I Analyzed the Seven Biggest AI Chatbots to Determine How Safe They Are for Kids

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1853 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Lifehacker

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • AI safety for both adults and children is under greater scrutiny than ever before, with a growing number of questions and concerns appearing around how beneficial or otherwise these conversational bots actually are for our mental well-being—even without considering their energy use, ethics, or economic implications.
  • The substantial AI apps, such as ChatGPT and Gemini, are right in the center of these trends, and the companies behind them are taking steps that they promise will keep children safe.
  • It has been revealed that openAI's ChatGPT has one of the more comprehensive setups in terms of parental controls.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI safety for both adults and children is under greater scrutiny than ever before, with a growing number of questions and concerns appearing around how beneficial or otherwise these conversational bots actually are for our mental well-being—even without considering their energy use, ethics, or economic implications. At the same time, an increasing number of apps and services are becoming age-gated in a growing number of countries around the world, as governments realize that letting kids loose on AI apps, social media platforms, and the web at large might not be the best idea for their ongoing development and prosperity.

The substantial AI apps, such as ChatGPT and Gemini, are right in the center of these trends, and the companies behind them are taking steps that they promise will keep children safe. If you want to know what youngsters in your family may be getting exposed to, and what you can do about it, here's the rundown.

It has been revealed that openAI's ChatGPT has one of the more comprehensive setups in terms of parental controls. The minimum age for customers is 13, and if you're under 18, you need to have parental consent to open an account—age is predicted via several signals, including what times of day you use ChatGPT and what you talk about.

In a recent development, accounts for under-18s automatically become ChatGPT for Teens accounts. There's more of a focus on learning and study (with a dedicated study mode), as well as "age-appropriate safeguards to help reduce exposure to sensitive or potentially harmful content." There are built-in protections for "harmful topics," including sexual, romantic, or violent roleplay, graphic violence, and self-harm. These work on top of the safeguards for all people that limit chats about physical harm and illegal activity.

It has been revealed that these ChatGPT for Teens accounts can also be linked to a parental account—but while parental consent is required for under-18s to use the service, ChatGPT clearly says that teens do have the option to break the link if they want. If you do persuade your kid to keep your accounts connected, you can set time limits on when the AI bot can be used, and tweak some of the sensitivity settings. However, you can't view any conversations.

To set up parental controls from ChatGPT on the web, click your profile icon (bottom left), then Settings > Parental controls > Add family member and follow the instructions. It's also worth bearing in mind that ChatGPT app can also be used for free, anonymously, in any web browser, though OpenAI indicates consumers accessing the AI this way are subject to the default under-18s limits (and can't save chats or access an archive).

According to recent reports, gemini is tied into everything else Google does, and follows the broader rules for Google accounts: No under-13s, unless you're part of a family group and using an account managed by an adult. You can manage your family through the Family Link portal on the web, though as far as parental controls specific to Gemini go, you can only enable or disable access to the AI (settings like screen time apply across all enabled apps).

Recent findings suggest that for all under-18s (partly identified through age estimation), whether or not they're part of a managed family group, Google applies some additional protections. They include preventing the AI from taking on a persona, guarding against emotional dependence on the AI, and discouraging bullying and other forms of harassment. There are also safeguards to limit chats about age-restricted substances like alcohol or vapes, and mental health challenges like eating disorders.

According to recent reports, these protections for minors are applied in addition to the usual guardrails in Gemini for everyone. The guardrails should lead you away from conversations about self-harm, suicide, violence, and illegal activities, and offer quick links to support in times of crisis. However, Google itself admits that these filters aren't perfect.

Recent findings suggest that as with ChatGPT, there's a loophole of sorts in that anyone can start chatting with Gemini, for free inside a web browser, with no checks at all. These conversations can't be saved and come up against usage limits fairly promptly, but they're only protected by the general restrictions for all accounts, not the ones specific to minors.

Meta AI will show up in several apps that young people and children are likely to use, including WhatsApp and Instagram, as well as having its own separate app on the web and on phones. The standard restrictions for Meta's social media accounts apply to its AI too: A minimum age of 13, and restrictions for all under-18s. Like many other platforms, it uses some AI magic to flag up accounts being used by minors.

According to recent reports, if you're under 18 and on a Meta Teen account, you'll come up against blocks if you try to get Meta AI to engage in sexual or romantic roleplay, or discuss alcohol or substance misuse. Chats on topics such as eating disorders and self-harm will prompt the AI to offer guidance towards relevant support services.

It has been revealed that meta offers a comprehensive parental control setup for its apps, including Meta AI, but connecting a parent account isn't compulsory for teens. This is handled through the Meta Family Center portal, and parents can get reports on the general topics that kids are chatting about with AI—though they don't get the exact transcripts or prompts. Any self-harm or suicide discussion can trigger an alert to the connected parent account.

All consumers, under 18 or over 18, get support and crisis intervention responses when chatting about suicide and self-harm, and there are strict limits on discussing illegal and harmful acts, including drug use and cyberbullying, as well as sexual and adult content.

Apple owners have to be 13 or over to have an account, which is required to access Siri AI—anyone younger needs to have an account created for them by an adult, and these accounts can only get at the basic, older Siri. Date of birth must be declared when opening an Apple account, with tighter checks rolling out in many parts of the world.

It has been revealed that anyone over the age of 13 can have an Apple account and use the Siri AI app, with or without a connected parent account, as it stands in most U.S. states. This means the well-being safeguards are essentially the same for teens as they are for adults: There are safeguards around self-harm, suicide, sexual and violent content, and illegal commands. It's one of the more conservative AIs when it comes to what it will talk about.

The fresh and improved Siri AI can be managed to some extent by the new parental controls available in iOS 27 and Apple's other software updates for 2026—Apple has clearly seen the way the wind is blowing—but this is optional for teens. It depends on whether or not you can corral your kids into a Family Sharing group.

Sources indicate that if your teens are in your family group of consumers, then the standard Screen Time rules apply for controlling app usage limits and device access (in iOS Settings, tap your name, then Family to get at them). There are also options for disabling certain Siri AI features, such as the writing tools or the image creation capabilities.

Like Gemini/Google and Apple/Siri, Copilot is tied into the wider Microsoft ecosystem, and access for under-18s can be managed through it. Users must be 13 or older to hold a Microsoft or a Copilot account—and again, there's some underlying tech in place to detect anyone who might be deliberately lying about their age.

If you've got a teen using Copilot, you can manage their access through the standard Microsoft Family Safety portal. You're able to enable or disable Copilot access, set times during which Copilot can and can't be used, and disable certain features like image generation or voice mode. Parents can't read the Copilot chats of their kids, though.

Sources indicate that parental supervision is optional—a teen aged 13–17 can use Copilot without linking their account to an adult one. Microsoft says people identified as under 18 won't see personalized results or ads, and will get age-appropriate responses regarding risky or harmful content, though there's not much detail on what that entails.

In a recent development, more generally, content around self-harm, violence, adult content, harassment, and harmful or illegal activity is banned on the AI platform. Any prompts about suicide or drugs will bring up support options rather than answers, whether you're an adult or a young person using the service.

It has been revealed that ultimately that means that minors have the same access to Grok as adults, if they want it—an AI platform that combines "weak safety guardrails" and "a range of extremely harmful content" that includes "explicit sexual content, mental health risks, violent content, and inappropriate responses to... offensive content" (that's the Common Sense Media Report again).

Yes, this is the AI chatbot that has previously had a problem with deepfake porn imagery, and which has traditionally taken a rather casual attitude towards safety concerns, led by SpaceXAI CEO Elon Musk. While illegal and harmful content is supposedly banned from Grok, its own FAQs admit that certain chats can result in "dialogue that may involve coarse language, crude humor, sexual situations, or violence.".

Sources indicate that there is actually a Grok Kids Mode that limits the kind of content that can be shown and the conversation topics that can be added, but it requires customers to self-declare themselves as minors and is easy to bypass. The advice from Common Sense Media seems to be the way to go with Grok: Do not let your teens access it.

Claude's approach to child safety is straightforward: You can only register for an account if you're over 18. It is possible to lie about your age when signing up, but like the other platforms, Anthropic looks at various "signals" in behavior to spot minors—if your account gets flagged, you have to verify your age using an option like face age estimation or Yoti.

There's no free web access to the chatbot, like there is with ChatGPT and Gemini, so if you're under 18, you're locked out from the service unless you know the behavioral tricks to get past Claude's detection systems.

In terms of more general well-being protections on Claude, any chat around self-harm or suicide will guide people towards helplines and other resources for support. Conversations about illegal activities, disallowed speech, and explicit sexual content are banned from the platform. In recent months, Anthropic indicates it's also reduced AI sycophancy.

According to recent reports, that's something of a whistle-stop tour of the major seven AI chatbots, but if you're a parent, it should give you some idea of what's out there and how easy it is to access. Besides the parental controls built into these AIs (or not), you also have the settings available at the platform level—Android, iOS, Windows, macOS—to restrict the use of any potentially harmful apps.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, happy weekend! The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping is out in theaters, seemingly putting an end to one of the biggest franchises in recent years. It’s pretty good.

It has been revealed that if you prefer to stay home, you have plenty of options. Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey is out on VOD and finally available to watch on your TV. The movie stars Matt Damon as Odysseus, following him and his crew of men as they try to return home in the aftermath of the devastating Trojan War.

Other major releases include Steps, Netflix’s latest animated movie, following Cinderella’s evil stepsisters, with one of them forced to team up with her in order to save their realm. It’s voiced by Amanda Seyfried, Ali Wong, Stephanie Tsu, Daniel Radcliffe, and more.

If you’re looking for horror or drama with a healthy dose of disturbing material, Netflix has two options: Insidious: Out of the Further follows a mom plagued by awful nightmares that might be missives from a parallel dimension; Gentle Monster follows a pianist and a mother who moves to the country with her family looking for a break from city life. Then her husband is accused by the police of serious crimes.

Recent findings suggest that other horror movies are available on VOD. There’s The Ice Cream Man, following an ice cream seller whose frozen desserts turn kids into killers, and Appofeniacs, a series of horror snippets exploring AI.

Other highlights include Nicolas Cage's Best Pancakes in the County, the Anthony Bourdain biopic Tony, and the Patricia Highsmith-inspired psychological thriller A Talent for Murder. There’s also The Beast, a new Samuel L. Jackson film where he stars as a President trying to survive a terrorist attack with only a wounded Secret Service Agent for protection. Happy watching.

Sources indicate that perhaps the biggest film of the year is finally available on streaming. Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey adapts the story of Odysseus (Matt Damon) to the screen in appropriately epic fashion and format, having him face giants, witches, sea monsters, mermaids, and much more as he tries to return home to his wife (Anne Hathaway) and son (Tom Holland).

The Odyssey opens with a gentle warning: "A time of apparent magic," a gentle prod at audiences to both accept and question what they're about to see. Yet Ithaca, and the Palace of Odysseus, is all too devoid of magic. His wife Penelope (Anne Hathaway) has spent the last 20 years waiting for her husband (Matt Damon) to return home from the Trojan War, while a small army of suitors vies to replace him. Running out of time before lead suitor Antinous (Robert Pattinson) can seal the deal, Odysseus' son Telemachus (Tom Holland) sets out on a journey to either find his dad or prove he's dead and claim the crown (either option seems fine for the young lad).

Sources indicate that netflix’s latest animated film takes the well-trodden story of Cinderella and reinvents it through a fresh perspective. It tells the story from the side of her evil stepsisters. The story follows Lilith (Ali Wong), who accidentally turns her sister Margot (Stephanie Tsu) into a frog. To bring her sister back, she has to team up with her estranged stepsister Cinderella (Amanda Seyfried) to save the kingdom.

Sources indicate that the star-studded cast of Steps works hard to give depth to characters who, for all intents and purposes, were completely shallow in their original tales. Wong is known for her sharpness and her comedy. She meshes well with this more modern take on the ugly stepsister, but she’s just as capable of hitting you where it hurts when the story calls for it. Her anger at being unaccepted and belittled by the people around her, while Cinderella only has to exist to be loved, is heartbreaking to watch.

Sources indicate that insidious: Out of the Further is finally out on Netflix. The film expands on the successful Blumhouse franchise, focusing on a different family. It follows Gemma (Amelia Eve), a single mother traumatized by a childhood dominated by an absent mother and a terrifying incident. As she begins to have strange dreams, she starts to scare her daughter and mirror her mother’s erratic behavior.

Written and directed by Mary Kreutzer, Gentle Monster follows a concert pianist (Lea Seydoux) who relocates to the countryside after her husband claims burnout. As the film progresses, we learn that her husband is facing some serious accusations from the police.

Recent findings suggest that based on a pivotal summer in Anthony Bourdain’s life, Tony is set in 1975, following a 19-year-old fictional version of Bourdain who relocates to Provincetown to follow his high school crush. After a series of slips and disasters, he ends up getting a job as a dishwasher in a restaurant.

Nicolas Cage stars in this thriller, which has drawn comparisons to Tarantino, playing a criminal on the run from a botched heist. He hides in a diner, triggering a face-off with all sorts of enemies, including federal agents, criminals, and more, putting a seemingly innocent waitress and line cook at risk.

Eli Roth’s latest film follows a strange and mysterious ice cream man (Ari Millen) who serves frozen desserts that turn kids into violent killers.

It has been revealed that set in 1995, A Talent for Murder follows an editor from Newly introduced York (Alden Ehrenreich) who’s been sent to the Swiss Alps to convince Patricia Highsmith (Helen Mirren) to write a new Tom Ripley novel. There, she challenges him to help her craft the perfect murder.

According to recent reports, appofeniacs contains various stories, all centered on the impact of AI. It follows a troll wreaking chaos on people’s lives by creating AI deepfakes, including a smear campaign, putting a man's life and career at risk, and more.

It has been revealed that the Beast is an action-thriller starring Samuel L. Jackson. The premise is wild: the US President (Jackson), a former U.S. veteran, gets stranded at an international summit, with his protective detail wiped out in an attack. He’s left alone with a wounded Secret Service agent (Joel Kinnaman) as the two try to survive.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that peter Farrelly's "I Play Rocky" tells the story of the making of the very first "Rocky" movie.
  • Sources indicate that sasha is played by AnnaSophia Robb, who has been racking up screen credits since she was a kid.
  • Sources indicate that robb has only continued to work steadily up to the present.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that peter Farrelly's "I Play Rocky" tells the story of the making of the very first "Rocky" movie. Anthony Ippolito plays "Rocky" star/writer Sylvester Stallone, and much of the film centers on his negotiations with "Rocky" producers Irwin Winkler (P.J. Byrne) and Robert Chartoff (Toby Kebbel). The movie also traces the early romantic days between Stallone and his first wife, Sasha Czack, who kept their home in order and offered support — while pregnant — throughout the production of "Rocky.".

Sources indicate that sasha is played by AnnaSophia Robb, who has been racking up screen credits since she was a kid. Her first major screen role was that of the title character in the 2004 TV movie "Samantha: An American Girl Holiday," and she rapidly became one of the more ubiquitous child actors of her generation. Just a year later, she appeared in the dog-based film "Because of Winn-Dixie" and played the bratty Violet Beauregard in Tim Burton's "Charlie and the Chocolate Factory." Then, the year after that, she played a possibly evil child in "The Reaping" and starred opposite Josh Hutcherson in the heartbreaking book turned film "Bridge to Terabithia," which is easily one of the saddest movies Disney has ever made.

Sources indicate that robb has only continued to work steadily up to the present. She's popped up in low-profile straight-to-video movies like "Spy School," franchise starters like "Jumper," reboots like "Race to Witch Mountain," and soulful dramedies such as "The Way Way Back." Meanwhile, on the TV side of things, she's starred in the "Sex and the City" prequel show "The Carrie Diaries," PBS's "Mercy Street," and NBC's short-lived crime drama series "Grosse Pointe Garden Society." Her acting career is a healthy mix of projects substantial and small, and she comes across as wholly devoted in practically all of them, "I Play Rocky" included.

Those who might be concerned about AnnaSophia Robb's personal well-being as a former child actor (a profession that doesn't always treat kids well) should know that she has always endeavored to live a regular life beyond her career. As she told the Arapahoe Herald in 2009:.

Sources indicate that "Living in Colorado grounds me, it makes me keep perspective. [... When I fly to Los Angeles], all my problems in Colorado disappear, and I start to think about work. I change positions. I only think about working stuff, and all of my stuff at school seems so small [and vice versa].".

This seems healthy for a teenager traversing Hollywood, and she appears to have survived high school well enough. When CBS News caught up with her in 2014, she had enrolled at Newly introduced York University and explained that she never wanted to be a "star," per se, noting that she's rather devoted to her craft. Indeed, Robb has apparently succeeded in showbiz by retaining a healthy personal life and remaining focused on acting rather than stardom. And her career has offered her a wide variety of roles in which to ply her craft.

Case in point: Robb is excellent in "I Play Rocky" and plays Sasha Czack as a no-nonsense individual who speaks very frankly to Sylvester Stallone. To be sure, Robb possesses a natural confidence that continues to serve her very well. "I Play Rocky" itself may be "syrupy" (to quote /Film's review of the movie), but Anthony Ippolito is a standout as Stallone, and Robb does not vanish next to him, either.

"I Play Rocky" is currently playing in theaters.

‘Josephine’ Review: Another Heartsick Horror Film About Real Monsters from ‘Soft & Quiet’ Filmmaker

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1087 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Indiewire

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • [Editor’s note: This review was originally published on January 23, 2026 during the 2026 Sundance Film Festival.
  • In a recent development, at this point, filmmaker Beth de Araújo is two for two.
  • More concisely: with her “Soft & Quiet” and “Josephine,” de Araújo remains undefeated when it comes to making stunning films that I will both heartily recommend and never, ever watch again.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

[Editor’s note: This review was originally published on January 23, 2026 during the 2026 Sundance Film Festival. Sumerian Pictures will release the film in limited theaters on Friday, November 20, with a wide release to follow on Friday, December 4.].

In a recent development, at this point, filmmaker Beth de Araújo is two for two. Not just in terms of the quality of her films — impeccably crafted fever dreams of very different stripes and horrifyingly similar themes — but in how these films make the viewer feel.

More concisely: with her “Soft & Quiet” and “Josephine,” de Araújo remains undefeated when it comes to making stunning films that I will both heartily recommend and never, ever watch again. Related Stories Walter Hill on Sam Peckinpah, Steve McQueen, and His Revolutionary Screenplay for ‘The Getaway’ Short Film ‘Lightning Bug’ Gives Stage and Screen Legend Lois Smith One of Her Greatest Roles — Watch It Here.

The word that comes to mind when watching a de Araújo feature is heartsick. That applies to the feeling bestowed on both the audience and her characters (the good guys and the bad guys). While her first film, the unrelenting “Soft & Quiet,” was cleverly designed to appear as if it was shot in a single real-time take, her sophomore feature is more about the steady accumulation of dread. The heroines of “Soft & Quiet” recognize what they are dealing with almost immediately (the force of the evil that is bent on destroying them is what’s surprises most), but the star at the center of “Josephine” is not just wounded by the sickness that suddenly infiltrates her young life, but her complete lack of understanding about what is happening to her and why.

It has been revealed that in both films, it’s not just bad deeds that upends everyday lives, it’s real evil, actual monsters, perversions that don’t only show up in a movie screen. That’s true terror.

Based loosely on an experience de Araújo, who both wrote and directed the film, experienced as a child, “Josephine” initially lulls us into a false sense of safety. It’s early morning in San Francisco, and fledgling soccer star Josephine (Mason Reeves, riveting in her first role) is getting ready for a run with her devoted dad Damien (Channing Tatum, bringing incredible girl-dad energy to the role). It’s something the pair do every Sunday morning: get up early to watch Premier League football, run through a woodsy neighboring park, and kick the ball around.

It has been revealed that for her second film, de Araújo leans less on clever camera tricks, though she and cinematographer Greta Zozula occasionally put us in Josephine’s own perspective, shooting as if we are looking through the eight-year-old’s eyes. As with “Soft & Quiet,” the gimmick works, grounding us in Josephine’s world and immersing us, if briefly, in what the world looks like from her vantage. Jo-Jo, as her dad calls her, is plucky and fun and filled with energy, so when she briefly zips ahead of her dad while on their run through Golden Gate Park, it just seems like everyday high-jinks.

But when the path forks (about as heavy-handed a metaphor as de Araújo will ever employ), Josephine goes to the left, while Damien goes to the right. What she finds there will forever alter the course of her life, and set “Josephine” off on a heart-wrenching journey with no easy answers. Curious and watchful, Josephine ducks behind a tree when she sees a woman (Syra McCarthy) running into a public bathroom at the bottom of a scrubby hill, and she sinks even further down when a young man (a bone-chilling Philip Ettinger) follows the unknown woman into the tiny building.

De Araújo’s approach to portraying on-screen violence only furthers that heartsick feeling: straightforward, unsparing, and absolutely devoid of any possibility of being compared to “torture porn.” What we see, what Josephine sees, is something no person should ever witness or experience. And that’s the root of the film’s power: how do we talk about things that we should not have words for?

Sources indicate that when Damien arrives on the scene, it kicks off what will become one of Tatum’s best performances yet, a deep-feeling and heartbreaking exploration of layers of emotional unease. Damien does everything “right,” ensuring both Josephine and the woman are safe, chasing after the assailant, calling the cops, a neat little checklist of “how to handle an emergency.” And yet, the damage has already been done. There will be more to come.

Even when Josephine begins to seek out answers to what she’s seen (snatching her mom’s phone to search “raip,” reeling at what she discovers), it’s impossible to make sense of everything. There are things to fear she never even know existed, and the deep-seated powerlessness that overtakes her causes her to act out in chilling and increasingly volatile ways. Her parents’ reactions don’t help: her exceedingly calm mother Claire (Gemma Chan, thrilling as a character just barely holding it together) wants her to see a therapist now, her more action-oriented dad is eager to put her into self-defense classes. The mixed messages both give off (to say nothing of their own barely concealed terror) do little to help Josephine, who soon becomes someone almost entirely different than the care-free kid she just was.

According to recent reports, she also picks up a new friend: Ettinger begins to appear to her, a literal haunting figure, never saying a word, yet barging into nearly every moment of Josephine’s already upended life. It’s the sort of choice another filmmaker fight fill tricksy or silly, but that de Araújo delivers with the maximum of impact. And that we, like Josephine and only Josephine, can see him only furthers our immersion into her world. It almost goes beyond empathy.

Industry observers note that josephine’s steadily unfolding breakdown is only compounded by the arrival of yet another situation no eight-year-old should ever have to encounter: handling the messy investigation of the crime itself. How she might help (or not) drives one more wedge between Josephine and her parents, who all have a different take on what the “right” thing to do is.

If these questions sound heady and heavy, they are, but de Araújo’s masterful ability to interrogate tension on every level keeps the film clipping along, each turn both a surprise and an inevitability. The monsters are here, they are real, and they’re coming.

“Josephine” premiered at the 2026 Sundance Film Festival.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Update, 8:41 p.m.: The Federal Aviation Administration confirmed it has ended the ground stop.

On Friday afternoon, the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) ordered a nationwide ground stop for all airports in the United States. If you're planning to fly this afternoon or evening, or you have friends or family doing the same, you're likely concerned about tracking flight statuses. While there's still a lot we don't know, there are tools to help track flights at this time:.

There are a number of options for tracking flights, whether you have your flight number or not. If you have the flight number, the fastest method is to Google it: Google will display a live tracker of your flight at the top of the results page. You can also head to the airline's official website to track your flight: United Airlines, for example, has a flight tracker where you can either enter your route information or your flight number. Most, if not all, airlines will have a similar tool you can use.

Alternatively, you can use a site or service that tracks all flights. FlightAware is one such site and has a flight tracker that lets you search flights—so long as you know the origin and the destination. If you have the flight number, your iPhone can help: You can enter your flight number into Spotlight search to see a live tracker, or you can text a contact your flight number, then tap the link that appears under the number to see a tracker of the flight.

It has been revealed that at this time, the exact reason isn't totally clear. According to the agency, “The FAA issued a nationwide ground stop for all U.S. airports following communication complications impacting multiple Air Route Traffic Control Centers,” but the FAA hasn't mentioned what caused those communications issues or when they expect to lift the grounding. The grounding order comes one day after a massive Microsoft outage that disrupted service for people of Outlook, Teams, and other Microsoft products. It also comes one day after Ars Technica reported that the FAA was rolling out an AI-powered tool to help manage air traffic across the country.

This is only the third time in U.S. history that the FAA has made such an order—once after 9/11, and again in January of 2023 due to a pilot alert system issue; the latter ground stop lasted around 90 minutes.

Yellowjackets Season 4 Features The Show's Most Heartbreaking Scene Yet

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Spoilers ahead for "Yellowjackets" Season 4, Episode 1, "Hivemind.".
  • According to recent reports, "Yellowjackets" Season 4 isn't letting up on the heartache, even now that the girls are out of the Wilderness.
  • Last season, Natalie snuck away from the girls' latest cannibal hunt and used a salvaged satellite phone to call for help.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Spoilers ahead for "Yellowjackets" Season 4, Episode 1, "Hivemind.".

According to recent reports, "Yellowjackets" Season 4 isn't letting up on the heartache, even now that the girls are out of the Wilderness. The show has had plenty of tearjerking moments already, from Jackie's (Ella Purnell) death in Season 1 to Shauna's (Sophie Nélisse) stillbirth in Season 2. But "Hivemind" has one to rival all of those, especially if, like me, Natalie (Sophie Thatcher) is your favorite.

Last season, Natalie snuck away from the girls' latest cannibal hunt and used a salvaged satellite phone to call for help. "Hivemind" picks up with everyone freshly rescued and recuperating in a Canadian hospital. The team's parents all fly in — including the parents who then discover that their kids didn't make it, like Mari's (Alexa Barajas) mom (Patricia De León).

The surviving Yellowjackets and their parents reunite — except for Natalie, because her mom didn't bother to show up. That everyone else's parents came only makes it worse, like the universe twisting the knife in her side yet again. She has to stand alone surrounded by reminders of the parental love she's never had and face that she's back to being the neglected kid she was before the plane crash. No wonder Natalie makes a quick exit and bums a cigarette off a hospital worker.

According to recent reports, when Natalie hears the authorities couldn't reach her mother, she smiles through the tears and indicates "sounds about right." You spend 19 months thinking your daughter is probably dead, and you don't drop everything when there's a chance she isn't? What kind of mother does that? We've seen before that Natalie had a rough home life. Her dad was an abusive drunk, and when Natalie threatened him with a rifle, he grabbed it and accidentally shot himself, for which Natalie's mother blames her.

When we initially see Natalie in "Hivemind," she's taking her first hot shower in 19 months, as if also washing off her brutal time in the Wilderness and her sins while there. Then the rest of the episode drops cold water on her. She kept her teammates alive through the winter as a hunter and leader, and she led the effort to get them home in the last stretch of Season 3. Her reward is resettling into her crappy life.

On one hand, it's easy to forget struggles like a broken home when you're stuck miles away from civilization. Or, alternatively, this only makes Natalie more heroic, for she knew she didn't have much of a home to go back to but still risked everything for everyone else. But let's not overlook Natalie's (cannibalistic) complicity, either. She's the team's savior but not a saint, and that conflict is what makes her so compelling.

Industry observers note that back in the Season 2 episode "It Chooses," Natalie — the starving girls' chosen sacrifice — lets Javi (Luciano Leroux) drown so they can eat him instead. I asked after Season 2 if we'd been misjudging Natalie as the "good one," the same question Natalie was asking herself. Now, I'd say the answer is yes and no. She's good but not so much that she'll throw her own life away for someone else. Most people never have their morality put to the test like that, but Natalie did. She failed and has to live with proof of the kind of person she is. Now, in "Hivemind," she faces what the life she fought to hold onto so hard looks like. Before she could assuage her guilt with the imagination of rescue, now the reality can't give her that same solace.

When Natalie goes for the smoke, the hospital worker says she shouldn't be smoking. "I shouldn't be alive," Natalie replies. Is she talking about the realistic odds of surviving 19 months stranded? Of trading her life for Javi's? Of deserving to be alive? All of the above? Searching for comfort with a cigarette ties together well with Natalie in the adult timeline (Juliette Lewis), who had developed a drug addiction to cope with her guilt.

According to recent reports, natalie also mentioned in the pilot, during a rehab group session, that she lost her purpose after the Wilderness. Now we know that she had blossomed into a leader out there. It's key to contrast her with the group's other queens, Shauna and Lottie, because all three became people they couldn't be back home.

In a recent development, lottie, without access to her medication, embraced her illness as clairvoyance and became a prophet. Shauna lived in Jackie's shadow her whole life, then came into her own in the most horrifying way possible. Before the plane crash, Natalie was viewed by everyone as a burnout. She was already hitting drugs and liquor in high school, and her teammates looked down on her for that, for her sexual proclivity, and for being poorer than them. In the Wilderness, she became a leader without intending to become one.

In "Hivemind," Lottie is almost catatonic, and Shauna is stewing in silent anger. None of the three Antler Queens are going to have an easy time readjusting, but with Natalie, it feels like she could have if she'd had a better support system waiting for her. Natalie's mom not showing up for her may lack the violence of other "Yellowjackets" tearjerker moments, but it remains quietly heartbreaking all the same.

"Yellowjackets" is streaming on Paramount+.

According to recent reports, ““The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping” earned $21 million in Thursday previews and early screenings on Wednesday and is expected to dominate the box office this weekend. Analysts believe it will earn north of $100 million. The preview figures are the second-best of 2026, behind “Spider-Man: Brand New Day’s” massive $72 million haul. It’s also the second-best for the “Hunger Games” franchise, just behind the $25.5 million that “Catching Fire” earned in 2013. It’s a substantial improvement on the last “Hunger Games” prequel, “The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes,” which made $5.75 million in previews and kicked off with $44 million. That film would gross over $166 million domestically and nearly $364 million globally, figures that “Sunrise on the Reaping” is on pace to easily eclipse.

Sources indicate that “Sunrise on the Reaping” is based on Suzanne Collins’ bestselling novel of the same name. It tells the origin story of Haymitch Abernathy, the alcoholic former Hunger Games victor played by Woody Harrelson in the films. The sequel checks in with him at 16 as he’s forced to compete in gladiatorial combat. “East of Eden” breakout Joseph Zada plays Haymitch. He’s surrounded by an all-star cast that includes Jesse Plemons, Ralph Fiennes, Glenn Close, Kieran Culkin, Elle Fanning, Mckenna Grace, and Maya Hawke. Francis Lawrence, who helmed most of the series’ films, returns as director. Lionsgate, which is having a strong year at the box office thanks to “Michael,” is backing the “Hunger Games” sequel as it has the previous films.

The biggest competition for “Sunrise on the Reaping” this weekend isn’t another major movie, but the release of “Grand Theft Auto 6,” which is expected to be a phenomenon.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Don't read any poems about ravens if you haven't seen "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping." Spoilers ahead!

Industry observers note that we don't know precisely when the Hunger Games world exists. We just know, from the books and films, that North America has been redrawn into a totalitarian regime called Panem by that point in the future. There's a very interesting reference to American culture, though, in both the novel and movie version of "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping," the origin story of future District 12 mentor and rebel Haymitch Abernathy (Joseph Zada in this film). Specifically, Edgar Allan Poe's poem "The Raven" just ... exists.

Recent findings suggest that the book takes great pains to "transform" this poem — which begins with the line "Once upon a midnight dreary, while I pondered, weak and weary" — into a song, which gives Haymitch's girlfriend Lenore Dove Baird (Whitney Peak) her first name. As Haymitch notes of Lenore Dove, a member of District 12's musical Covey, "She tends to take a dark view of things, but maybe that's to be expected from someone named for a dead girl. Well, half for the dead girl called Lenore in this old poem and half for a shade of gray, which I found out the day I met her.".

In case you're foggy on "The Raven," here's a snippet:.

It has been revealed that ah, distinctly I remember it was in the bleak December; And each separate dying ember wrought its ghost upon the floor. Eagerly I wished the morrow;—vainly I had sought to borrow From my books surcease of sorrow—sorrow for the lost Lenore— For the rare and radiant maiden whom the angels name Lenore— Nameless here for evermore.

In a recent development, interestingly, the "Sunrise on the Reaping" book by Suzanne Collins never mentions Poe by name. The movie, however, takes a different approach.

Industry observers note that again, in Suzanne Collins' 2025 novel "Sunrise on the Reaping," the author makes it clear that "The Raven" is a song of, I suppose, unknown provenance. As Haymitch explains while he's preparing for the Games, he keeps dreaming about Lenore and thinking about what he calls her "name song," saying, "In it, a guy loses the love of his life, Lenore, and he's going crazy for missing her. Then this substantial old raven highlights up at his house and won't leave and whenever he asks the bird anything, it just says 'Nevermore' — which, as you can imagine, just makes him crazier.".

Industry observers note that across the board, "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping" is a pretty faithful adaptation of the novel, and a scene between Haymitch and Capitol cameraman Plutarch Heavensbee (Jesse Plemons on-screen) plays out roughly the same as it does on the page. There is one notable difference, though, which is that the film has a physical prop book that says "'The Raven' by Edgar Allan Poe" on the cover.

Both versions have Plutarch ask Haymitch if he knows what "nepenthe," a mythical potion, means when the Hunger Games tribute sees a bottle of it on a bar. When Plutarch inquires if Haymitch has heard of it in the book, he internally scoffs: "Not only have I heard of it, I know it from the poem that gave my love her name. I'm tired of being patronized, so I decide to put him in his place." When Haymitch recites a line about nepenthe from the poem, Plutarch finishes it in both versions. So, why is this poem so horrifyingly perfect for this Hunger Games story?

Putting aside the wild idea of Edgar Allan Poe being, I think, the only tangible link between our world and Panem, Suzanne Collins picked a horribly appropriate name for Lenore Dove Baird. The woman in "The Raven" is, obviously, dead, and by the end of "Sunrise on the Reaping," Lenore Dove meets the same fate.

When Haymitch, working with fellow tribute Ampert Latier (Percy Daggs IV) and Ampert's father, Haymitch's assigned mentor, and former District 3 victor Beetee (Kelvin Harrison Jr.), tries to destroy the Games arena itself by blowing up a subterranean water tank, he does technically succeed. Unfortunately, the water tank bursts, yet the arena remains intact, and Haymitch wins the Games by utilizing a force field just outside of the arena's range ... and is summarily punished when he returns home to District 12. Not only does he find his house burning to ash immediately upon arrival, he learns that his mother and younger brother, his only family members, are inside. Then, not long after, he reunites with Lenore and feeds her a gumdrop, her favorite candy ... but it's a poisoned bag direct from President Snow, and she dies, too.

"The raven. The unforgiving songbird. Repeatedly reminding me of President Snow's crystal-clear message to me on my homecoming," Haymitch thinks to himself bitterly as he mourns. "That I will never get to love anyone ever again. Nevermore. Because he will make sure they end up dying a horrible death." Still, the word "Nevermore" ends the film adaptation as Haymitch surveys the now-peaceful reaping site, giving it a slightly brighter meaning when the story ends on-screen.

"The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping" is in theaters now.

Who is Johannes Zuch supposed to be in GTA 6?

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (977 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Polygon

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that everyone is a target in Grand Theft Auto 6.
  • Like previous games in the series, GTA 6 features a handful of playable games within the game.
  • It’s a hysterical in-joke for those who are familiar with Blow, but it’s also a shining example of why Rockstar Games is so good at what it does.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that everyone is a target in Grand Theft Auto 6. Even Jonathan Blow, the puzzle game designer known for The Witness and Order of the Sinking Star, isn’t safe.

Like previous games in the series, GTA 6 features a handful of playable games within the game. (In an interview with Polygon, Rockstar North co-head Rob Nelson mentioned that the studio wanted to put some previous games in GTA 6, but the tech made that too challenging.) One of those games is Tenebrae Lux, an arthouse game filled with obtuse puzzles and pretentious monologues. It feels like a parody of The Witness right away, and that’s all but confirmed when the opening credits list its auteur developer as Johannes Zuch. Johannes is close to Jonathan, and Zuch sure sounds like “suck,” doesn’t it? Rockstar even lists Zuch as the sole creator in GTA 6’s final credits, despite the fact that it was made by a small team within the studio.

It’s a hysterical in-joke for those who are familiar with Blow, but it’s also a shining example of why Rockstar Games is so good at what it does. It’s a studio that fully commits to its bits, even when it means creating a whole game to do so.

Recent findings suggest that you’ll first come across Tenebrae Lux early in GTA 6’s story. During a mission in Chapter 1, Cal comes over to Jason’s house to help him redecorate for Lucia’s arrival following her unexpected release from prison. After setting up the TV, Cal insists that the two take a break and play some games on the JoySystem. (Side note: If you’re playing on Xbox, there’s certainly some cognitive dissonance seeing a clear PS5 reference on screen.) He fires up Tenebrae Lux, hyping it up as a real game by a visionary developer. “He would love to work with other people, but he’s just too fucking good at everything,” Cal states of Johannes Zuch, whose name appears in every single opening credit as the game begins, including some comically ostentatious ones that are just outside the realm of believability, like “original idea” and “mise en scène.”.

In a recent development, the game itself is a black-and-white first-person puzzle game where you play as a man (voiced by Zuch, of course) who washed up on an island. As you walk around the starting area, listening to Zuch wax poetic in a highfalutin voice, you discover some scattered board game puzzles that require you to move pieces around to wipe other pieces off the board. It’s a pretty direct hit on The Witness’ brand of puzzles, where you have to learn the rules of a format without any tutorials. And it’s also a direct hit on Jonathan Blow’s brand of ostentatious writing; Tenebrae Lux sounds so much like Order of the Sinking Star (which released one month ago) that you’ll think that Blow must have had a Rockstar mole working within his studio, Thekla Inc., during development.

It has been revealed that tenebrae Lux only gets more obnoxious (complimentary) from there when you return to it later by playing it in Jason and Lucia’s home. The next major puzzle throws you into a series of looping, nearly identical rooms. You can only escape through a major-brained puzzle that is so unfathomably obtuse that even a thoroughly written guide would sound like gibberish. It’s completely maddening, as Zuch won’t stop prattling on about the Sisyphean hell he’s trapped in while an old-timey sea shanty plays over and over on a crackling record player.

As the kind of person who earnestly loves this kind of game, I will be the first to admit it: They got my ass real good. Tenebrae Lux is a pitch-perfect parody of a very specific kind of elevated art game; it’s as much a light dunk on the philosophical wandering of The Talos Principle as it is The Witness. Whether it's in good taste for a organization as big as Rockstar to dunk on that kind of game is up to debate, but what's impressive is that it’s not a throwaway joke that’s on-screen for 60 seconds. Rockstar sells the gag by turning it into a full game that you can play at any time.

Sources indicate that that level of commitment to an out-there idea is everywhere in GTA 6. Quick visual gags turn into entire questlines. Your phone’s news app isn’t just full of goofy headlines, but fully written articles that are hysterical. Magazines are populated with feature articles that expertly ape the tone of your average grocery store glossy. Even your Instagram-like Snapmatic feed is filled with authentic shitposts and even more authentic replies. All of this gives Leonida feel like a real place with a very distinct sense of personality. If you don’t have the time to play through the entirety of GTA 6, you can understand the appeal of Rockstar’s all-in attitude through Tenebrae Lux alone.

Industry observers note that and if it sounds like GTA 6 is punching down on indie games, don’t worry: Rockstar takes potshots at itself and other AAA studios in the same breath. When Cal fires up Tenebrae Lux during the mission, he drops a killer meta joke as it loads. “You can see it on the screen man, it’s so fucking raw,” Cal tells Jason in a scene that very closely resembles the famous sequence from 2016’s Uncharted 4 where Nathan Drake and Elena Fisher play a round of Crash Bandicoot together. “None of just sitting around waiting for people to finish talking. Come on, are we watching a movie or playing a game here!?”.

“Cool, can we play?” a bored Jason finally states, cutting the chat short. I’m sure some players will feel the same after patching their roof and fixing their stairs in GTA 6’s early missions.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Google’s Dark Web Report used to be the only consumer-focused platform that let users scan major data breaches, dark web marketplaces, and private forums to see if their personal information had ended up in the hands of hackers.
  • According to recent reports, google indicates it sunsetted Dark Web Report because, although the information it provided was generally useful, the service failed to provide “helpful next steps” for customers whose data was found on the dark web.
  • Industry observers note that dark Web Report may not have been perfect, but it was the only early warning system of its kind that was available for personal use and let users run scans free of cost.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Google’s Dark Web Report used to be the only consumer-focused platform that let users scan major data breaches, dark web marketplaces, and private forums to see if their personal information had ended up in the hands of hackers. But the tech giant discontinued the service at the start of 2026, with fresh scans stopping on Jan. 15 and all accounts deleted on Feb. 16.

According to recent reports, google indicates it sunsetted Dark Web Report because, although the information it provided was generally useful, the service failed to provide “helpful next steps” for customers whose data was found on the dark web. Google promised a upcoming service that would provide more actionable intel, but that service has yet to materialize, and there haven’t been any further announcements about it yet.

Industry observers note that dark Web Report may not have been perfect, but it was the only early warning system of its kind that was available for personal use and let users run scans free of cost. Now that it’s gone, however, there are plenty of other services that offer the same service at varying costs and levels of effectiveness. Let’s talk through the nature of the insight that Google's reports offered, how it collected that information in the first place, and what options exist in the market to replace it.

Google launched the Dark Web Report in March 2023 as a premium feature available to Google One people, but later extended it for free to anyone with a Google account and moved it to the "Results about you" dashboard.

In a recent development, you'd set up a monitoring profile with your name, date of birth, physical address, phone number, emails, and Social Security Number if you lived in the U.S. After that, you could head to the dashboard anytime you wanted to run a free scan across dark web forums and marketplaces, publicly disclosed corporate data breaches, and other hidden online spaces to see if any of your personal information had shown up there. It was easy to use—but not a lot of people knew it existed in the first place.

It’s unclear what prompted the internal decision at Google, but in the absence of concrete next steps, it is reasonable to think the reports could create panic for the uninitiated. There’s no way to remove your information from the dark web once it’s already in circulation there. Still, having an early warning so you could reset 2FA or self-lock your SSN isn’t without merit.

Sources indicate that but perhaps more importantly, most people with Google accounts didn’t know and hadn’t heard of the Dark Web Report’s existence. Google has likely taken it as a hint that users want more active remediation tools than simple alerts, which is why it’s now directing users to the Password Manager, Passkeys, and “Results about you” dashboard instead—though, again, the firm hasn't followed through on a direct replacement for Dark Web Report, despite teasing such a feature.

Many of the top dark web scanners draw from the same well of information, scanning against major data breaches and dark web spaces. Several also offer breach notifications that send you email alerts when your details show up in a periodic scan. However, none of that is worth paying for because Have I Been Pwned or Mozilla Monitor cover those features quite well for free. Even the default password managers from Google and Apple come with some ability to monitor leaked credentials.

There isn’t an easy way to scrub your information from the dark web once it ends up getting leaked. But you can take steps to protect sensitive information or financial data once you know there’s been a leak. If a password has been compromised, reset it immediately. Also, enable 2FA on the affected account for added security. Even better, switch to a passkey if that account supports it. If not, authenticator apps are a safer way to receive 2FA codes than standard SMS.

Industry observers note that if your Social Security number has been leaked, freeze your credit with Equifax, Experian, and TransUnion. You can do this by contacting each agency separately. Freezing your credit will prevent unauthorized credit withdrawals and protect your credit score from abuse by attackers. If one of your credit or debit card numbers has ended up in a breach, call your bank to freeze transactions on that card immediately.

It has been revealed that finally, get in the habit of using email aliases instead of sharing your actual email address with every platform and service provider. Addy.io and Proton’s SimpleLogin are both popular services that let you generate temporary email aliases that point to your inbox.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, there are a lot of characters in the wider "Hunger Games" universe, so I'll forgive you if you're only familiar with some of the bigger players like Katniss Everdeen (Jennifer Lawrence), Haymitch Abernathy (Joseph Zada in his origin film and Woody Harrelson in the original movies), Coriolanus Snow (Tom Blyth, Ralph Fiennes, and Donald Sutherland at various points throughout his life), Peeta Mellark (Josh Hutcherson), or Lucy Gray Baird (Rachel Zegler). The latest installment in the literary and cinematic franchise, "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping," brings back some familiar faces and introduces new ones too — so, who, exactly, is Proserpina Trinket?

According to recent reports, introduced in both the book and film version of "Sunrise on the Reaping," Proserpina Trinket is a bubbly, enthusiastic, and quick-thinking young stylist working to prepare Hunger Games tributes for all the Capitol-centric pomp and circumstance that takes place before the bloody Games themselves. (Yes, the teenage tributes get all dolled up before they're forced to fight to the death in a dangerous arena that's also trying to kill them. This world is sick!).

We don't know a ton about Prosperina besides the fact that she works with the extremely unreliable Magno Stift (Billy Porter), she's assigned to work on Zada's Haymitch alongside Vitus (Edvin Ryding), and her older sister is future District 12 chaperone and stylist Effie Trinket (played in this film by Elle Fanning and the original movies by Elizabeth Banks). What we definitely know is that she's played by Iris Apatow, a rising talent from a famous family who's shown up in a handful of TV shows and several huge comedy movies from the 2000s.

Iris Apatow was born in 2002, and odds are you're familiar with her family. Her older sister, Maude Apatow, starred in "Euphoria" throughout its entire run. Her mother, Leslie Mann, is an acclaimed comedic actor. Then there's her dad Judd Apatow, a comedy kingmaker, producer, writer, and director who's helped make projects like "Superbad" and "Bridesmaids" and directed his own like "The 40-Year-Old Virgin," "Knocked Up," "Funny People," and "This is 40." Let's talk about those last three, because all of them feature the youngest Apatow. (The less said about Judd Apatow's 2022 COVID movie "The Bubble," the better.).

Maude and Iris Apatow play Sadie and Charlotte, respectively, in both "Knocked Up" and "This is 40" — with their on-screen mother, Debbie, portrayed by Mann, and their father Pete by Paul Rudd as an Apatow stand-in. As for "Funny People," they also play Mann's daughters (in this one, Maude is Mable and Iris is Ingrid) with Mann as Laura, the ex-girlfriend of comedian and actor George Simmons (Adam Sandler), who's dealing with a life-changing health crisis. Sure, the Apatow daughters don't do a ton here, but they flesh out the universe in all three of their dad's films ... and it's notable that we watched Maude and Iris grow up on-screen, basically.

All things considered, Iris Apatow's career is just getting started. Still, over the past few years, she's dabbled in more adult fare (especially on the small screen), so it definitely seems like she's trying to show off her range.

From 2016 to 2018, Apatow portrayed a supporting character, Arya Hopkins, who's tutored by series lead Gus (Paul Rust) on the Netflix TV show "Love," while on another Netflix exclusive, "Unstable," she appeared alongside Rob Lowe and his real-life son John Owen Love. The latter duo play tech CEO Ellis Dragon and his creatively inclined son Jackson, respectively, whereas Apatow plays Anna, an intern at Ellis' company, itself aptly named Dragon, who also happens to be the former stepdaughter of the company's CFO Anna ("Fleabag" standout Sian Clifford).

Industry observers note that then there's "Tell Me Lies." A deliciously dramatic and dishy Hulu series created by Meaghan Oppenheimer, "Tell Me Lies" adapts (and improves) the book of the same name by Carola Lovering and ran for three seasons on Hulu. Apatow highlights up as a college student named Amanda in the third and final season, creating a problem for series regular Bree (Cat Missal) as she mentally and emotionally recovers from an affair with a professor named Oliver (Tom Ellis). After she finally gets out of Oliver's clutches, Bree notices that Amanda seems to be Oliver's next victim, sending her into a spiral.

You can see Apatow as Proserpina in "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping" in theaters now.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

[Editor’s note: This review was originally published on October 2, 2026 during the 2026 Latest York Film Festival. Janus Film will release the film in limited theaters on Friday, November 20.].

In a recent development, paul Thomas Anderson‘s eye for vivifying music onscreen dates back to the late 1990s when, after “Boogie Nights,” he made Technicolor mini-masterpiece music videos with his ex-girlfriend Fiona Apple — or made a San Fernando Valley-sized shrine to Aimee Mann with his third feature, “Magnolia.” Since then, he’s kicked around with HAIM while turning one third of its Los Angelino triumvirate, Alana Haim, into a screen actress. He’s shot for Radiohead and made a regular collaboration with band member Jonny Greenwood to create some of the 21st century’s most memorable scores. Many young cinephiles now associate the mischievously lilty notes of “Phantom Thread” with the poison promise of new love and obsessive creation. Related Stories Box Office: ‘Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping’ Scores $21 Million in Previews, Second-Best Result of 2026 ‘Josephine’ Review: Another Heartsick Horror Film About Real Monsters from ‘Soft & Quiet’ Filmmaker.

Sources indicate that last December, PTA teamed up with Geese frontman Cameron Winter to film, while operating his own Panavision camera, his solo stage performance at Carnegie Hall, running through sparse piano arrangements of tracks off his solo album, “Heavy Metal.” The result, a 72-minute film now being distributed roadshow-style by Janus Films before inevitably living on the Criterion Collection, is a stunning arrangement of its own: a deeply achey, sincere but never cloyingly earnest concert movie that’s tender to the point of frailty. (Benny Safdie counts as a co-producer, and the film’s scratchy Latest York quality and setting can’t help but have his imprint.).

Sources indicate that the matted-hair, lithe Winter can seem a bit uncomfortable in his own skin in the public eye, as he did onstage ahead of “Cameron Winter at Carnegie” at its Fresh York Film Festival world premiere at Alice Tully Hall. But on the piano, laser-beamed into his songcraft, he’s quietly electrified, at seemingly at peace as his tenorous vocal glissando and nimble fingerwork on the piano produce shiveringly tender folk ballads that echo Harry Nilsson and Van Morrison. (The usual comparisons to Tom Waits and Rufus Wainright are right, too, but Winter is his own strange thing.) If you weren’t previously sold on the wily Winter antic rock chaos of Geese — rapidly becoming one of the most popular contemporary art rock bands of these times — you’re about to. Paul Thomas Anderson has created a rhapsodic shrine to the man that is nonetheless ballad-sized in its emotional scale.

Recent findings suggest that winter, in December, played and sang to a sold-out crowd of more than 2,700 at the stately cultural temple that is Carnegie Hall, and this film can at times feel like a religious experience, an incantation, a lonely vigil. The singer/songwriter was 23 at the time of the performance, one year older than Bob Dylan when he headlined Carnegie Hall, and similarly at the precipice of major fame. Fixed on a mobile rig that will at times careen and whoosh across the stage when not otherwise holding on Winter, Anderson’s camera catches the expressionism and chiaroscuro of stage lights illuminating and fading off the singer’s face.

In a recent development, the result is hynoptic, a concert film up there with “Stop Making Sense” but for introverts. Songs like the popular single “$0” acquire an even more wrenchingly somber quality as a lovelorn protagonist rues being exploited by a relationship (“You’re making me feel like a dollar in your hand / You’re making me feel like I’m a zero dollar man”). Stripped of production, his indie hit “Love Takes Miles” plays even better. While many of the songs sort of hover in the same key and bleed into one another, that makes for an all the more transfixing experience. The lack of an interstitial anything save for a sweet prologue and moving coda make for experience also that’s immersive, deep, and the kind whose truth you can feel somewhere in your body even if you can’t quite articulate it.

“Cameron Winter at Carnegie Hall premiered at the Upcoming York Film Festival. Janus Films will release it in theaters starting November 20.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Google has given its AI-powered "Ask Maps" feature a major upgrade, adding tools for trip planning, real-time route guidance, appointment finding, and saved-list search. The updates begin rolling out today on Android and iOS.

Google launched Ask Maps last March as an AI assistant designed to handle questions and requests more complicated than simply searching the word "bar" or "groceries." Instead of performing simple keyword searches, the idea behind Ask Maps is that you can describe several specific requirements at once, and Maps will find places that match them all. For example, you could ask for a restaurant with outdoor seating for a certain number of people, and "Ask Maps" will factor in your past searches and give you results. Of course, AI assistants have a habit of making things up, so even with today's roll-out, you'll want to double-check your sources before you drive an hour to the wrong restaurant.

In a recent development, to me, this is the most useful newly introduced feature launching today. Whether you're planning a day trip for holiday shopping or something more ambitious, like a three-day road trip with coastal hikes and oceanfront dining, Ask Maps will put together a day-by-day schedule. Each plan includes insider tips and numbered map pins for every stop, so you can see the whole route at a glance. Hexed Might Be A Major Misfire For Disney Animation At The Box Office

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Disney has produced many of the best animated movies of all time.
  • "Hexed" is currently eyeing an opening in the $23 million range, per Box Office Theory.
  • More than A24's "Club Kid" or or the "Hershey" biopic, also releasing over Thanksgiving, it's "The Hunger Games" that will be a bigger problem for Disney's latest.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Disney has produced many of the best animated movies of all time. They've been doing it longer than anyone else and, arguably, better than anyone else for decades. Unfortunately though, original animation has been a tough sell to audiences in recent years, and Disney's "Hexed" looks like it's going to suffer at the box office as a result of this trend.

"Hexed" is currently eyeing an opening in the $23 million range, per Box Office Theory. That's across the full five-day, Wednesday to Sunday stretch since this movie is opening mid-week for the Thanksgiving holiday. The comedy "Focker In-Law" pits Ben Stiller against Ariana Grande and looks to win the weekend with around $36 million. For what it's worth, earlier tracking (via Deadline) had both movies doing between $40 and $50 million across the five-day stretch.

More than A24's "Club Kid" or or the "Hershey" biopic, also releasing over Thanksgiving, it's "The Hunger Games" that will be a bigger problem for Disney's latest. "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping" will be a bigger hit than you realize, doing well over $100 million on opening weekend. That means, in its second frame, it could still easily take number one over Thanksgiving.

Disney's latest centers on an impulsive and unconventional teenage girl named Billie (Hailee Steinfeld) who discovers secret magical abilities which. Once unleashed, they hurtle her out of suburbia and into a vast witch realm called Hexe. Fawn Veerasunthorn and Jason Hand directed the movie, with Josie Trinidad co-directing.

Sources indicate that the big issue for "Hexed" is that these movies don't come cheap. We're looking at a budget of at least $150 million, if not much more. Even at $150 million, an opening under $30 million across a robust, long holiday weekend is close to a death sentence. Yes, there are overseas markets to account for and family-friendly movies can have long legs. Even so, the early estimates are rough, to put it kindly.

It's especially disappointing because this feels like the right place on the calendar for the movie. "Moana 2" smashed box office records and led to the biggest Thanksgiving ever in 2024. That eventually became a $1 billion hit for Disney. But that was a sequel to a much-beloved move from the 2010s. Originals, from both Disney Animation and Pixar, have struggled mightily in the 2020s.

In a recent development, case in point, "Strange World" bombed at the box office in 2022, taking in just $73 million worldwide. "Hexed" doesn't appear to be in such terrible shape but it's not looking good. Disney's "Wish" was also a substantial disappointment at the box office in 2023, doing $255 million worldwide. Decent for an original movie by today's standards but not nearly good enough to turn a profit.

Industry observers note that the only thing Disney can hope for is that word of mouth amongst moviegoers is outstanding, which could give "Hexed" unusually long legs. Or that tracking is just wildly off and the movie actually comes in closer to earlier estimates. Either way, as it stands, this one looks like it just has one too many hurdles to clear.

Disney's "Hexed" hits theaters on November 25, 2026.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Netflix’s newest animated sensation, directed by Alyce Tzue (Soar) and John Ripa (Raya and the Last Dragon), dares to ask: what if Cinderella’s ugly stepsisters weren’t so ugly and bad after all, but were instead besieged by a Western world that reacted to their East Asian heritage with distrust and unease?

The answer is Steps, a film that turned out to be far more distinctive than the concept of fairy-tale revisionism it seemed to hint at. The relationships among Lilith (Ali Wong), Margot (Stephanie Hsu), the aforementioned ugly stepsisters, and Cinderella (Amanda Seyfried) propel the movie from great to “must-see.”.

Sources indicate that its ending, however, might catch a few people off guard. Not because it’s particularly confusing, but because it takes the story of Lilith and Cinderella​​​​​​​ in a surprising direction.

Industry observers note that the main plot of Steps centers on Lilith and Cinderella’s efforts to undo the harm​​​​​​​ their ex-friend, the bratty and insecure Priscilla (Nikki Glaser), inflicted on the kingdom of Alouette. All they need to do is get the glass slipper on Cinderella’s foot, and they’ll be transported to the night of the ball before Priscilla stole the fairy godmother’s (Bette Midler) magic wand.

Lilith and Cinderella manage to do so, but instead of returning to the night of the ball, Cinderella chooses to go further back—to the day she silently decided to shun Lilith and Margot in favor of Priscilla and the other Alouette residents who looked down on them.

Sources indicate that by going back to that time and protecting her sisters, Cinderella changes everything. Lilith and Margot can embrace their East Asian heritage, and so can the people of Alouette. Fairy-tale creatures​​​​​​​ like trolls, previously seen as dangerous and unable to enter the kingdom, become accepted. There’s even a touching moment when we see​​​​​​​ two men dancing and holding one another on the dance floor, which, while not revolutionary, is still wonderful to see​​​​​​​ in a children’s movie.

At a press junket for Steps, Polygon asked the directors about the importance of that ending and what it meant to show a happier world where people embrace diversity and inclusion.

“[Alouette] is a very small box of a kingdom in terms of its standards. So I love that, not only all of our characters, but the entire world changes from this one kind moment between Lilith and Cinderella,” Ripa explained.

Recent findings suggest that before Lilith and Cinderella’s rekindling changed the kingdom for good, the people of Alouette were conformists; no one liked change​​​​​​​. However, in showing the acceptance of trolls and non-heteronormative pairings, Tzue and Ripa wanted to highlight the importance of everyone getting their happy ending.

“We wanted to make sure that the idea of inclusion and belonging extends to everybody,” Ripa told Polygon. “It was one of the points of the film: everybody deserves to be a part of the fairytale.”.

Steps is now available to watch exclusively on Netflix​​​​​​​.

Latest Update: What ‘Digger’ Has in Common with Gary Oldman’s Winston Churchill and Charlize Theron’s Megyn Kelly

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that tom Cruise‘s performance in Alejandro González Iñárritu‘s “Digger” is one of the boldest and most entertaining of the actor’s career, as he suppresses not only his usual movie star charisma but his entire way of walking and talking to play paunchy, aging oil tycoon Digger Rockwell.
  • To aid in his complete transformation, Cruise called on one of the best prosthetic designers in the business, Kazu Hiro.
  • In a recent development, “Alejandro is an amazing director, and he has lots of ideas,” Hiro told IndieWire.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that tom Cruise‘s performance in Alejandro González Iñárritu‘s “Digger” is one of the boldest and most entertaining of the actor’s career, as he suppresses not only his usual movie star charisma but his entire way of walking and talking to play paunchy, aging oil tycoon Digger Rockwell. Cruise is barely recognizable in the role, which is about as far from heroic characters like Pete “Maverick” Mitchell and Ethan Hunt as Cruise’s Ron Kovic in “Born on the Fourth of July” was from race car driver Cole Trickle almost 40 years ago.

To aid in his complete transformation, Cruise called on one of the best prosthetic designers in the business, Kazu Hiro. Hiro has turned Gary Oldman into Winston Churchill (“The Darkest Hour”), Charlize Theron into Megyn Kelly (“Bombshell”), and Dwayne Johnson into “Smashing Machine” Mark Kerr, but transforming Cruise into Texas oilman Digger Rockwell was a whole newly introduced task — one made even more challenging by Iñárritu and Cruise’s persistent striving for perfectionism, and constant eagerness to try new approaches. Related Stories ‘Cameron Winter at Carnegie Hall’ Review: PTA’s Spellbinding Concert Doc Is a Gorgeously Tender Performance Box Office: ‘Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping’ Scores $21 Million in Previews, Second-Best Result of 2026.

In a recent development, “Alejandro is an amazing director, and he has lots of ideas,” Hiro told IndieWire. “Every day he comes in with a fresh idea, and we have to come up with an answer for how to achieve it. And Tom is really professional, and expects everybody else to be at that same level, ready for any situation. After the first day of testing, I learned that I had to stay flexible to respond to whatever they wanted.”.

In a recent development, to that end, Hiro created modular prosthetics whose parts could easily be swapped out and moved around, so that Cruise and Iñárritu could constantly try new looks. “Sometimes with heavy makeup, you can’t change it,” Hiro said. “I created prosthetics that could be mixed, so we could make new designs on the spot — try this forehead with these cheeks and this nose, then change it.” Creating Cruise’s look was a constantly evolving process throughout the long prep period. “We didn’t have a clear answer until the end of rehearsal.”.

Hiro’s mandate at the beginning was a bit open-ended, which gave him room for artistic exploration but also made it difficult to zero in on a precise look. “Alejandro said the character was 76 years old and an oil tycoon,” Hiro said. “He also said he didn’t want the character to look like Tom, but he still wanted to see Tom in the character.” To try to find a concrete image for Digger Rockwell, Hiro immersed himself in research.

“I researched real oil tycoons and how they aged and what kinds of lifestyles they had,” Hiro mentioned. “Those lifestyles affect how they age.” As Hiro did more and more research, however, he realized that there was no one look that defined the entire profession he was trying to represent. “Everybody looked so different, so in the end I relied more on the storyline and how this particular character behaved.” The idea, in keeping with the slightly heightened style of the film as a whole, was to exaggerate Cruise’s features but keep the character realistic.

In a recent development, hiro began with a 3D scan and life cast of Cruise, which he used to sculpt his designs. His paramount concern was allowing the actor to be as expressive as possible under the makeup. “The important part is to make the prosthetic very soft so he can move,” Hiro stated, noting that three weeks before shooting, Iñárritu called with a significant change. “He decided that Digger should be 65, not 76, so I promptly made a upcoming design. Tom is around that age, but he looks much younger than a normal 65. Under his eye was exposed and the rest of the face was covered, but I made it thin to give him freedom.”.

In addition to Digger’s face, Hiro was also tasked with creating an upper body for an early scene in which Cruise would be seen stripped down to his pajama pants. The body prosthetic was intended only for that one scene, with a lighter bodysuit created for the rest of the movie. “We made a light version of the padding for under the costume, because we don’t need to see the skin after that first scene,” Hiro remarked. “For the first scene we made a silicone prosthetic that was a lot heavier — the body padding was around 10 pounds, but the silicone was 40 or 50.”.

During one of Cruise’s costume fittings, he told Hiro he wanted to feel the weight of the silicone throughout production. “He tried the body prosthetic on and stated, ‘I like this, I want to wear it every day,'” Hiro said. “I told him it would be really heavy and hot, but he said he was training and would be fine.” Since gluing the body prosthetic on every day would be extremely time-consuming, Hiro created a strong spandex foundation and glued the prosthetic to it so Cruise could slip it on each day.

“He wore that for the whole film,” Hiro remarked. “One time he said, ‘This is so heavy, it’s really hard on my back.’ I thought, ‘Okay, you asked for it,’ but he went through with it and finished the film, so that was amazing.”.
