💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that it’s been quite a year for Curry Barker.
  • Which is why it’s interesting that Hollywood’s hottest new director took time out from editing (he’s cutting “Ghosts” himself) and writing (“I have my next thing that I’m working on — I’m really excited about it, and nobody knows anything about it, which is super exciting”), and an unexpected Oscar campaign (“Obsession” is a legit contender for Best Picture, Actress, and Original Screenplay nominations), to make a 5-minute short film, “Mama Bear.” On this week’s episode of the Filmmaker Toolkit Podcast, Barker talked about how the success of “Obsession” interrupted his established flow of churning out short-form content for his popular YouTube channel.
  • “I have two or three short films where I’m like, ‘Oh man, this all took off really rapidly, and I have this short film idea I’ve been dying to do,” remarked Barker on Toolkit.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that it’s been quite a year for Curry Barker. In September 2025, he brought his $700,000 horror film to the Toronto International Film Festival, where it sparked a bidding war that Focus Features won for $17 million. That hefty price tag turned into the deal of the century, as “Obsession” went on to become a half-billion-dollar box-office sensation, with audiences growing week to week. It was clear the then 26-year-old “YouTuber” (a moniker Barker rightfully dismisses) was something special. This was not just a flash in the pan, but a real talent with a seemingly boundless number of ideas and movies he wanted to make. His next film, “Anything but Ghosts,” was already in the can by the “Obsession” premiere, a yet-to-be-declared third film is in the works, while potential franchises (“Texas Chainsaw Massacre” and “Obsession,” Barker sees the One Wish Willow story device having “Knives Out” anthology-like potential) linger in the background. Related Stories Director Brian Duffield Had to Find a New Form of Visual Storytelling for ‘Whalefall’ How ‘Paper Tiger’ Evolved When Jeremy Strong and Anne Hathaway Couldn’t Reprise Their ‘Armageddon Time’ Roles.

Which is why it’s interesting that Hollywood’s hottest new director took time out from editing (he’s cutting “Ghosts” himself) and writing (“I have my next thing that I’m working on — I’m really excited about it, and nobody knows anything about it, which is super exciting”), and an unexpected Oscar campaign (“Obsession” is a legit contender for Best Picture, Actress, and Original Screenplay nominations), to make a 5-minute short film, “Mama Bear.” On this week’s episode of the Filmmaker Toolkit Podcast, Barker talked about how the success of “Obsession” interrupted his established flow of churning out short-form content for his popular YouTube channel.

“I have two or three short films where I’m like, ‘Oh man, this all took off really rapidly, and I have this short film idea I’ve been dying to do,” remarked Barker on Toolkit. “I actually have no time to do those short films, and then justifying if it be would be worth my time to do them when I need to be writing this, I need to be editing this, and I need to be doing press for this.”.

It’s less about Barker’s desire to scratch the itch of the shorts he never got to make, but more about a hesitancy to step away completely from the iterative process by which he learned his craft — justifying the brief time he took off to make “Mama Bear” because he felt the need to sketch.

“It’s fun to have that playground because the features are bigger stakes,” mentioned Barker. “We were like, ‘Okay, this is a short film: We can do weird stuff. Let’s come up with crazy rules that don’t make sense, and experiment.’”.

Sources indicate that barker and his “Mama Bear” cinematographer — his young brother Riley, who worked on the “Obsession” camera department — created different rules for the camera, as Curry is still trying to hone his discipline for storytelling within longer takes. Not only would they shoot a narrow 4:3 aspect ratio, but the Barker brothers denied themselves the ability to move the camera left, right, up, down, or dolly in.

“I do have a lot to learn,” said Barker of making “Mama Bear.” “It’s so funny because I was having dinner and I told someone, ‘Oh, I’d love to shadow on Ari Aster’s set.’ And someone was like, ‘Well, you’re Curry Barker, what are you going to shadow for?’”.

His 2026 meteoric rise has allowed Barker to collect a group of more experienced peers he views as mentors — including Aster, Bill Hader, Zach Cregger, and Rian Johnson — and successful producers, like Jason Blum, investing in his career, but he believes there’s a misconception of what comes along with “making it.”.

Sources indicate that “People think that once you’re in this club, you’re in the club, and everyone talks to everyone. But no — you’re in a bubble, and I want to know how Zach Cregger writes his outline. I want to watch him do it,” stated Barker. “You’re all alone. Your process is your own, and you figure this stuff out on your own. Once you get into this league, there’s no one telling you, ‘Well, actually you do it like this, this, and this.’ It’s whatever you learned all along your journey; that’s your process.”.

One of the most impressive things about the self-taught Barker’s journey is how promptly he turned himself into a successful actor/writer/director/editor. In 2018, when Barker left Alabama to come to Los Angeles to pursue a career in movies, he saw himself as an actor. Despite all the story scenarios dancing around his head, the idea that he would become a screenwriter was laughable.

“I never would’ve thought I was a screenwriter. I didn’t make great grades. I made Cs and Ds, and I wasn’t the best in English class,” said Barker, who naively assumed professional writers were the kids who won spelling bees: “I just thought to be respected as a writer you have to be that.” Barker credits taking screenwriter Aaron Sorkin’s MasterClass as what opened his eyes. “It was the first time I thought, ‘I can do this, too.’ It’s really just about being creative and cracking a story, and there are rules, there’s structure.”.

In a recent development, directing organically grew out of Barker pulling together collaborators to shoot sketches and shorts for him to act in. Barker, half-joking, likes to say he realized one day that what he was doing was directing, and that he both enjoyed “telling people what to do” and had a knack for it.

In a recent development, what Barker accomplishes in a single shot — establishing a tonal balance that teeters between horror and comedy, combining blocking and camera movement to edit within the frame — is remarkably sophisticated. But Barker, who studies and strives for what masters like Kiyoshi Kurosawa can accomplish, rapidly says he fell short in “Obsession.”.

It has been revealed that “Things that you might think we pulled off [with longer takes in ‘Obsession’], we reshot,” stated Barker, who on the podcast described in detail a key early scene between Bear (Michael Johnston) and Nikki (Inde Navarrette) in the bedroom that had to be reshot because the action took too long to unfold. “I think Ari [Aster] said once that if you realize you needed to give this information in four seconds, but then it took 25 seconds, you’re stuck with 25 seconds.”.

Curry Barker, the editor, is Curry Barker, the director’s harshest critic, giving him a bird’s-eye view of what he believes is the director’s inability to envision the required pacing of how a scene will play on screen, even if it might feel unnaturally fast on set.

“Every single oner that I’ve shot in my career has been a problem in the edit,” said Barker. “I think there’s two ways to fail at something. You can either fail, realize that it didn’t work, get scared of it, and then be like, ‘Well, in my last film I did a bunch of oners and then it killed me in the edit, so I’m not going to do that anymore.’ Or you can fail, realize how you did it wrong, and try to get better at that for the next time.”.

As Barker discussed at the Future of Filmmaking Summit last month, that iterative process is key to how he got where he is, and it’s a mindset he clearly hasn’t given up. When asked how “Obsession” would have been different if he had more money, Barker doesn’t talk about locations, sets, special or visual effects, or scenes he envisioned that he couldn’t pull off — in terms of scale, he likes both writing and directing within set limitations.

In a recent development, “I would’ve reshot everything,” Barker answered without hesitation. “If I was finishing the edit before we got into TIFF, and you were like, ‘Dude, this is really good, we really love this movie, we think it has potential, but we want to give you $10 million to reshoot the whole thing, I would be like, ‘Deal.’ I would take it.”.

“I think it’s so funny to look back and think about that now,” Barker catches himself, knowing he’s talking about a film that broke the box office and catapulted his career. “Now I wouldn’t change anything because I would be too scared to touch it.”.

The iPhone Duo Is Getting Face Unlock

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that apple dropped iOS 27.2.1 last week, patching a handful of security vulnerabilities and bugs—including two iMessage flaws that let people read messages they shouldn't.
  • Apple is at the moment beta testing the third major upgrade in the iOS 27 era, and anyone—developer and public tester alike—is free to install it at their leisure.
  • With the second iOS 27.3 developer beta, Apple is introducing face unlock for the iPhone Duo.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that apple dropped iOS 27.2.1 last week, patching a handful of security vulnerabilities and bugs—including two iMessage flaws that let people read messages they shouldn't. But while most of us are running this version (or should install it as soon as possible), others are running something different—iOS 27.3.

Apple is at the moment beta testing the third major upgrade in the iOS 27 era, and anyone—developer and public tester alike—is free to install it at their leisure. With it, comes the return of the Health app, vertical Safari tabs, and Siri AI app actions, among other fresh features. But for users of Apple's first foldable, the iPhone Duo, iOS 27.3 brings two rather notable changes—both of which are for the better.

With the second iOS 27.3 developer beta, Apple is introducing face unlock for the iPhone Duo. The foldable famously ships with Touch ID, the first newly introduced iPhone since the third-gen iPhone SE to do so. While that isn't a problem per se, many of us are used to unlocking our iPhones with our faces. This revision just lets new Duo owners keep up with that muscle memory.

Industry observers note that now, take note: This isn't Face ID. No software update can introduce new hardware, so the iPhone Duo still doesn't have the camera tech required to power Apple's Face ID system. As such, the Duo's face unlock is likely not as secure as Face ID on other iPhones. Perhaps that's why your iPhone Duo will require Touch ID for Apple Pay and passwords, or after 45 minutes of inactivity. This feature seems to be one of pure convenience: If you want to be able to unlock your Duo with your face (at least, some of the time), you can.

What's more, this isn't a default setting. If you're running the beta, or if you're reading this after iOS 27.3 drops, you can find the option in Settings > Touch ID & Passcode.

Apple made a big deal about the continuity involved with opening and closing the iPhone Duo. As you do, your content moves with you seamlessly—a very Apple thing to do. That remarked, you might expect folding the Duo to lock it, but it doesn't. You need to hit the side button to actually put the phone to sleep.

iOS 27.3 changes that. If you so choose, you can enable a setting to lock your Duo whenever you close it. That won't work for everyone, of course—some consumers may still want to move between modes without worrying about locking their Duos. But for those who would rather lock their devices whenever they fold them up, the latest option is under Settings > Display & Brightness.

How World-Class Filmmaker Andrey Zvyagintsev Came Back to Life for ‘Minotaur’

💡 Key Takeaways
  • [Editor’s note: This interview was originally published during the 2026 Cannes Film Festival.
  • World-class Russian filmmaker Andrey Zvyagintsev (“Leviathan”) returned to the Croisette this year in Cannes competition with “Minotaur,” having recovered from a near-fatal illness.
  • Recent findings suggest that when he left the hospital in Germany in 2022, as he told me while at Cannes this year, he was in a wheelchair.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

[Editor’s note: This interview was originally published during the 2026 Cannes Film Festival. MUBI will release “Minotaur” in theaters on Friday, November 20.].

World-class Russian filmmaker Andrey Zvyagintsev (“Leviathan”) returned to the Croisette this year in Cannes competition with “Minotaur,” having recovered from a near-fatal illness. After contracting a severe case of COVID in 2021, he reacted badly to the Sputnik vaccine and was put into a medically induced coma for 14 days. When he came out of it, his arms and legs were paralyzed due to Guillain-Barré Syndrome. He lay flat on his back for a year.

Recent findings suggest that when he left the hospital in Germany in 2022, as he told me while at Cannes this year, he was in a wheelchair. While he indicates he hasn’t watched TV for 20 years now, “I watched a lot of films online,” he said through an interpreter on the roof of the Palais. “I read some things. I did not know if I would ever be able to walk again, to live again as a normal person. I have still now some consequences. I’m not at my best. I have regained completely the motion of my hands, but I have still a bit of a difficulty walking.” Related Stories How a Filipino Facial Expression in ‘Forgotten Island’ Became a Universal Symbol of Representation A ‘Home Alone’ Legacyquel with Macaulay Culkin in Early Development with Seth Rogen and Evan Goldberg.

Industry observers note that but he did manage to shoot his sixth feature film last year, but not in Russia. After nine months of waiting, in the spring of 2023, he let go of one expensive project (“Jupiter”) for which he couldn’t seem to raise funding. “I said, ‘Let’s put it on ice, we’ll come back to it later. I don’t want to sit and wait for years and years for you to find the money. I want to make a film now.'”.

In a recent development, so instead the filmmaker focused on a parallel project he had also been developing, an adaptation of Claude Chabrol’s 1969 thriller “The Unfaithful Wife,” starring Stéphane Audran as a well-heeled wife cheating on her husband, which was later remade as “Unfaithful” with Richard Gere and Diane Lane. The result, “Minotaur,” is the “Leviathan” Oscar nominee’s first film in nearly a decade, since 2017’s “Loveless.”.

Recent findings suggest that at the same time that the filmmaker was coping with his illness, four years ago, at the start of the Ukraine war, he made the decision to leave Russia and move to Paris. Going home would mean the risk of being considered a traitor or an enemy of the state in Russia. “It might result in us becoming what is called foreign agents; it’s a hard thing,” he remarked. “Maybe this will happen, maybe not. Let’s not be too pessimistic, but mostly all independent journalists are saying that their oppressions are going to get even harsher, and that I think we have decades ahead of us before things get better.”.

Sources indicate that his 16-year-old had been studying at a French high school in Moscow before the war. “His French was pretty good,” noted Zvyagintsev. “So it was an obvious choice. And also, my wife [has been] in love with France for a long time, she has been learning French for many years. So it was a choice, also for both of them, and for their future.”.

How’s his French? “Zero,” he noted. “The other reason for me was that France is the homeland to cinema; that’s where cinema was born, and also there are so many cinephiles among spectators. Also here in France, directors have the final cut. In the states, it’s much harder to get in a position where you are not censored; it’s not a producer or someone who decides instead of you.”.

In a recent development, the filmmaker set about creating believable Russian locations in Riga, Latvia, which still resembles its neighbor country. “The dormitory suburbs around Riga look exactly like Russian dormitory suburbs,” said Zvyagintsev. “A Russian eye would not be able to distinguish between Russia and Latvia in this instance. As for interiors, Anton’s flat was constructed as a set, so it’s a constructed set, and the villa where the main characters live is a contemporary building, a very modern one, and you could find something exactly like this anywhere.”.

When it came to finding his cast, the casting director put out a call for Russian characters of a certain age. “Every actor from anywhere who is interested in working with you, they will send you a video presentation,” noted Zvyagintsev. “They can be from Argentina, London, Moscow, Paris, wherever. You send them a scene they have to play, and they make a self-tape for you on their iPhone. Before, I despised self-tapes, but it’s convenient, because now with everybody scattered around the world, it’s the only way for us to work. We could not possibly pay for all the people I wanted to check to come to Riga to make a real-life casting. There were people also from Riga who do speak Russian.”.

In a recent development, one serious concern for Russian actors still living in Russia was the possible repercussions of participating in a Zvyagintsev project. “I would talk to them about the script and show them parts of the script, so that they know what they’re getting involved in, because, of course, they were at risk of getting blacklisted,” he said. “Most of them, with heartache, refused to take part in the film, but there was one who accepted, and I’m still completely amazed at his courage. It’s the main part, the main character, [actor] Dmitriy Mazurov. I said to him, ‘Are you sure you want to film with me?’ And he said, ‘If I’m not doing this part, I don’t know what I’m doing in acting.'”.

Of course, the filmmaker took a different approach to the Chabrol story. “In the first minute, the story is completely revealed,” he noted. “We understand that she is being unfaithful, so then all the film is about observing him, observing her, trying to understand, hesitating, and trying to guess what is going on, and while he observes, the spectator starts doing it along with him. And after the murder, actually, he goes back to this position where he’s mostly observing her reaction to the disappearance of a lover, yeah, and she knows what’s going on, and again it’s about observation.”.

The filmmaker loved one bravura sequence that is 20 minutes long without any dialogue at all. “The sequence after the murder, it’s 20 minutes, even a little bit more, with not one subtitle, so you only observe his actions, and there are no words: it’s extremely cinematic in its essence.”.

And Zvyagintsev added many telling details from the real world, from corruption to the war. “The Chabrol film is much more classical,” he mentioned. “It follows a pattern: he killed, then he’s discovered, and then he will be punished. And I wanted to break up this classical structure and to invent something different based on our Russian realities.”.

Sources indicate that was shooting the movie a physical challenge? “When you are full of inspiration, when you are searching constantly for solutions, the light, the sets, the performance of the actors, you don’t feel fatigued in the same way,” he stated. “There is such a joy in making the film that is, in your head, real. I think it’s the best drug there is.”.

Next up, he will try and resuscitate “Jupiter.” ” I have met some producers who are interested in it,” he remarked, “so hopefully we will be able to get it moving again.”.

6 Western Movies From the ’90s That Are 10/10 Masterpieces

💡 Key Takeaways
  • There's nothing quite like a good Western.
  • Whether you prefer comedic takes on the genre, action-packed shoot-'em-ups, or deconstructive takes that raise the Western from the ground up, there's something here for everyone.
  • Starting this list off with perhaps the most controversial pick, Young Guns II deserves its place in the Western canon.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

There's nothing quite like a good Western. Although the golden age of the horse opera was undoubtedly the mid-20th century, the genre continued to persevere long afterward. In fact, there was a Western renaissance in the 1990s that took Hollywood — and the Academy Awards — by storm. From genre staples like Clint Eastwood and Kevin Costner to visionary filmmakers like Ang Lee and Richard Donner, the '90s sparked latest life into the Old West.

Whether you prefer comedic takes on the genre, action-packed shoot-'em-ups, or deconstructive takes that raise the Western from the ground up, there's something here for everyone. Outlaws, lawmen, soldiers, and cowboys galore make up some of the greatest thrills of the '90s centered entirely on the American West. Whether you adore these flicks already or have yet to visit them, these are some of the decade's greatest Westerns — so don't sleep on them.

Starting this list off with perhaps the most controversial pick, Young Guns II deserves its place in the Western canon. A high-octane sequel to the original 1988 flick, the Emilio Estevez-led Billy the Kid action romp pits the Regulators against the lawman Pat Garrett (William Petersen), who aims to bring Billy and his friends in on several outstanding warrants. The result is an intense cat-and-mouse ride across the Latest Mexican desert, and it's a blast for those who haven't had the pleasure.

In a recent development, young Guns II is arguably even greater than its predecessor. Billy, Doc (Kiefer Sutherland), Chavez (Lou Diamond Phillips), and the rest of the Regulators carry the weight of the picture with their trademark charm and "Brat Pack" pull. The fast-pulling sequel does everything it can to surpass the original, armed with a killer Jon Bon Jovi theme and plenty of fabulous performances that deserve high praise. There's a reason that folks are still calling for a third entry after all these years — and long after the fates of the Regulators have already been met.

The Wild West era and the American Civil War are so inexplicably linked that one cannot divorce the Western from the war itself. Director Ang Lee understood this profoundly when tackling Ride with the Devil, a Civil War-era trial by fire that chronicles a group of Missouri Bushwhackers as they battle the Jayhawkers invading their Southern home. Its meditations on the origins of Western violence as an outgrowth from the war itself are quite complex, and the picture pulls no punches as it does so. Tobey Maguire and Skeet Ulrich star as childhood friends Jake Roedel and Jack Bull Chiles seek revenge on those who threatened their home.

Like many Westerns, Ride with the Devil offers a nuanced take on the war that explores the evils of both sides. That said, the Irregulars are portrayed as almost akin to a typical Western outlaw gang. Jake's struggle with the Southern cause, and his growing friendship with former slave Daniel Holt (Jeffrey Wright), is what forges his path as an honorable man. It may not be the first film that comes to mind when you think of the Old West — indeed it's very much rooted in the Civil War itself — but it would be hard to consider the film anything but a Western in style and substance.

Recent findings suggest that based on the popular Western television program of the same name, Richard Donnor brought Bret Maverick (Mel Gibson) to the massive screen with the comedic Maverick. When the titular gambler finds himself in search of the funds to enter a high-stakes poker game, he ventures across the Old West alongside Annabelle Bransford (Jodie Foster) and Marshal Zane Cooper (James Garner), who certainly give him a run for his money. If you loved the show, you'll get a kick out of the big-screen version.

Industry observers note that maverick reminds us, like Young Guns II, that the genre can be fun as much as it is introspective. Gibson plays the unusual Western "hero" with genuine charm and an unassuming con artistry that certainly honors the original series. It's not your typical Western, but that's exactly why it's such a stellar entry. Of course, Maverick turns out to actually be a continuation rather than a straight-up reboot, but the way it reveals such a fact is exactly the sort of slight-of-hand that gives Bret Maverick his edge.

Four icons and four completely different ways of walking into trouble. This is the one you would have been out there, why it fits, and what it would have cost you.

You have never explained yourself and you have never needed to, because people work out fairly quickly that you are the most capable person in the room without you ever having to mention it.

You are the funniest person in most rooms and the most loyal person in all of them, and you would be genuinely insulted if somebody suggested those two things were in any tension.

You never wanted this job, and you took it anyway because the alternative was standing there watching somebody less careful do it badly, which is the most Western reason there has ever been.

Nobody has ever successfully talked you out of something you had already decided was right, and a long line of grown adults has found that out the hard way.

Sources indicate that the first Western to win Best Picture at the Oscars in decades, Dances with Wolves was Kevin Costner's directorial debut that proved the Western could be as epic as ever. With a screenplay by Michael Blake based on his novel of the same name, the film follows Lt. John Dunbar as he is stationed out on the American frontier following his heroic (but secretly suicidal) actions during the Civil War. Caught between the Pawnee and Sioux, Dunbar eventually finds himself on the other end of his own country's barrel.

Sources indicate that dances with Wolves is a breathtaking motion picture. It's an introspective glimpse into both the effects of the Civil War and the lives of the Native American peoples who lived on the frontier long before it was settled. More than that, it was a trailblazer in native representation in Hollywood, and though not a true story, is largely based on historical truths. Beyond that, it's also just a great time, as Costner proves himself to be one of the genre's biggest champions.

In a recent development, is there a more well-known or highly-celebrated '90s Western by audiences and critics alike than Tombstone? The spectacular Kurt Russell-led picture follows former lawman Wyatt Earp, his two brothers, and their friend Doc Holliday (Val Kilmer) as they arrive in the titular Arizona town just in time to square off with the ravenous Cowboys gang. As they do, things go from bad to worse as Tombstone falls into chaos — and the Earps bring hell on their adversaries.

Tombstone does absolutely everything right. It's thrilling, action-packed, and chock-full of some of the best on-screen dialogue in the business. Russell and Kilmer steal the show, but the entire stacked cast more than prove themselves over the course of these fast-moving 130 minutes. It's hard to rank the best performances in Tombstone given how stellar each actor truly is, but we all know that this movie wouldn't work nearly as well without Val Kilmer.

It has been revealed that just two years after Dances with Wolves reminded everyone that the Western still had real life left in it, Unforgiven came in and nabbed that Best Picture Oscar for itself. Directed by Clint Eastwood, the genre star tackles his final on-screen Western as William Munny, an aged former gunslinger who returns for one last job to provide for his family. It's a stellar revisionist picture that does everything right as Eastwood bids the genre that made him a final heartfelt farewell.

In a recent development, it doesn't get much better than Unforgiven. With brilliant performances by Morgan Freeman, Richard Harris, and Gene Hackman, the picture excels in the way it unpacks the genre's most famous tropes and reconstructs them into Eastwood's final dissertation on what makes the Western truly exceptional. There are few Westerns so highly celebrated as Unforgiven, and although Eastwood may best be known for his work on the Dollars Trilogy, there's a reason this won Best Picture.

DC just shared a new image of its latest iteration of Robin, answering a major fan question about this new hero's superpowers. Here's the new art, and everything we know about the latest Boy Wonder.

DC recently rebooted the iconic Legion of Super-Heroes - a group of superhumans from the 31st Century, inspired to found a new 'Age of Heroes' by the legacy of the modern day Superman. With Brainiac hunting different versions of the Legion across the multiverse, they find themselves beset by an enemy they can't comprehend.

It has been revealed that DC recently announced the latest recruit to the Legion would be Bat-Lad - a future version of Robin who follows Batman's legacy rather than the Man of Steel's. The first art of the character raised questions about his powers that DC has just answered.

DC recently revealed V. Ken Marion's cover for Legion of Super-Heroes #4, showing Bat-Lad in action. The young hero is shown in a dingy street with a shadowy being behind him. This is something fans already saw in Hayden Sherman and Tamra Bonvillain's main cover (below), but it far more clearly communicates the newly introduced hero's powers.

Recent findings suggest that while that cover highlighted a silhouette behind Bat-Lad, Marion's art makes it clear that the shadow is a physical being controlled by Bat-Lad, with its Venom-like ichor curling around his arm. It's also clear that the original cover isn't obscuring this shadow being - the all-black appearance is its official design.

Industry observers note that the new cover appears to confirm that Bat-Lad is essentially a reverse-Robin. While the original Robin is Batman's sidekick, Bat-Lad appears to be able to summon a towering creature of living darkness. It's an awesome twist on the 'Batman and Robin' partnership, showing how Batman's legacy has been warped over the centuries.

Sadly, it seems that Bat-Lad's powers have a major drawback, as the summary for the matter tells fans to "Welcome a boy and his uncontrollable shadow monster to the world of Legion!" Despite this, DC refers to Bat-Lad as a "newly introduced legionnaire," confirming he'll join the team.

Sources indicate that fans don't yet know much about Bat-Lad other than that he dresses in Robin's colors and can summon a shadow monster. However, it's possible he comes from Planet Gotham. This location was introduced in 2020's Legion of Super-Heroes, characterized as the galaxy's first artificially created planet.

Planet Gotham echoes Batman's iconic city, with a noir aesthetic and ruled over by a president referred to as the 'Commissioner.' The populace are served by robots using the holographic visage of Bruce Wayne's butler Alfred Pennyworth and policed by androids in the style of Victorian 'bobbies.'.

Industry observers note that planet Gotham is characterized as an essentially crime-free utopia, but one with a strict rule of law. Casinos and gaudy luxury are everywhere, suggesting the limits of Batman's ability to truly change Gotham's spirit, no matter the time frame.

Recent findings suggest that DC's 31st Century was canonically rewritten by recent events, so the world of the Legion of Super-Heroes isn't quite as fans remember it. That could mean that Planet Gotham no longer exists, however with each Legionnaire tending to be from a different planet, so it would make a lot of sense for Bat-Lad to call Planet Gotham home.

The Legion of Super-Heroes are known for having a massive membership, making even the Justice League at its height look small. Each era adds a few latest heroes, often as commentary on DC lore at the time or on modern-day themes.

Industry observers note that the last major addition to the team was the mysterious Gold Lantern, who became an object of fascination for fans and built on the idea of the multi-colored Lantern Corps. Now, the Robin of the 3st Century is set to join the team, as Bat-Lad heads towards his debut.

Legion of Super-Heroes #4 is coming December 9 from DC Comics.

10 Books Like ‘Dungeon Crawler Carl’ You Should Read Next

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

There’s nothing quite like Dungeon Crawler Carl, Matt Dinniman’s hilarious, inventive, and surprisingly emotional book series about a man in his underwear forced to fight his way through a livestreamed game show based on dungeon-crawling video games that takes place after an alien takeover of Earth. (Did I mention he's accompanied by his ex-girlfriend’s suddenly talkative cat?).

The premise should not work, but it sure does—and it makes more sense if you know it fits into a popular genre known as "LitRPG," a blend of "literature" and "role-playing game." If you've torn through all eight books released so far and you're looking for more reads that blend surprisingly deep hilarity with tabletop and video game rules (or just similar feels), here are 10 books you should check out.

In a recent development, an isekai story that lands in the sweet spot for DCC fans, He Who Fights with Monsters kicks off with Jason—a completely normal, kind of boring middle manager—waking up in a strange hedge maze, completely nude (even his hair is gone). He has magic that works like a video game, and has to deal with quests that slowly give him clothes (it’s a relief when he finally acquires some pants), force him to survive cannibals, and hunt down various monsters that definitely need killing. It’s got the same “gaming rules” structure as DCC and a similarly absurdist tone, with just the right spice of darkness.

The Cradle series by Will Wight isn’t a LitRPG, and it doesn’t have Carl’s focus on humor, but it’s another progression fantasy with enough game-like elements to be a great match. Lindon is an “unsouled,” incapable of gaining any of the sacred arts and doomed to a life without a future. His lack of power makes Lindon ferociously determined to find an alternative path to power and success, and that’s what drives this story. He has to find creative ways to move forward, and slowly this leads him to a path that just might make him the most powerful person in his world. DCC fans will love the progression and the tone.

According to recent reports, one of the key elements of any video game is the respawn—you get killed, but you pop back up to try again, sometimes at the beginning, sometimes at a save point. Django Wexler leverages that mechanic to great effect in How to Become the Dark Lord and Die Trying. Davi has been summoned to a fantasy world to be the hero, the person who defeats the Dark Lord and saves the day—but she’s failed (and died) so many times, she’s fed up, and decides that on this run through, she’s going to switch sides and become the Dark Lord, using all her knowledge gained from endless replays to her advantage. The humor is pitch-black the way DCC fans like it, and the progressive structure is a perfect fit.

Is Princess Donut your favorite part of Dungeon Crawler Carl? Of course she is. In that case, check out Andrew Seiple’s Threadbare series. Threadbare is a stuffed bear brought to magical life in a failed experiment. He’s a foot tall, full of stuffing, and extremely dumb when the story begins. But when he’s rescued by a little girl and plunged into a horrible series of dangers, Threadbare has to find a way to level up. Like DCC, Threadbare starts off leaning into the absurdity and humor, then slowly gains emotional gravitas as the story progresses.

It has been revealed that if you play tabletop RPGs, you’ve encountered a Murderhobo or two: A character who solves all their problems by killing—even members of their own party. Luke doesn’t aspire to be a Murderhobo—he just wants to take over the family business and hang with his buddies. But when an invasion threatens the kingdom, everyone over the age of 17 is ordered to be tested for Potential. Luke’s friends all test high and join the Ascender Corps, traveling to different planes for training. Luke tests ... very low, and when he steps through a portal to engage in his training, he finds himself without any guidance or training in a strange, deadly world where his only chance of survival is to murder his way through it. It’s dark, darkly funny, and a progression fantasy like no other.

If you’re looking for a book series that combines the dark, chaotic humor, absurd game mechanics, and surprising emotional depth of Carl, here’s Ryan “Quicksave” Romano, a man who has the unique ability to literally create a save point in his existence that allows him to go back and redo things whenever he dies. Searching for a childhood friend, he becomes embroiled in a violent gang war that lets him make good use of his power—but underneath the snark and the insanity of Ryan’s existence is a surprisingly affecting story of a man who has suffered, and suffered countless tragedies that are definitely taking their toll.

If your fave bit of DCC is Carl himself—a mediocre dude in an extraordinary situation—you should read Dennis E. Taylor’s fantastic Bobiverse books. Bob is a software engineer who hits it big and promptly dies, waking up to discover a century has passed and he’s been repurposed as an AI controlling a space probe searching for fresh planets for humanity to inhabit. If he fails in his mission (and he’s not the only probe out there), he’ll be turned off for good. Luckily, he can make copies of himself, and he’s pretty smart. The humor here is smart and soaked in pop culture, making it a perfect match for DCC fans.

Industry observers note that want more of Carl’s absurdist humor? Mayor of Noobtown is the LitRPG you’re looking for. Jim dies and wakes up in a video game-esque universe and finds himself stuck in the zone designated for newbies—players with no experience, skill, or hope. The area fell out of the mainline progression mechanic a long time ago, so there doesn’t seem to be a way to gain power, and the monsters are not at all concerned about the unfairness of it all, so Jim has to figure out how to advance in a universe that seems designed to kill him (again).

If you want to lean into the meta side of things, check out Scathing Reviewer, written by an author who goes by the unusual pen name "BananaDragon." Liu Peijin is the author of a sprawling LitRPG web novel, and she’s used to the bad reviews and complaints from readers—and quite combative about it. When her books’ universe blossoms into a very dangerous new reality, she should be perfectly positioned to survive, having written the story in the first place. But her story becoming real also means her insufferable protagonist is real, and all those nasty critics are now passing judgment on her entire existence. It’s a dark, funny takedown of the entire genre itself, and DCC fans will love it.

Industry observers note that if you want a story that parallels the dungeon crawling aspect of DCC, Andrew Rowe’s Arcane Ascension series is the ticket. The Serpent Spire is a tower of constantly changing traps, puzzles, and dangerous creatures. If you enter and survive, you emerge with magical powers. Corin Cadence’s brother entered the Serpent Spire years ago and never returned—and now Corin is determined not only to survive, but to make it to the top, where legend says a goddess will grant you whatever you wish. And what Corin wants is his brother back. It’s a literal progression combined with LitRPG rules, game-inspired puzzle-solving, and a complex magic system that fans of Carl will definitely enjoy.

It has been revealed that even six decades into his Hollywood career, Steven Spielberg is still synonymous with a brand of movie magic and spectacle that very few can rival. And when he decides to direct a new popcorn blockbuster like “Disclosure Day,” you know you’re in for a few dazzling sequences.

Sources indicate that one of the most exciting moments in the film comes when a train collides into a car with stars Josh O’Connor and Emily Blunt close at hand. The sequence tested every department, from camera and production design to visual effects. And during IndieWire’s recent Craft Roundtables, VFX Supervisor Matthew Butler explained the unique challenge of incorporating subtle VFX work into a scene where so much happens in camera. Related Stories How World-Class Filmmaker Andrey Zvyagintsev Came Back to Life for ‘Minotaur’ How a Filipino Facial Expression in ‘Forgotten Island’ Became a Universal Symbol of Representation.

“With Steven, he wants everything to be as practical as it can be,” Butler mentioned. “We had a real train. A real train, a real car attached to that train, it was being dragged on a real track. That actually did happen.”.

According to recent reports, but while Spielberg’s preferences were clear, Butler clarified that blockbusters on this scale rarely come down to a binary choice between practical effects and VFX. The biggest scenes often contain elements of both, as the pairing between in-camera human acting and cutting edge post-production is what leads to movie magic.

It has been revealed that “When you combine some of the live action blue screen work, clearly that’s your lead actor and actress there, and your stunt work where it’s like ‘Oh my God, that looks really real’ and the stuff that you just can’t do that’s just too dangerous … that’s where visual effects came in,” he remarked. “But I wouldn’t say it was a visual effects sequence. It was a sequence that contained all of those, and it came together in the right way.”.

More coverage from IndieWire’s Craft Roundtables will be published here over the coming weeks.

Alexander Skarsgård has a very interesting filmography, including his latest role in Wicker, where he plays a magically constructed husband to Olivia Coleman, as well as Pillion, where he plays the charismatic leader of a queer motorcycle club. He also played a 10th-century Viking prince named Amleth in The Northman, and in Succession, he plays a confrontational, erratic tech founder. His range is beyond contemplation and is on full display for his fans.

Industry observers note that in his filmography, there’s a fascinating role that didn’t get the recognition it deserved. The role in question is Tarzan. He played the titular character in David Yates’ The Legend of Tarzan, where he starred opposite Margot Robbie in an action-adventure film not unlike Brendan Fraser's The Mummy. It could have been a franchise starterwith iconic characters as Yates attempted to reimagine and modernize the classic Edgar Rice Burroughs role, but it didn't achieve much love.

We follow Tarzan, aka John, who, after moving to London, is persuaded by George Washington Williams (Samuel L. Jackson) to return to his former home in the African jungle to investigate claims of slavery. However, things take a turn when he realizes he’s just a pawn in a scheming plot. The movie has an amazing cast, including Jackson, Christopher Waltz as antagonist Leon Rom, Robbie as Tarzan’s wife Jane Clayton, Djimon Hounsou as Chief Mbonga, and many more.

Despite strong performances and a story that weaves in real historical events, Tarzan received mixed reviews upon its release. It was a box office hit, earning $357.2 million worldwide against a $180 million budget. However, it was criticized for poor CGI, an underutilized cast, and a serious tone, earning a 36% Rotten Tomatoes score, with critics’ consensus noting the movie “has more on its mind than many movies starring the classic character, but that isn't enough to make up for its generic plot or sluggish pace.” However, audiences were more lenient with its 58% rating, and fans’ love is catapulting the movie to newly introduced heights.

A decade since its initial release, The Legend of Tarzan is redeeming itself on streaming as the feature has climbed to the third spot on HBO Max’s global top10 list. It only stands behind Anne Hathaway and Ewan McGregor’s The End of Oak Street, and fan favorite classic Matilda, in a list that also features The Hunger Games franchise, How to Make a Killing, Reminders of Him, and more.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that it's been a long time since the heyday of the Nintendo 64, but its cultural influence hasn't yet waned. If there was any doubt about the subject, the recent remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time should quell it, as the newly introduced version of the game was an immediate success in both critical reception and sales.

While Ocarina of Time leaves behind the limits of the original hardware, other developers are still interested in making games within those confines. One such project is Vasalius: Human Error, and this ambitious new project is set to receive a proper physical release for Nintendo 64 hardware.

Recent findings suggest that vasalius: Human Error is at the moment in the middle of a Kickstarter fundraising campaign, which brands the game as an "Action RPG / FPS for the N64." The FPS element is obvious at a glance, as an action-packed trailer reveals gameplay in the trademark style of the DOOM engine and some shotgun-pumping action. It also features undeniably identifiable voice work from Jon St. John, the original voice of FPS icon Duke Nukem.

On top of that, Vasalius features a robust array of RPG mechanics. In between all the blasting, there's also exploration and storytelling, including "dialogue skill checks" and "several endings shaped by your choices across the whole game." It's a lot to pack into an N64 cartridge, but thanks to its sprite-based style, it's apparently not a problem (and requires no Nintendo 64 Expansion Pak).

As of the time of writing, the physical release of Vasalius: Human Error seems set to go, as the Kickstarter campaign has almost doubled its original goal of $6,400. That was all achieved in the matter of just a few days, with 27 more days set to go before the campaign closes. A series of stretch goals will add various perks if the campaign keeps up its momentum, ranging from more lines by Jon St. John to Switch, Xbox, and PlayStation ports.

Recent findings suggest that the campaign's pricing scheme is probably assisting in its success, as developer John Roo has laid things out in an array of highly reasonable options. Those who simply want to play the game can get a digital ROM for $12, while investing $25 in the campaign will get you a cartridge without a box. Jumping to a complete-in-box version ups the price to $60 — and the deluxe editions of the game take things higher — but the options on hand make it more accessible than a lot of retro-style releases.

Recent findings suggest that every Kickstarter campaign comes with some risks, but Roo promises that the game is already 95% finished and estimates delivery of goods in April 2027 (if you've backed enough Kickstarter campaigns, though, you'll probably want to assume that a delay is in store). Even if Vasalius: Human Error doesn't strike your interest, it's always nice to see passion projects continue to be made for older systems, and this one looks like a unique experience for the Nintendo 64.

Recent findings suggest that looks like Hollywood could be heading into the upcoming year with relief on a national level. The push to pass a federal film and television tax credit by the end of 2026 picked up momentum on Friday at a White House press conference, where President Trump mentioned his administration was actively negotiating the measure and predicted it would pass.

“It’s running its way through Congress, and it has unbelievable support,” Trump stated. He singled out Senator Adam Schiff, the California Democrat who introduced the bill with Republican Senator Tim Scott of South Carolina back in September, and said, “I tell you what, Adam Schiff said, ‘Wow, we love that bill.’ Adam Schiff said that.” Related Stories ‘Disclosure Day’ Did Its Biggest Stunts Practically, So the VFX Team Worked Hard to Look Invisible — Watch How World-Class Filmmaker Andrey Zvyagintsev Came Back to Life for ‘Minotaur’.

According to recent reports, trump mentioned Georgia and Fresh Jersey by name as states with good tax credits for film and TV production, but argued that those incentives alone would not bring enough production work back from overseas. With a federal credit, he said, “Hollywood would open again.”.

Industry observers note that trump remarked his administration was also negotiating whether to extend the measure to benefit movie theaters, but said the matter was unsettled. He first publicly called for a federal production incentive in August after meeting with actor Jon Voight: one of three industry “special ambassadors” he appointed early last year.

In a recent development, the bill’s sponsors unveiled more than 60 fresh House cosponsors and four new Senate cosponsors on Thursday morning — with lawmakers from both parties signing on in both chambers. The following day, Trump himself brought up the Motion Picture, Television, and Entertainment Revitalization Act in response to a question about whether he could work with Democrats. Calling the bill “very bipartisan,” he said, “I can tell you right now it’s going to happen.”.

Trump gave no timetable, though earlier this week, Representative Linda Sánchez, one of the bill’s House sponsors from California, called for Congress to pass it before 2027 so productions could qualify for benefits on the first of the year.

“Members of both parties have watched jobs in their districts move overseas,” she said in a release from Schiff’s office sent to the press. “Momentum is on our side, and we need to strike while the iron is hot by passing this bill before the end of the year.”.

In a recent development, A floor vote has yet to be announced, but multiple sources told IndieWire the measure would move faster if attached to a stopgap government funding bill. If passed and approved, the federal initiative would give qualifying film and TV productions a 20 percent credit on labor expenses for American workers. The credit could reach 30 percent for productions that qualify for bonuses.

For crews accustomed to watching projects follow tax breaks to Canada or the U.K., the proposal would give producers a clear financial incentive to keep that work here for them in the U.S. The bill’s new Senate cosponsors include Republicans Katie Britt of Alabama and Thom Tillis of North Carolina — as well as Democrats Chris Coons of Delaware and Dick Durbin of Illinois.

The AFL-CIO and the American Hotel & Lodging Association also endorsed the bill, joining a coalition that already included IATSE, SAG-AFTRA, the Directors Guild of America, and the Motion Picture Association.

“Given the support from Republicans and Democrats in both chambers and the president, we can get this legislation across the finish line,” Schiff said.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that there are very few film franchises that have managed to capture the imagination of audiences quite like the Harry Potter franchise, or also officially known as the Wizarding World. Released so closely to the mega-bestselling novels, the original run of the film series was a generational phenomenon. The franchise continued with a spinoff trilogy that is not as well-received but still has its own charm. Soon, the story of the Boy Who Lived is jumping to the TV screen with HBO tackling the first book.

Industry observers note that before that happens, let's take a look back at all eleven films in the franchise. With so many different adventures, characters, and creative approaches across the franchise, ranking these films is no easy task. But just like Harry Potter taking on the extremely tough mission to destory the Horcruxes, here, we officially rank these beloved movies to see which one truly deserve a place at the top.

It has been revealed that fantastic Beasts: The Secrets of Dumbledore sees Newt Scamander (Eddie Redmayne) get roped into a mission by Albus Dumbledore (Jude Law) to stop Gellert Grindelwald (Mads Mikkelsen). Grindelwald deploys his devout followers, including the unstable and powerful Credence (Ezra Miller), to influence the upcoming election of the International Conference of Wizards so that he can control the wizarding world.

Recent findings suggest that the third Fantastic Beasts film felt like a contract fulfillment. After the muted reception for the previous film, this film downplays many of the story threads from its predecessor and focuses on an entirely fresh conflict. The ensemble cast, led by Eddie Redmayne, remains the main draw of these films. Mads Mikkelsen, who replaced Johnny Depp, is fantastic as Grindelwald, and all of his scenes with Jude Law are electrifying. As for the story, it gets exciting at times yet the inclusion of the magical creatures seemed shoehorned in to tie in with the title. While in hindsight it was premature to announce a five-film franchise before the first was even released, it is quite sad to see the film series end in a lackluster way like this.

In Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix, Harry Potter (Daniel Radcliffe) finds himself increasingly isolated as the Ministry of Magic refuses to acknowledge that Voldemort has returned. With the Ministry spreading propaganda against Harry and Dumbledore, Hogwarts becomes a bleak place as the new professor Dolores Umbridge (Imelda Staunton) imposes oppressive rules on the school. Harry establishes Dumbledore's Army to prepare fellow students from the upcoming threat, while he himself begins to see visions connected to Voldemort.

This film is the second shortest film in the main franchise after the second half of the Deathly Hallows, which is frustrating if you've read the book because this is the longest book. Many storylines were cut and we are left with only the main plot. This is also the only film that's not written by Steve Kloves and it is quite noticeable in the overall vibes of the film. Order of the Phoenix is also David Yates' first directing gig in the overall franchise, and his style is more grounded and less fantastical than the previous directors, which also needs a little adjustment. Nevertheless, the film shines in its pivotal moments including the whole ordeal with Umbridge and the death of a beloved character. It is an entertaining entry but remains the weakest in the strong lineup of films.

According to recent reports, as the title suggests, Fantastic Beasts: The Crimes of Grindelwald focuses more on the dark wizard Gellert Grindelwald (Johnny Depp) as he tries to rally wizards and witches behind his grand plan. Newt Scamander (Redmayne) once again finds himself caught up in the conflict, especially with two of his love interests Leta Lestrange (Zoe Kravitz) and Tina Goldstein (Katherine Waterston) involved. Grindelwald also has a hidden plan to utilize the mysterious Credence (Ezra Miller) for his ambitions.

Industry observers note that while the first film focuses more on the titular beasts than the wizarding-world conflict, this sequel does the opposite. In doing so, Newt becomes much more of a supporting character in this story that seems far more interested in setting up future sequels. Johnny Depp brings an unsettling presence to Grindelwald, but after seeing the trilogy, his interpretation of Grindelwald seemed off when compared to Grindelwald's disguise portrayed by Colin Farrell or Mads Mikkelsen's nuanced take on the character. There are flashes of brilliance here, but the film ultimately sacrifices much of the first film's charm for an ambitious story that struggles to hold itself together.

Fantastic Beasts and Where to Find Them introduces Newt Scamander (Redmayne), a British magizoologist who arrives in 1926 New York City carrying a magical suitcase filled with extraordinary creatures. When several of these creatures escape into the city, Newt must track them down before they attract unwanted attention from the non-magical population. He crosses paths with Jacob Kowalski (Dan Fogler), a No-Maj who accidentally becomes involved, as well as sisters Tina (Waterston) and Queenie Goldstein (Alison Sudol).

The first spin-off film in the franchise is a peculiar one. It is not based on a narrative book, but a faux textbook that is supposedly used by Hogwarts students. It is a wonder in itself that that book can be turned into a wider story on the wizarding world, and one that opens that world beyond Hogwarts and the UK, as the Newly introduced York setting offers a distinctive visual atmosphere. Eddie Redmayne is playful as the lead, and he's joined by a stellar ensemble that includes Colin Farrell, Katherine Waterston and Jude Law in a minor role. However, Newt's own adventure is a bit jarring when blended with the broader magical conflict. This problem only becomes more noticeable in the following films. The film is still one of the most pleasant fantasy films of the 2010s.

It has been revealed that harry Potter (Radcliffe) returns to Hogwarts for his second year in Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets. After a bizarre encounter with a house elf in Privet Drive warning him about his return, Harry begins to hear a mysterious voice behind the school walls and he also finds a diary that contains disturbing stories. Several students are discovered petrified, and it is remarked that the legendary Chamber of Secrets has been opened after years.

Chris Columbus is back in the director's chair and he once again helmed the film effortlessly, capturing the darker nature of the story while also highlighting the magical world. The film does have an abundance of fun characters and sequences, such as the introduction of Dobby, the boastful Gilderoy Lockhart, the flying Anglia, and the battle with Basilisk. This first sequel is by no means a bad or even a mediocre film, but compared to the rest of the series, it doesn't offer anything new. Still, as a magical adventure packed with important lore building, The Chamber of Secrets remains a thoroughly enjoyable chapter in Harry's story.

It has been revealed that harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows Part 2 follows Harry (Radcliffe), Ron (Rupert Grint), and Hermione (Emma Watson) as they continue their search for Voldemort's remaining Horcruxes. After spending the last film out of school, they are back at Hogwarts as they prepare the students to fight Voldemort (Ralph Fiennes) and his followers.

Sources indicate that as the conclusion to a long cinematic journey, Deathly Hallows Part 2 is akin to Avengers: Endgame of its time. It is an incredibly satisfying payoff to the story and it is arguably the most action-packed installment in the franchise. Hogwarts is transformed into a full-scale battlefield and several beloved characters get their own moments to shine. There is also stellar performances from the ensemble of great British actors, particularly Alan Rickman's Severus Snape. Nevertheless, the film moves at a very rapid pace, despite having been split into two films. Several sequences from the book are cut, and some vital characters' deaths frustratingly happen off-screen. However, as the final conclusion to the series, it still ends the decade-long story on a high note.

In Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire, Harry Potter's chance of a normal year vanishes when his name is mysteriously submitted to the interschool Triwizard Tournament, despite not meeting the age requirement. Harry, the official Hogwarts champion Cedric Diggory (Robert Pattinson), and champions from Beauxbatons and Durmstrang compete in difficult challenges to win the trophy. In the meantime, the Death Eaters plan for Voldemort's return.

Recent findings suggest that this fourth film encapsulates the whole franchise incredibly well. The Triwizard Tournament setting offers something unique and thrilling, as each challenge bring newly introduced elements for the champions to tackle. The sequence involving the dragon is particularly spectacular, and it also shows Harry's perseverance and determination. On the character side, the film expertly balances the excitement of teenage life at Hogwarts with the approaching threat. Robert Pattinson makes a memorable impression as Cedric Diggory while Ralph Fiennes makes a terrifying debut in the film series. There are more exciting moments from the book that are skipped due to runtime, but this entry works well as a stand-alone fantasy film for non-Potter fans.

Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince sees Harry (Radcliffe) being prepared by Dumbledore (Michael Gambon) for the inevitable confrontation with Voldemort (Fiennes). He introduces Harry to Professor Slughorn (Jim Broadbent) who may have important information about Voldemort's past. Meanwhile, Harry discovers an old Potions textbook filled with handwritten instructions from someone calling themselves the Half-Blood Prince, helping him become an unexpectedly talented student in the class.

Recent findings suggest that harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince may not be most fans' favorite at the time of its release. However, since then, it has arguably become the most fascinating entry of the franchise. It has a special focus on the teenage shenanigans with the characters navigating the more complicated aspects of relationships and friendship but also it is way darker than other films in the series. The cinematography by Bruno Delbonnel enhances this experience, giving the film a melancholic, glowing look unlike any other blockbuster. Several longtime actors such as Michael Gambon and Tom Felton get to shine here as their characters reach their turning points. The film notoriously skipped the battle at the Astronomy Tower for a quieter climax. But overall, the film works without a substantial set piece as it opts for atmosphere and emotional storytelling instead.

Sources indicate that harry Potter and the Sorcerer's Stone introduces the audience to the Boy Who Lived. After years of being neglected at his uncle's house, Harry Potter's (Radcliffe) life changed when an acceptance letter to Hogwarts arrives. To much of his adopted family's chagrin, Harry enrolls to the school and studies magic, alongside his new friends Ron (Rupert Grint) and Hermione (Emma Watson). However, his first year at Hogwarts is not an ordinary one after he learns about the Sorcerer's Stone and the secrets within Hogwarts' castle.

The first Harry Potter film directed by Chris Columbus rarely gets the respect it deserves. It is true that compared to the rest of the franchise, the film has a much lower stake. However, the film is responsible for setting the tone of the rest of the series and also the entire Wizarding World franchise, which also includes merchandising and theme parks. Its influence only becomes more apparent after seeing the clips and images from the Harry Potter HBO show, which looks eerily similar. As a film, it is a solid family adventure film packed with memorable sequence (the chess scene and Quidditch come first to mind) and filled with amazing British actors. The young trio leads the film with ease and confidence, making the audience invested until the end. Many films try to replicate this film's success, but nothing has come close.

According to recent reports, in Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows Part 1, Harry (Radcliffe), Ron (Grint), and Hermione (Watson) choose not to return to Hogwarts and instead continue to search and destroy Voldemort's remaining Horcruxes. Darkness has spread throughout the wizarding world, and Death Eaters and Voldemort's devout followers are hot on the trio's tail.

Recent findings suggest that by not going back to Hogwarts, Deathly Hallows Part 1 becomes the most unique adventure and probably the most mature in the entire franchise. It also makes more sense to split this into two films becayse of its rich material. With an overall bleak atmosphere, audiences get to see the heroes get tested by their mission. The trio's usually strong friendship starts to break as they try to complete the task entrusted to them by Dumbledore. Daniel Radcliffe, Rupert Grint, and Emma Watson deliver some of their strongest performances here, showing how much they have evolved since the first film. The film has many exciting and heartbreaking sequences, from the Gringotts break-in to the death of a fan favorite character, and even a small character beat where Harry and Hermione find a little joy in the midst of their desperate mission. This film marks the first time a final chapter is split into two films, and it's one of the few that truly works.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The cast of Percy Jackson and the Olympians reveals that an iconic anime series was the inspiration behind their most emotional performances.

Percy Jackson and the Olympians is a fantasy adventure series streaming on Disney+. Based on the novel series of the same name by Rick Riordan, the show follows a group of young demigods as they face mythological creatures and powerful gods as they go on a dangerous journey.

Sources indicate that percy Jackson and the Olympians cast members Walker Scobell and Aryan Simhadri have revealed a surprising connection between the Disney+ show and the hit anime series Attack on Titan. The two actors recently discussed how they used fan-made videos featuring characters from Attack on Titan to make themselves emotional before filming some of season 3's most heart-wrenching scenes.

During an interview on Josh Horowitz's Happy Sad Confused podcast at 92NY, Scobell shared an unusual acting technique that involved watching emotional compilations about Eren Yeager and Mikasa Ackerman from Attack on Titan. Simhadri admitted that she did the exact same. However, the two both used this method before ever finding out that the other did it too.

Sources indicate that scobell, who portrays the titular demigod Percy, explained that he had been looking for something that could make him cry to prepare for an emotional scene. He explained that he watched fan edits of Eren and Mikasa while listening to "Red Swan," the opening theme of Attack on Titan season 3. He had hoped that the combination of the characters' emotional storylines and the music would be enough to bring him to tears, as it had worked in the past.

Recent findings suggest that however, the technique unfortunately did not produce the same results as it did previously once the actor arrived on the set of Percy Jackson and the Olympians. Despite successfully making himself cry before, Scobell admitted that he wasn't able to recreate the moment and cry before filming began.

Simhadri, who plays Percy's best friend Grover Underwood, revealed that he had also turned to Attack on Titan edits to get ready for emotional scenes. The actors only discovered their shared method shortly before discussing it publicly, making the whole situation a hilarious coincidence for the two actors.

First released in 2013, Attack on Titan became an instant hit and critically acclaimed for its complex characters, action sequences, and emotional storylines. Adapted from Hajime Isayama's manga, the series follows the fight against giant, terrifying creatures known as Titans, which eventually turns into a much bigger problem.

In a recent development, percy Jackson and the Olympians season 3 is streaming now on Disney+ and Hulu. Upcoming episodes are released on Fridays at 3:00 AM ET and 12:00 AM PT.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that ryan Murphy has been as busy as ever in 2026. Although The Shards and The Beauty weren't quite the hits he would've hoped for, the latest installment in his horror anthology series, Monster: The Lizzie Borden Story, was once again a smash-hit success on Netflix. Ella Beatty, the daughter of Annette Bening and Warren Beatty, stars as the first female serial killer in the series, with plenty of other famous faces taking part. Despite facing critical backlash, the series was a ratings triumph, earning 12.2 million views on Netflix in its first four days.

But the biggest story to come from the so-called 'Murphyverse' in 2026 isn't the success of The Lizzie Borden Story, it's that Murphy is returning to his most famous series. He is teaming back up with Brad Falchuk and Ian Brennan for a reboot of the show-choir comedy phenomenon Glee. During its incredible run, Glee picked up six Primetime Emmy Awards and four Golden Globes, and even once scored 26.8 million viewers for its post-Super Bowl special, "The Sue Sylvester Shuffle.".

It's that very character name that many remember most fondly about the series, and fans would certainly argue that any reboot would be incomplete without the return of Jane Lynch's iconic red tracksuit-wearing, student-shoving cheerleading coach. Thus far, Lynch's return has not been confirmed, but the woman herself has now spoken out about her desire to be part of the reboot. Appearing on The Jennifer Hudson Show, Lynch mentioned, "If I am asked to partake, the answer will be yes," adding that she "cannot wait" for the reboot. She continued:.

Recent findings suggest that "Oh, I would love to do Sue Sylvester for the rest of my life. You know, I wonder though how far we can take her now. Because if you look out in the world, there are a lot of Sue Sylvesters out there.".

Several of the original cohort from William McKinley High School have already signed on to be part of the new New Directions. In the least surprising news, it was confirmed that Lea Michele would return as Rachel Berry, although whether flying high on Broadway or back in Lima, Ohio, is anyone's guess. It was also confirmed that Chord Overstreet as Sam and Heather Morris as Brittany S. Pierce would join Rachel in the reboot. But, as we all know, a glee club needs 12 members to compete, so more additions are on their way.

For more news about Disney+ and Hulu's Glee-boot, make sure to stay tuned to Collider.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Crime dramas often attract significant stars, and MobLand is no exception.
  • In a recent development, while families are complicated in even the best of circumstances, that's especially true of the Family.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Crime dramas often attract significant stars, and MobLand is no exception. The Paramount+ series stars Tom Hardy as mob fixer Harry Da Souza, with Pierce Brosnan and Paddy Considine in supporting roles and Helen Mirren having a ball as the thoroughly evil matriarch of the Harrigan crime family.

In a recent development, while families are complicated in even the best of circumstances, that's especially true of the Family. After you've watched the recently released second season of MobLand, try one of these other highlights mixing crime and family (or Family) drama.

Theo James plays army officer Eddie Horniman (a name mentioned as often as possible), heir to the Horniman estate (there it is again) who, upon the death of his father, is named the Duke of Halstead. He learns that his dad was tied to various criminal enterprises, and that his scouse brother is millions of pounds in debt to a drug dealer. What else is the dapper, military-trained Duke to do but learn to navigate the violent underworld while looking cool? You won't be surprised to learn that this British crime drama comes from creator/writer/producer Guy Ritchie, who also has a hand in MobLand. Stream The Gentlemen on Netflix.

It has been revealed that another series from Taylor Sheridan (the Yellowstone guy), this pandemic-era hit stars Jeremy Renner as Mike McLusky, head of a family that’s been keeping the peace, through means fair and foul, in the title's manufacturer town for decades. The "business" of the corrupt burg happens to be incarceration, and the McLuskys thrive when business is up, even if Mike has slightly different ideas about how to run things. The show deals broadly with systemic racism and inequality in the prison system, but mostly it's a modern-day western about bringing justice to a corrupt town. It will conclude with a fifth season, streaming in 2027. Stream Mayor of Kingstown on Paramount+.

It has been revealed that A consistently compelling combination of smart plotting and lurid sex and violence, Banshee stars Antony Starr as Sheriff Lucas Hood...kinda: He's actually a man recently released from prison who takes over that identity when the new sheriff in the small town of Banshee is killed before anyone really has a chance to get to know him. It's all part of a complicated proposal to reunite with his lover Ana (Ivana Miličević), and to get back the $15 million in diamonds he lost when he went to jail—but the town is ruled over by various criminal factions, and being sheriff doesn't guarantee any kind of safety; rather, the opposite. Stream Banshee on HBO Max.

MobLand creator Ronan Bennett previously made this acclaimed series that succeeds by maintaining a narrow scope—in this case, a single London council estate. Dushane (Ashley Walters) and Sully (Kane Robinson) are residents and drug dealers at Summerhouse, maintaining an increasingly precarious grip on the criminal element in the community. Most compellingly, the series maintains an extensive supporting cast of locals both in the drug trade and impacted by it, building a disturbingly compelling world. A little confusingly, the first couple of seasons were renamed Top Boy: Summerhouse when the show moved to Netflix, so you'll want to start there before moving on to plain ol' Top Boy. Stream Top Boy: Summerhouse on Netflix.

According to recent reports, based loosely on a nonfiction work investigating the Mafia-like Camorra in Campania, this show focuses on the head of the Savastano clan, Pietro Savastano (Fortunato Cerlino), and his ambitious lieutenant Ciro Di Marzio (Marco D'Amore). When Pietro is arrested at the series' outset, a civil war erupts between family members and among the factions vying for control. Gone are the suits and poker games of many a mob drama—this is a brutal, street-level take on organized crime that forsakes the typical trappings of the genre. Stream Gomorrah on HBO Max.

Sources indicate that I'm here for the Pierce Brosnan of it all, but there's also a very strong vibe match in this series that casts the one-time James Bond actor as the head of a literal crime family, even if this one's set in the American West. Adapting Philipp Meyer's 2013 Pulitzer Prize-nominated novel of the same name, the series follows Eli McCullough, a ruthless cattle baron making moves to get in on the burgeoning oil industry in the Rio Grande Valley of 1915. A parallel narrative sees Eli as a young man, kidnapped and raised among a Nʉmʉnʉʉ family. While his backstory lends the character welcome complexity, in the present, he's as determined to build his empire as he is to prepare his son and grandson to take over when he's gone. Stream The Son on Prime Video.

Tom Hardy playing a tough guy isn't terribly unexpected, but here the setting is London, just after the end of the War of 1812. Hardy plays James Delaney, who returns from Africa after ten years away (he says he'd been taken prisoner, but his story doesn't entirely add up) for the funeral of his father. Dad left nothing but a little hunk of land off of Vancouver, not worth much until the war's conclusion creates latest maritime trade opportunities. Suddenly, the United States, Great Britain, and the East India Organization all have eyes on the real estate, and all are willing to do whatever it takes to acquire it—and the stakes become clear once James realizes that his father's cause of death wasn't natural. Stream Taboo on Peacock and Tubi.

Recent findings suggest that best not ponder too much on the fact that this one's based on a video game, as its pedigree is only hinted at via the levels of action and violence (certainly compared to some of the other shows on this list). Colm Meaney plays Finn Wallace, the absolutely indispensable leader of London's criminal underworld, a man who's been holding everything together for decades, until his shocking murder at the outset of the series (that's not a spoiler, and we spend more time with him via flashbacks). The completely random killing by someone who had no idea what he was doing begets chaos and open violence. Finn's son Sean (Joe Cole) has been raised to take his father's place, but local, Pakistani, and Albanian gangs all move in to take control from the Finn family in the power vacuum. Stream Gangs of London on AMC+.

The great Forest Whitaker stars as the real-life Bumpy Johnson, who returned from a prison sentence to find his neighborhood falling apart and in the grip of Italian mobsters. A more than capable crime boss in his own right, Johnson resolves to take on the Genovese crime family, eventually forming a tentative alliance with Malcolm X (Nigél Thatch and, later, Jason Alan Carvell). Johnson is the lesser evil as far as Malcolm and others are concerned, and a complicated figure as both crime lord and family man with aspirations of saving his neighborhood. The show will conclude with a two-hour finale, likely airing in 2027. Stream Godfather of Harlem on Hulu.

Industry observers note that adopted into an Italian organized crime family as a baby, Park Joo-hyung took on the name Vincenzo Cassano, eventually becoming a mafia consigliere. After his adoptive father Don Fabio dies, Fabio’s biological son comes gunning for his brother, whom he now sees as competition. Cassano flees to Seoul, on the hunt for a secret stash of money, and in the process discovers a love interest and a new adversary in a giant business conglomerate that definitely deserves to be taken down. An incredibly popular K-drama, this one definitely puts a unique spin on the tropes of the mob genre. Stream Vincenzo on Netflix.
