💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, grand Theft Auto VI offers a size befitting the 13-year wait.
  • Like millions of gamers worldwide, I dived into the game at midnight, the very second it unlocked on my PS5 Pro.
  • So, if you’re heading to Leonida over the weekend, here are three major mistakes I've already made, and most importantly, how you can avoid doing the same stupid things as me (all spoiler-free).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, grand Theft Auto VI offers a size befitting the 13-year wait. Not only is the Vice City map absolutely huge, but it’s the most system-rich and mechanically deep game in the Grand Theft Auto series to date. There’s an overwhelming amount of things to see, do, and learn.

Like millions of gamers worldwide, I dived into the game at midnight, the very second it unlocked on my PS5 Pro. I’ve since put five hours of playtime into GTA 6, and while I’m still getting my head around all that the game has to offer (my completion percentage is a mere 12%), I’ve already learnt a few lessons the hard way. Yes, mistakes have been made.

So, if you’re heading to Leonida over the weekend, here are three major mistakes I've already made, and most importantly, how you can avoid doing the same stupid things as me (all spoiler-free). Learn from my errors!

After 13 years of waiting, Grand Theft Auto VI has arrived. Set in the state of Leonida, with Vice City at its heart, you play Jason and Lucia, two criminals forced into an increasingly dangerous situation as they seek their fortune, discovering the darker side of the sunniest spot in America.

Sources indicate that GTA 6 introduces a fresh money system in which you can hold cash either on your person or stashed securely at your safehouse. If you get “wasted” or “busted” by the cops, you’ll lose all the money you’re carrying, but the funds kept under the floorboards at Jason's beachside home are protected.

Industry observers note that as a cautious type, I took this to mean never carry any money on your person for fear of losing it, which pretty quickly proved to be an oversteer when an early mission required me to buy a gun, and I literally had $0 in my wallet. This forced a trip back to the safehouse, where I counted out the exact number of bills required to buy the weapon.

In a recent development, once I returned to the Ammu-nation store, I bought my gun and then was presented with a range of attachments (some with a limited-time discount), which I couldn’t buy because, again, I’d only brought the specific amount required to buy the gun itself. Frustrating.

This taught me not to fear actually carrying money in your wallet. Sure, running about Vice City with your entire bank balance on hand is probably unwise, but you’re going to want, and need, some money in your pocket. At this early stage, I’ve been opting for a 50/50 split, keeping half my ill-gotten gains in my stash, and the other half within instant reach.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

My approach to previous GTA games tended to be this: Complete a few story missions, and then go on a psychotic rampage to blow off some steam (I swear I’m not a total psycho).

According to recent reports, GTA 6 is different. For pretty much the first time in the franchise’s history, the game actively discourages you from causing carnage without purpose through the fresh “Criminal Profile” system. Your in-game actions are tracked and contribute to the type of criminal Jason (and later Lucia) is becoming. Ranging from a “professional” all the way to a full-blown “psycho.”.

Sources indicate that during my first GTA 6 session, after completing the mandatory prologue, I decided to see how many wanted stars I could rack up with just the starter pistol, and pretty quickly the game warned me that my criminal spree would have consequences. It felt like that old Tellale’s The Walking Dead warning message, “Clementine will remember that…”.

Rockstar has confirmed your “Criminal Profile” will impact how the story plays out, and I certainly don’t want to receive a “bad” ending; such was my concern about how my early game rampage would impact how my GTA 6 story plays out, I opted to reload to a previous save to instantly wash away the worrying amount of blood already on Jason’s hands.

It has been revealed that so, in GTA 6, it pays to show restraint. You will commit many crimes, of course, but resist the urge to go full GTA and instead commit your criminal acts with purpose and even planning.

Recent findings suggest that speaking of planning, from what I’ve played so far, GTA 6 is the most ambitious Grand Theft Auto yet in all areas, including mission design. Previous GTA games present players with cinematic but largely linear missions; if you tried to get creative, the game would quickly shepherd you back onto the golden path with instant fail states for any deviations.

To be clear, GTA 6 does have these types of missions as well, but there’s a larger focus on player choice and letting you pick your approach. As an early (spoiler-free) example, a Chapter 1 mission asks you to retrieve a red sports car from a police impound lot.

According to recent reports, you’re dropped off right outside the main gate, with an on-screen prompt encouraging you to break the lock. Naturally, I obliged, and the impound’s alarms started blaring; every cop in the area was instantly alerted, and the mission pretty much went further south from there.

One reload later, I was back at the mission start, and this time, I slowed down. I cased the joint first, walking the perimeter, trying to find a subtler way to access the impound lot. And what do you know, a conveniently placed scissor lift around the corner got me onto the roof, allowing me to quietly drop into the compound without setting off any alarms or alert cops.

It’s a reminder that in GTA 6, thinking before you act can pay off, and when you factor in the “Criminal Profile” system, there is real merit in completing missions without having to shoot your way out of trouble.

GTA 6’s 30 FPS lock broke my PC gamer brain — until I turned on the one TV setting I swore I’d never touch

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (944 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tomsguide

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • If you’ve ever bought a new TV and invited a tech nerd like me into your living room, you already know I’m grabbing your remote, diving into the picture settings, and disabling motion smoothing.
  • Sources indicate that for movies and prestige TV, it is a crime against humanity — turning a cinematic masterpiece into an episode of "Days of Our Lives" shot on a camcorder.
  • And yet, here I am, playing Grand Theft Auto VI with motion smoothing cranked on, and refusing to turn it off.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you’ve ever bought a new TV and invited a tech nerd like me into your living room, you already know I’m grabbing your remote, diving into the picture settings, and disabling motion smoothing.

Sources indicate that for movies and prestige TV, it is a crime against humanity — turning a cinematic masterpiece into an episode of "Days of Our Lives" shot on a camcorder. I hate it. Tom Cruise hates it. You should hate it too.

And yet, here I am, playing Grand Theft Auto VI with motion smoothing cranked on, and refusing to turn it off.

To understand how I ended up committing TV heresy, you have to understand the shock to the system that is GTA 6’s frame rate. Coming straight from my monster PC rig playing games like Resident Evil Requiem at up to 214 FPS, dropping back down to a strict 30 FPS console lock feels like wading through treacle.

Industry observers note that but on top of that, as I’ve seen (and you’ve seen on Digital Foundry’s test), that 30 FPS lock isn’t an actual lock. It can dip into the mid-20s during heavy scenes. Coming from super fluidity, that 30 FPS is brutal to adapt to.

So out of sheer desperation (and because we’re stuck waiting for the PC port), I broke the golden rule and toggled my TV’s smooth motion setting on.

And I hate to admit it, but it’s basically bootleg DLSS Frame Generation for your living room.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

Just like PC frame generation tricks of old, your TV’s motion interpolation processor looks at two real frames from your console, guesses what should happen in between them, and inserts an artificial frame to smooth out the motion.

Recent findings suggest that the moment I flipped it on in GTA 6, that nauseating camera stutter when cruising down Ocean Beach vanished. Panning around a crowded street or taking a high-speed corner suddenly felt dramatically more fluid — nowhere near 60 fps, and definitely not my desktop rig, but miles smoother than the choppy presentation.

It has been revealed that before the AV forums come for my head with pitchforks, let’s be completely honest about the trade-offs. There is no such thing as a free lunch in frame interpolation:.

Because your TV has to wait for the next frame before it can invent the one in the middle, motion smooth adds latency between pressing a button and seeing the result on screen. In twitchy, competitive games, that’s a death sentence.

But in a Rockstar open-world game — where character movement is already famously weighty and deliberate — I never noticed that extra latency.

It has been revealed that your TV’s processor is just guessing after all, and while it is a good guesser, there are some moments of weird shimmering around fast-moving objects and some boiling around on-screen elements like subtitles. Probably compounded by the fact GTA 6 is already running its own resolution scaling tech under the hood.

Standard Game Mode and VRR (Variable Refresh Rate) automatically lock out motion smoothing on many TVs. Depending on your set, you either have to turn on the dedicated low-latency Game Motion Plus mode (found on newer Samsung and LG sets) or sacrifice VRR to unlock it.

The silver lining, though, is that with this being a 30 FPS game, it’s not high enough to require VRR anyway.

If GTA 6’s 30 FPS cap is giving your eyes a workout and you want to test the dark arts yourself, don’t just blindly max out every slider.

If your TV has a low-latency interpolation option (like Samsung’s Game Motion Plus or LG’s TruMotion tweaks), use that before turning off Game Mode completely.

Recent findings suggest that set Judder Reduction to a middle ground (around 5-7 out of 10) rather than maxing it out. You want to take the harsh edge off camera pans without turning your car into a blurry smudge.

This is optional based on personal taste. Test how your TV’s smoothing looks with GTA’s built-in motion blur turned off. For a lot of OLED owners, letting the TV handle the smoothing cleanly beats stacking two different blur effects on top of each other.

Do I want to play GTA 6 at native 240 FPS on my PC rig? Obviously. The second Rockstar drops the PC version, I’ll be uninstalling this hack from my brain and never looking back.

According to recent reports, I still wouldn’t be caught dead watching a movie with motion smoothing turned on. But until PC gamers get their turn in Vice City, breaking the ultimate TV rule is the best survival trick I’ve found for making a 30 FPS masterpiece actually feel better to play.

Also yes, my wife has taken note of the fact that I share the same name as the male protagonist. And yes, she is side-eyeing how I treat Lucia hard.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Vanessa Piña has been writing as a journalist for over two years. As a senior writer, she focuses on timely coverage of the latest anime releases and popular comic franchises.

When it comes to works that explore the differences between humans and robots, the first name that comes to mind is likely Isaac Asimov, one of the world's most acclaimed science fiction authors. While many of Asimov’s stories have been adapted for the screen, such as Apple TV's Foundation series, Netflix’s catalog also features a single-season masterpiece that draws significant inspiration from his writing and brilliantly incorporates the principles that he proposed in his book I, Robot.

The first principle of the "Three Laws of Robotics," devised by Isaac Asimov, states that a robot must not injure human beings. In I, Robot, Asimov uses these rules, which are embedded in the robots as basic instincts, to craft a compelling mystery centered on the loopholes that could lead these machines to cause harm. The 2023 Netflix anime series Pluto also centers its narrative on this premise, presenting a future society where technology has advanced to the point where AI robots have become fully integrated into human life until one of them is linked to a series of murders.

Recent findings suggest that pluto is a reinterpretation by Naoki Urasawa, creator of Monster, of the "The Greatest Robot on Earth" story arc from Osamu Tezuka's Astro Boy. Darker and more introspective than Astro Boy, rather than a typical murder mystery focused on identifying a culprit or a human versus robot war, Pluto explores the blurred lines between humanity and artificial intelligence, much like Isaac Asimov's works. Beyond these parallels to Asimov's work, Pluto also draws heavily from the philosophical themes of Ghost in the Shell, one of the major cyberpunk franchises in history.

Industry observers note that in Pluto, robots enjoy rights similar to those of human beings: they have jobs, get married, and can take vacations. There are even advanced models that are indistinguishable from humans at first glance. The series then follows special investigator Gesicht, who discovers that both robots and humans are being targeted by a killer who leaves behind the same signature mark. As the investigation unfolds, the murders reveal a far-reaching scheme targeting the seven most advanced robots in the world.

Industry observers note that this coexistence between humans and robots, the dangers of AI spiraling out of control, and even details like robots being capable of dreaming strongly resemble works by Isaac Asimov, such as Robot Dreams. Pluto also uses these machines to propose profound philosophical questions, such as what truly defines humanity, a theme it also shares with Ghost in the Shell. Another thing they have in common is that both stories take place in a futuristic setting, within a society that treats individuals' memories and visual information as digital data.

According to recent reports, while in Ghost in the Shell, cybernetically enhanced individuals challenge humanity's boundaries, Pluto delves into whether machines programmed to mimic feelings can develop a "true heart" to the point of experiencing negative emotions such as grief and hatred. Furthermore, both Pluto and works like Ghost in the Shell: Stand Alone Complex peel back the layers of a larger conspiracy, digging into military conflicts, political intrigue, and moral dilemmas with a similar mature tone. Yet Pluto is mostly a slow-paced thriller, introducing the lives of various robots while inviting the viewer to reflect on what it is that makes life.

In a recent development, what's fascinating about the sci-fi genre is not always seeing creative future technologies but rather observing how humanity itself is shaped in response to it. In Pluto, for instance, robots are simultaneously treated as humans (mourned and respected) and viewed as potential weapons of mass destruction. That way, the series focuses on depicting trauma, the consequences of war, and discrimination from the perspective of these robots, adding a deep psychological layer that presents contradictions and truly embodies the philosophy behind robotics advancements.

According to recent reports, on the other hand, longtime fans of the sci-fi genre will notice that characters from Astro Boy, such as Atom and Dr. Tenma, appear in Pluto, accompanied by numerous references that those familiar with the classic anime will surely recognize. Even so, since these figures serve as secondary characters in Pluto, the series remains fully enjoyable even for those unfamiliar with the original story or the anime industry in general. That's because Pluto is a masterpiece that excels in every respect, from its visual quality, action sequences, and narrative to its well-developed characters, having established itself as one of the best short anime series of the past decade.

Recent findings suggest that across its eight episodes, each approximately an hour long, Pluto gradually unfolds its core mystery, offering a highly satisfying resolution as its various subplots converge. Thus, while it may feel heavy at times (as is often the case with slow-burn crime series), Pluto constitutes an ideal choice for binge-watching, as it is difficult to look away once it begins to unravel its story, being a thought-provoking work that will undoubtedly stir viewers' emotions just like the writings of Isaac Asimov or the universe of Ghost in the Shell.

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 2m • 📖 Standard (488 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚠️ Warning 🌐 Lifehacker ↗ Open Full Page

'Ghost Accounts' Are Putting Your Security at Risk, but You Can Protect Yourself

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (488 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Lifehacker

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that these so-called "ghost accounts"—all the old, forgotten logins that are still active but not in use—could expose your data in the event of a breach, increasing the risk of your information being used in malicious ways.
  • As McAfee describes, ghost accounts may retain lots of sensitive data, such as your contact details (phone numbers, emails, and addresses), purchase histories, payment details, and passwords.
  • Recent findings suggest that you're less likely to be keeping tabs on activity in older accounts, which may also have weak or reused passwords that haven't been updated in years.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that these so-called "ghost accounts"—all the old, forgotten logins that are still active but not in use—could expose your data in the event of a breach, increasing the risk of your information being used in malicious ways. That's why it's important to go through the effort to find and delete dormant accounts. Here's how to get started.

As McAfee describes, ghost accounts may retain lots of sensitive data, such as your contact details (phone numbers, emails, and addresses), purchase histories, payment details, and passwords. While this doesn't mean your information is sure to be compromised, the more places it lives, the more opportunities there are for bad actors to get ahold of it.

Recent findings suggest that you're less likely to be keeping tabs on activity in older accounts, which may also have weak or reused passwords that haven't been updated in years. If that organization or service experiences a data breach, not only is your stored data there exposed, but that information (including your password) can be used to access other accounts using tactics like credential stuffing and phishing. This also increases the risk of identity theft, as threat actors can use your name, birth date, and other information to open fraudulent accounts.

According to recent reports, unfortunately, finding and removing forgotten accounts can be tedious. If you have a password manager, the easiest way to start is to audit older items as well as look at security reports that identify weak or reused passwords, as well as data breaches that have impacted your accounts. If you've saved credentials in your browser keychain, go through the same process to find dormant accounts.

According to recent reports, next, audit accounts you've created using single sign-on, such as Google, Apple, or Facebook. For Google, this is under Account Settings > Linked apps. For Apple, go to System Settings > [Your Name] > Sign in with Apple on your Mac (or the same path in the Settings app on iOS). On Facebook, this is under Settings & privacy > Apps and websites. Disconnecting these accounts won't automatically delete them, but you can add them to the list to take action. Finally, you can search your email(s) on HaveIBeenPwned and username(s) on IDCrawl or WhatsMyName to find dormant accounts.

Recent findings suggest that once you've found accounts you no longer use, the next step is to deactivate or delete them, which you may be able to do through the settings or by reaching out to customer support. At the very least, remove all identifying information and change the password, and if possible, patch the address to a burner using your browser's or password manager's hide-my-email feature. If you no longer have access to an old account, that doesn't mean it's been deactivated and your information removed, so you may need to reach out to customer support to find out how to access and delete it.

  • According to recent reports, to rank Christmas Carols, you have to decide what A Christmas Carol is to you.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Charles Dickens’ A Christmas Carol is the greatest story about Christmas ever written—even better than the one with Mary and Joseph and the manger. The 1843 tale of a miser browbeaten by self-righteous ghosts is (probably) the most filmed story of all time. Dozens of cinematic adaptations of A Christmas Carol have been released in theaters and on TV since Scrooge; or Marley's Ghost came out in 1901. Hundreds or thousands if you count re-imaginings and very special episodes of sitcoms. But which version is the very best?

I've carefully considered every major theatrical and TV adaptation of A Christmas Carol and rated each in terms of holiday spirit, Dickensian whimsy, and Scrooge-osity to arrive at the definite, no-argument-possible best-to-worst list of Christmas Carols.

According to recent reports, to rank Christmas Carols, you have to decide what A Christmas Carol is to you. My criteria for inclusion: It has to be full-length (at least around an hour long); it has to have been released widely, either in theaters, on network television, or through a larger streaming service, and it has to be fairly close to a direct adaptation—modernizations, re-imaginings, sequels, and that episode of The Six Million Dollar Man don’t count (sorry, Scrooged fans). Using those criteria, I’ve winnowed the Carols down to the 17 you see below, ranked from best to worst, along with where you can stream each one.

It's tough to pick a single adaptation of A Christmas Carol as the absolute best of all time, but the 1984 TV movie version starring George C. Scott is unassailable. Other versions do some things better, but this one does everything right—no mistakes. It stays close to the original text; it's perfectly produced; and it has a consistency of tone and vision that makes it the most balanced of all versions of the story. A Christmas Carol might not have the best Scrooge of all time, but George C. Scott's performance is a solid nine out of ten, and this version features the most adorable and pitiable Tiny Tim of all and the best Ghost of Christmas Present, played by Edward Woodward, who played the policeman in The Wicker Man.

Where to stream it: Roku, Tubi, Pluto TV.

Shot in the midst of the Great Depression, the first sound version of A Christmas Carol digs deeper into the despair and horror of the story than any other adaptation. It’s a bleak, German expressionist Christmas flick, and Seymour Hicks’ sickly, haunted portrayal of Ebenezer Scrooge fits the tone perfectly. Instead of delighting in his own crapulence, Hicks plays Scrooge like Satan in The Divine Comedy—he's not the ruler of Hell; he's its most tormented prisoner. Scrooge's miserliness is played as pathology. He wears dirty, torn clothing and shivers miserably while eating gruel because he can’t bring himself to burn a single scrap of coal. Even when he converts, it seems like a manic episode instead of Christmas spirit, suggesting this could be a story about an old man going mad.

Where to stream: Sadly, the version on free streaming services like Tubi and Plex is colorized, but you can watch it on YouTube in glorious black and white.

This massive-budget musical take on the Yuletide classic turns Dickens up to 11. Scrooge is huge, a raucous, crowd-pleasing musical with hundreds of extras, elaborate sets, and a scenery-chewing central performance from Albert Finney to hold it all together. But Finney and company also manage to keep the emotional core of the story intact. The music is great, with memorable tunes like “I Hate People,” a song that Finney snarls instead of sings. Scrooge has the best ghosts of any version of A Christmas Carol, too—you can't beat the cheesy awesomeness of big-money 1970s special effects.

Where to stream it: Tubi, Pluto TV, Plex.

Before Hallmark devoted its corporate life to forgettable holiday-themed romantic comedies, it co-produced one of the best versions of A Christmas Carol ever made. This entire movie belongs to Patrick Stewart, whose nuanced, layered portrayal of Scrooge is the best that has ever been done. His "conversion" scene is so visceral and honest, it brought a tear to my eyes, even though I've seen the exact scene performed in at least 40 other movies, stage plays, and episodes of 1980s sitcoms. Sadly, the paucity of basic cable budgets in the 1990s results in some chintzy-looking sets and laughable special effects that mar an otherwise top-notch production.

Where to stream it: Digital rental only.

Sources indicate that horror director Ti West's Carol adaptation muddies the moral clarity of Dickens' tale and suggests there's something deeply troubling beneath all the Victorian holiday catharsis. With a few exceptions, Ebenezer hits the familiar beats of A Christmas Carol: It delivers the crowd-pleasing rich-jerk-turns-good story moviegoers expect, but West layers in subtle hints along the way that suggest the floorboards are rotten, and if you dance with Christmas joy too hard, you'll fall into the dark basement below. Ebenezer seems to whisper to audiences, "How much does the conversion of one miserly wretch matter in the face of systemic injustice? And isn't he going to snap out of it when the fright wears off anyway?" Bonus: As you'd probably expect from a Ti West movie, the ghosts are genuinely scary.

Where to watch it: In theaters now.

I'm sticking A Muppet Christmas Carol randomly here on the list because you can't reasonably compare it to other versions of the story. The Muppet version is a thing unto itself. Like the Ol' Dirty Bastard, its style has no father. A Muppet Christmas Carol is absolutely delightful from start to finish, for children, grown-ups, cats, dogs, space aliens, and anything else you got. It shouldn't even work to set Michael Caine's serious portrayal of Ebenezer Scrooge against a supporting cast of puppets, but somehow it all seems natural.

In a recent development, alastair Sim takes Ebenezer Scrooge on a real journey in this movie. In the first act, he plays Scrooge like Capitalism personified, an uncaring, amoral monument to pure acquisition. He seems like a Scrooge who'd scare away ghosts, but when Marley demonstrates up dragging his trademark chains, Sim is instantly reduced to pop-eyed fear, like the single chink in his armor is the supernatural. Scrooge then regresses to a childlike, bashful figure as ghosts lead him to different visions, finally emerging from his symbolic death to his rebirth as a Christmas-obsessed guy who lives to serve others. This movie might be among the best of the genre, but an unnecessary subplot about Scrooge's business sandbags the movie through part of the second act.

According to recent reports, mr. Magoo's Christmas Carol was the first animated version of A Christmas Carol and the first animated holiday special ever shown on American TV. The main character, Mr. Magoo, was the star of a one-joke, limited-animation cartoon popular in the early 1960s about an old man who couldn’t see very well, so it’s surprising how carefully crafted and effective this version of A Christmas Carol is. It's weirdly meta too: Jim Backus voices Mr. Magoo, who is a (blind) actor performing as Scrooge in A Christmas Carol on Broadway, so the play is bookended with "this guy can't see!" bits. The songs are strange, memorable and funny (listen to "Razzleberry Dressing" above once and you'll never forget it), but the emotional core of the story remains surprisingly powerful. Jim Backus is amazing.

Where to stream it: Peacock, Roku, Tubi.

Industry observers note that I'm breaking my own rule about not including shortened versions of the story because this animated Carol is that great. Its evocative, graceful, hand-drawn look belongs to animation legend Richard Williams and was inspired by the illustrations from the original version of A Christmas Carol. It's a cartoon, but it's not a kiddie cartoon, so the darkness of the ghosts isn't glossed over. Plus, Scrooge is voiced by Alastair Sim, reprising his role from 1951's Scrooge.

Sources indicate that there's nothing wrong with this brightly lit, by-the-numbers take on A Christmas Carol, but it seems designed to appeal to as broad an audience as possible, so the rough edges of the story have been sanded off. The ghosts aren’t that scary. Scrooge isn’t that miserly, etc. It’s fine for a Christmas movie to be lighthearted fun, but the lowered stakes ultimately blunt the emotional resonance of the climax, leading to a mediocre Christmas Carol.

I'm including this version of A Christmas Carol because it's Lifehacker editor Meghan Walbert's favorite. Sorry, Meghan, but this flimsy 1970s TV movie adaptation hasn't aged well. Henry Winkler does a good job as Scrooge, and it's cool to see Burgess Meredith and other old-timey stars, but overall, this is a schmaltzy, plodding film that unwisely replaces a lot of Dickens' best writing with the work of 1970s TV hacks.

Where to stream it: Pluto, Tubi, Amazon Prime.

Sources indicate that I really wanted to like Disney’s A Christmas Carol. Robert Zemeckis is a great director and Jim Carrey is a force of nature, but I couldn't get through it. There might be a lot to recommend this version of the story, but using 2009’s technology to create realistic-looking characters was such a puzzling choice. The whole movie looks like a video game cutscene from a PS3 game, and I kept wanting to hit “A” to skip ahead to the gameplay.

It doesn't seem like the producers of this obscure 2012 straight-to-streaming feature had much money to work with, which is too bad. If they had, they might have been able to better realize some of the intriguing ideas behind this movie. It's a straight-up horror take on the tale, but it just isn't scary. Sadly, you can't carry a feature film on good intentions. Overall, a swing and a miss.

Where to stream it: Tubi, Amazon Prime.

The animation in this 1997 musical cartoon version of A Christmas Carol is dated, pedestrian, and ugly. The songs are forgettable, and Scrooge has a pet bulldog for some reason. (The one good joke is that he named his dog "Debit.") It’s just not good, which is a shame, because the cast is overflowing with talent, including Tim Curry as Scrooge, Ed Asner, and Whoopi Goldberg.

Where to stream it: Roku, Pluto TV, Xumo.

In a recent development, this BBC drama goes for a philosophical, moody version of Scrooge, but it doesn’t come together. It’s dark, grim, and so ponderously self-serious that it collapses under its own weight. In an effort to present aspects of A Christmas Carol that haven't been seen before (like "How Marley got his chains"), A Christmas Carol rewrites the original text from the ground up, but it comes across like Dickens' first draft with a bad case of Surf Dracula.

Where to stream it: Hulu, Disney+.

It has been revealed that the current state of Dickens adaptation is not good. Netflix's uninspired, sappy, CGI version of A Christmas Carol tries to tart the story up with slapstick, songs, and jokes, but it’s all cynical, lowest-common-denominator horseshit. The dialogue has been dumbed down and joked up. Scrooge has a silly dog for comic relief. They added scatological humor. Think about this: The minds behind Scrooge: A Christmas Carol read Dickens and concluded, “This story would be better with a wacky dog and fart jokes.”.

Recent findings suggest that A Christmas Carol is such a solid story, even a grade-school production of it can be fun to watch. But a cynical production of it is extra terrible, given the message of the story. This terrible ego project is a bottom-of-the-barrel Christmas Carol because it feels like a money grab. Kelsey Grammer sucks as Scrooge, mugging his way through a lightweight performance. Jason Alexander sucks as Marley. Jennifer Love Hewitt is, well, actually pretty good as Scrooge’s Christmas-past romantic interest. She is a rare bright spot in this dreary movie, however. Everything else is mid to terrible. It’s shot and lit like a TV show; the sets are bland and the songs forgettable. Overall, it has the cynical feeling of assembly-line, “let’s get this shit over with” TV production.

Where to stream it: Tubi, Pluto TV, Plex.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, while many shows experience shakeups as networks make programming scheduling decisions, Fire Country has enjoyed a pretty stable schedule on CBS since it premiered in the 2023-2024 TV season. The series has remained largely undisturbed because it was a major hit at its premiere and rapidly became a powerhouse anchor for the network's Friday night lineup, airing consistently at 9 pm ET. Co-created and led by SEAL Team fan favorite Max Thieriot as Bode Donovan, the firefighter drama became one of broadcast television's top-performing shows, drawing massive live and streaming audiences each week. Its reliable success and steady Friday night presence even allowed CBS to build an entire franchise around the fictional town of Edgewater, paving the way for its first official spin-off, Sheriff Country.

However, that steady routine is changing dramatically for the 2026–2027 broadcast season. To make room for a more crowded scripted lineup, CBS has shaken up its Friday night schedule and trimmed Fire Country's fifth season to a shortened 13-episode run, down from its usual 20-episode order. Rather than stretching across the traditional fall-to-spring television calendar, the firefighter drama is set to wrap up its season unusually early in February 2027. Once Fire Country concludes its run, Sheriff Country will slide into the 9 p.m. time slot to clear space on the schedule for Matthew Gray Gubler's latest procedural, Einstein.

Some more disappointing news for fans is that there will be no new episode of Fire Country this Friday, November 20. Instead, the series is entering an unexpected four-week fall hiatus, leaving viewers waiting until December 11 for the action in Edgewater to resume. This pause adds to the frustration of an already condensed season, cutting into the show's usual fall momentum just as storylines heat up. While CBS fills the Friday night gap with reruns and holiday programming, loyal viewers will have to be patient to see what emergency next rocks Edgewater and tests Station 42.

You are two steps ahead and you rarely mention it. Bobby is the one who finds the thing that unlocks the case, usually from a desk, usually about ninety seconds before anybody realises they needed it.

Recent findings suggest that you turn up, change the temperature of the room, and leave people arguing about you. Russell is Colter's brother, ex-military, and the show has never once let the audience settle on whether he is a help or a problem, which is exactly why he keeps coming back.

In the December 11 episode titled "Fight the Future," the show picks up continuing storylines, including the latest data center in Edgewater and Sharon's luck. But first, Station 42 races against time to save a man who has been buried in a frozen industrial accident. Meanwhile, Sharon (Diane Farr) finds herself trapped in a desperate life-or-death situation that threatens to expose a dangerous secret. Could this have something to do with the bag of money she found and has used part of, but the owner has come to reclaim?

Shameless: How Old The Characters Are At The Beginning And End Of The Show

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, with all the chaos in the Gallagher household, it can be challenging to keep track of the Shameless characters' ages from the beginning to the end of the show.
  • The Shameless characters' ages are somewhat hard to get a concrete answer on, even though there are some distinctive clues about their ages throughout the show's run.
  • Working out the age of the Gallagher family in Shameless can be difficult thanks to the show's somewhat muddy timeline, but it's not impossible.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, with all the chaos in the Gallagher household, it can be challenging to keep track of the Shameless characters' ages from the beginning to the end of the show. When the comedy-drama series debuted on Showtime in 2011, all the Gallagher kids, except for Fiona, were still minors. By the time the series wrapped up with the season 11 finale in the spring of 2021, all except Liam were adults with jobs and, in some cases, kids of their own, showing the incredible timeline of the long-running show. Shameless, for all of the difficult storylines and painful moments, was a journey for the Gallagher family.

The Shameless characters' ages are somewhat hard to get a concrete answer on, even though there are some distinctive clues about their ages throughout the show's run. There's a distinct division between the younger and older Gallagher siblings, with Fiona, Lip, and Ian being in the older tier, and Debbie, Carl, and Liam in the younger. However, this apparent split does nothing to determine any actual age outside of an abstract idea of what stage of life each of them is in. Regardless, throughout Shameless' 11-season run, some hints and clues are given about the ages of the Gallagher children.

Working out the age of the Gallagher family in Shameless can be difficult thanks to the show's somewhat muddy timeline, but it's not impossible. The ages of the characters in Shameless can be determined thanks to the introduction of Debbie's daughter Franny in season 6. Since Franny was born when Debbie was 15, and celebrates her fifth birthday when Shameless season 11 ends, it's possible to work out the ages of the Gallagher family at the start and end of Shameless using Franny's season 6 birth as a starting point.

The Shameless timeline isn't set in stone, and about nine years pass during the show. This means that there is really no detail about how old they exactly are when the show comes to an end, but there are some good hints about their ages, with almost all of them known at the start. Here's the age of every member of the Gallagher family in Shameless in season 1 and season 11.

Fiona Gallagher is 21 in Shameless season 1, which is set in 2010. This puts her birth year around 1989-1990. She had it tougher than anyone else in the family because she was 16 when her mother walked out on the family. Fiona had to take control and was the one who raised her younger siblings while her father was out drinking and ignoring his responsibilities. She was who her brothers and sisters came to when they needed help, which caused her to lose her independence when she needed to grasp hold of it.

Sources indicate that her father even came to her for help when he got into trouble, and Fiona had to be the grownup in the house despite being a teenager. By the time the show started, she was 21 and still unable to have her own life, as she was still watching out for her siblings. However, she finally had enough and left home in season 9 to finally take control of her own future. She never appeared in the Shameless season finale — set in 2020 — but by that time, she would have been around 30.

Sources indicate that in season 1 of Shameless, Lip Gallagher is 16, meaning he would have been born around 1994. Lip might be the most tragic of all the Gallagher kids. While Fiona was forced to act as a mother when she was still a teenager and raise the kids, Lip was the only one who had a clear way out of this life. He was the smartest of the kids, with a high GPA and a genius-level IQ. However, Lip's worst enemy was himself, as he was irresponsible and self-sabotaging every chance he had to escape.

He was still someone who, at only five years younger than Fiona, was there to help out as he got older, protecting his younger siblings and being someone who was more responsible than his father, even with his own bad traits. Sadly, his sense of abandonment, thanks to his mom leaving and his dad being an absentee authority figure, led to him making bad decisions and ending up with a juvenile criminal record. Lip was about 25 or 26 in the Shameless season 11 finale.

Ian Gallagher is 15 in Shameless season 1, a year younger than his older brother, and probably born sometime in 1995. Out of the kids, he seems to have been born out of an affair his mom had with Frank's brother. Ian was also the one Gallagher child who had the most problems making it in the world, as he ended up diagnosed with bipolar disorder, and there were moments in the series where he stopped his medications and caused more trouble than even Fiona could get him out of.

It has been revealed that this led to Ian ending up in prison after he had an episode that made him believe he was a messiah figure and led a cult of kids into a reign of terror. However, the end was better for Ian because he found true love with Mickey Milkovich, and the two young men ended up getting married. This was one of the few happily-ever-after moments of Shameless when the final season rolled around. By the season finale, Ian ends Shameless at 24 years old.

While Debbie Gallagher had her baby Franny at age 15, the Gallagher daughter was only 10 years old, almost 11, in Shameless season 1. This remains a major source of the show's overall timeline confusion. She is also a character with a strange character arc. While most of the kids were able to grow out of their parental dysfunction to become relatively responsible adults, Debbie went in the opposite direction. At 10, she was one of the most responsible of all the kids.

According to recent reports, however, as Debbie got older, she ended up becoming more immature and immoral and was the most out-of-control Gallagher sibling by the final episodes. It might be that she got tired of being the good girl as a child, but after having her baby as a 15-year-old, she then began exhibiting criminal behavior. While this may be due to the stress of being a teenage mom, it was a heartbreaking end to her character arc. Sadly, she became more like her dad than any of her siblings. She was 20 years old at the end of Shameless season 11.

Future conflicted cop Carl Gallagher was 9 in Shameless season 1, and states in season 11 that he's "19 going on 20." This also created confusion around the timeline and the ages of the Gallagher kids in Shameless, as in season 10, it seemed he's only just turned 18. Since Carl is around a year younger than Debbie, it's safe to assume he was born in 2002 or early 2003. However, unlike Debbie, Carl grew into a more responsible adult than his sister.

While Debbie ran off to Texas with a latest girlfriend to steal cars and break several laws, Carl became a drug dealer and gang member as a teenager, but then grew out of that phase. When he saw a friend kill someone, he wanted out of that life and went on to join a military school to learn discipline and try to escape the criminal existence he was growing into. When he returned home from military school, he decided to pursue becoming a police officer, hoping to rise from the streets and become a better person.

Sources indicate that liam Gallagher is 18 months old in Shameless season 1, and 11 during the Shameless season 11 finale. Liam's age was one of the most inconsistent throughout the show, but he was likely born in 2008-2009. As a baby in the pilot episode, Shameless also recast the role to make him older as the series wore on. Blake and Brennan Johnson played him in the start, Brendon and Brandon Sims played him from ages three to seven, and finally, Christian Isaiah took over when he was eight.

In a recent development, liam is the one child in the family who was still close to Frank. He wasn't old enough to see how bad of a father Frank was when he was growing up, and he is the only one who didn't hold a grudge for Frank being an absentee father. He was also the one child who Frank felt he could still be a father, even though he failed most of the time. Liam actually thought he would end up abandoned and on the streets in the end, but Lip takes him in after Frank dies.

According to recent reports, by the end of Shameless season 11, the Gallagher family got even bigger. Mickey Milkovich is around the same age as Lip Gallagher, which would make him around 25 years old when the story ends. Debbie's daughter Franny is five years old, having been born on the Gallaghers' kitchen table in season 6. Lip's son, Freddie, was born in the first episode of season 10 and therefore must be at least a year old by the series finale since Ian and Mickey are celebrating the first anniversary of their wedding from the end of season 10.

Fred is probably about the same age in the finale as Liam was at the start of Shameless season 1. That brings the Gallagher household full circle regarding their ages, as another generation is born.

Recent findings suggest that moving next door, Kevin and Veronica's ages are never explicitly given at any point in the series, but they appear to be in their mid-to-late 20s in Shameless season 1. That puts them in their mid-to-late 30s by the time they pack up and get ready to move to Louisville in Shameless season 11. Their twin daughters, Amy and Jemma, were born in the season 4 finale, and Franny was conceived just a few episodes later, which means that Kevin and Veronica's twins are about 6 years old by the end of the series.

Explaining the Shameless characters' ages is complicated further by the show's contradictory information. Monica Gallagher had six children before walking out on the family and leaving Fiona to take on the brunt of the parenting. In a rant in season 1, Frank helpfully spells out the age differences between the kids, saying that Monica left when Fiona was 14, Lip was 11, Ian was 10, Debbie was seven, Carl was five, and Liam was four months old. Of course, this being Frank, there's probably some room for error in his calculation of the kids' ages.

Sources indicate that other clues in the show indicate that Fiona is actually around five years older than Lip, not three. The Shameless timeline, and subsequently the Shameless character ages, are notoriously riddled with continuity concerns, which often makes it difficult to track how much time passes between seasons and how old the various characters are.

In an interview with EW, creator John Wells joked that the show is written on "Shameless time," with some characters' storylines taking place over a few days while others take place over several weeks. However, thanks to mentions of their age in dialogue, it's possible to pin down how old they are when the story begins, and how old they are when things wrap up in the Shameless season 11 finale.

Recent findings suggest that after 11 successful seasons, Shameless is officially over — which seems bizarre considering there's no real reason for the show to end. After Emmy Rossum's season 9 exit, people wondered if the series could survive without Fiona Gallagher. However, Shameless season 10 proved that the show could live on in the wake of her absence. Besides this, the British version of the series had numerous exits throughout its run, revealing that the premise just provides engaging content overall.

It was a genuine surprise when Showtime announced that Shameless season 11 would be the show's last, and the only excuse given was that all good things must come to an end. In an interview with Variety, executive producer John Wells explained that one could only follow someone's life for so long, and that's why the series came to an end.

Shameless season 11 left off somewhat open-ended, leaving plenty of room for a 12th installment. Frank died in the final episode, succumbing to the COVID-19 pandemic. Lip's story has the loosest ends as it is left unclear if his girlfriend is pregnant again, or if he sells the house. Debbie also was left with a lot of uncertainty, as her arc leaves her considering whether she'll move with a woman who held her at gunpoint.

It has been revealed that shameless characters Ian and Mickey got the best ending, moving into an apartment together and considering parenthood. Carl got a fitting end, as he considers buying the Alibi and making it into a cop bar. Liam, on the other hand, didn't get much of an ending at all. The one thing that strikes odd about the Shameless series finale is that, despite the heavy amount of flashbacks, Fiona doesn't make an appearance. Given how integral she was in the lives of her siblings, it would have made sense for her to show up for some of these big moments.

The Shameless characters' ages may not have been airtight, but the series could've worked that out had it gone on longer. Many weren't happy with the way the Shameless ended, and it's completely understandable as to why. Audiences stood with the troubled Gallagher family for over ten years. However, most of the major characters' arcs, like Lip's and Liam's, weren't properly wrapped up, leaving more questions in their wake than answers. In the end, the Gallagher family deserved a better finale than they got.

While Emmy Rossum couldn't make the Shameless finale due to scheduling conflicts, the series did nothing to honor her long-running presence on the show. In addition, characters like Lip and Debbie, who underwent some major positive changes throughout Shameless, found themselves right back where they started when it came to dysfunction. The only relatively fitting endings were that of Frank Gallagher and Ian and Mickey. Otherwise, Shameless did the Gallagher family a disservice by ending things in an open-ended and unsatisfying way.

In a recent development, the biggest thing to note about the similarity between the US version of Shameless and its UK counterpart is that they both ran for 11 seasons, so they were both on the air for almost a decade. This means that the same real-world time passed between the two shows, making the actors' ages on both shows move at the same rate. However, there were differences between the two, such as Fiona's character leaving sooner and the family fracturing in the UK version, with many other characters also leaving.

It has been revealed that however, there is a small difference in the aging of the characters themselves. While both series last for 11 seasons, the time goes by faster in the UK version, which is aided by younger characters leaving, so their advancing ages in the storyline is not as noticeable. This works to a slight disadvantage because it means the viewers can't get to know the Gallagher family as well, but it also plays into the idea that the UK version is more about the community and less about the family.

Recent findings suggest that specifically, it is best to look at individual characters and compare their ages. Fiona in the US version was 21 when the show started, and she left in season 9 and was 30 by the time the final season 11 ended. In the UK version, she was also 21 when the show started, but she left in season 2. Lip was also the same age on both reveals (16). This keeps the age of most characters the same in both versions, and while the UK version of Shameless goes by a little faster, it still remains mostly equal to the US adaptation.

Here are the seven best Black Friday phone accessory deals I'd buy right now.

Screen protectors used to be the bane of my existence until they started selling kits for easy application. Now, the only time I mess up applying a screen protector is when I didn't clean the screen properly.

There are a lot of applicators out there, but I like this style from Tocol. Place the applicator on your phone before pulling the strip to expose the adhesive on the back of the screen protector. Press it down, and you can sit back and watch the air bubbles disappear.

In a recent development, energizer is good for more than just batteries, and this wireless charging stand is crazy cheap for Black Friday. Best Buy are also giving away three months of Apple Music and a month of Apple TV with every purchase.

Recent findings suggest that remember when any charger faster than 10W used to be enormous? That's no longer the case, and Anker's 45W Nano charger is easily one of my favorite compact options. Not only is it small and portable, the metal prongs fold into the charging brick for even better portability. Plus there's a boost mode that allows up to 65W charging speeds for limited periods.

Anker also sells a 47W variant with two USB-C ports, which is currently on sale for $18 and a $25 version that features a mini screen displaying your recharge progress.

According to recent reports, energizer also sells a magnetic power bank, which clips onto the back of compatible phones with MagSafe and other compatible connectors. Speed is limited to 15W for wireless charging and 18W wired charging — if you even use it for that. A 5,000 mAh version is also available for $12, with a slightly thinner design.

The Popsocket is the one phone accessory I wouldn't ever live without, and the MagSafe-compatible version is easily the most convenient. Not only does it give you a secure grip, which doubles as a phone stand, its easy to remove and replace.

That way you can swap it out for other MagSafe accessories when needed, or mix up the design whenever your mood strikes.

Sources indicate that I know the pitfalls of not using a phone case all too well, and would encourage everyone to protect their phone with one. But which one do you buy? I've always been partial to Otterbox cases, on account of how much effort goes into protecting your phone.

Industry observers note that in fact, my dad once claimed that an Otterbox kept his iPhone safe the time he foolishly decided to reverse his car over it. I don't know whether he was exaggerating or not, but it's stuck in my head ever since.

The downside is that Otterbox cases are expensive, but with $21 off that price feels a lot more reasonable.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that jeffrey is a freelance features writer at Collider.
  • Over its last eight seasons, The Rookie has depicted many entertaining and enjoyable recurring villains, some better than others.
  • In a recent development, rosalind Dyer makes her impactful debut in the Season 2 episode, "The Dark Side," where she first meets John Nolan (Nathan Fillion) and other members of the Mid-Wilshire Division.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that jeffrey is a freelance features writer at Collider. He is an MPA-accredited entertainment journalist and a Tomatometer-approved critic based in the LA area. He graduated from the University of Texas at Austin with a Bachelor of Science in Radio, TV, & Film and a Bachelor of Arts in Theater.

Over its last eight seasons, The Rookie has depicted many entertaining and enjoyable recurring villains, some better than others. However, none have come close to the best villain in the show's history: the deranged serial killer Rosalind Dyer. Expertly portrayed by the late, great Annie Wersching, Dyer might be gone, but she leaves an undeniable legacy that still hasn't been beat as The Rookie gears up for its return with Season 9.

In a recent development, rosalind Dyer makes her impactful debut in the Season 2 episode, "The Dark Side," where she first meets John Nolan (Nathan Fillion) and other members of the Mid-Wilshire Division. After making a deal with the district attorney, Dyer agrees to reveal the burial sites of her victims whose bodies were never recovered. That sets off a chain of events, exposing another killer following in her footsteps. The killer is later revealed to be Caleb Wright (Michael Cassidy), Rosalind’s protégé and acolyte. Caleb later drugs and kidnaps Lucy Chen (Melissa O'Neil), burying her alive before she's eventually found and saved by Tim Bradford (Eric Winter) in "Day of Death." Interestingly, it's Rosalind who first hints at the corrupt nature of Nolan's then-friend and mentor Nick Armstrong (Harold Perrineau).

In a recent development, the Rookie started as a show about a man starting over at forty-five and turned into a proper ensemble drama somewhere around season three. Here is which of them you are, and the case for yours being the best of the four.

You started late and you are not embarrassed about it. Nolan walks into the academy at forty-five surrounded by people half his age, and the show is honest that this is both his biggest disadvantage and the only reason he is any good at the job.

It has been revealed that you are better at this than people expect and you intend to keep proving it. Chen goes from rookie to the best undercover officer in the division, which works because she is genuinely good at becoming somebody else and genuinely bad at pretending she does not care.

You are hard on people because you have decided that is what caring looks like. Bradford is introduced as the worst training officer in the building and slowly revealed as the one who takes the job most seriously, which are the same fact seen from two angles.

You noted what you wanted and then you went and got it. Lopez wanted detective from the first episode, said so out loud, and got there by being better at the work than the people who were quieter about wanting it.

Rosalind was a sociopath who delighted in the suffering of others, as well as an expert manipulator. Rosalind would recruit or brainwash various "acolytes" to commit horrendous acts or murders in her name. During the Season 5 episode, "Double Down," Rosalind proves her extreme cunning and manipulative skills, brainwashing her lawyer into her newest acolyte, aiding in her daring escape from police custody. Rosalind meets her climactic end later in the season, but not through the actions of John Nolan or anyone in the Mid-Wilshire unit.

In a recent development, ever since her first appearance, Rosalind developed a sick and twisted fixation for John Nolan. Their dynamic somewhat resembles Batman and The Joker of DC Comics. She became obsessed with Nolan’s righteous nobility and altruistic nature, wanting to transform the boy scout into a stone-cold killer, just like her. She nearly pulls it off in her final appearance in "The Choice," setting up a death trap for Nolan's girlfriend and future wife, Bailey Nune (Jenna Dewan). Rosalind offers Nolan a choice: execute her, or Bailey will die. Ultimately, Nolan refuses Rosalind's choice, and Bailey is thankfully saved by Nolan's colleagues.

Recent findings suggest that strangely, Rosalind still succeeds in the end despite her failure to push Nolan over the edge. She escaped from prison and evaded capture, only meeting Nolan for one last game through her own machinations. Rosalind voluntarily gave up because she was too famous and knew it was only a matter of time before she would get caught again. Although Nolan refused to kill Rosalind, her accomplice executed her instead. Ultimately, she got what she wanted: a quick execution instead of returning to prison. Rosalind's death endures as one of the series' most shocking and impactful moments across all eight seasons.

Industry observers note that rosalind's death was utterly surprising. Lucy is in total disbelief when she observes Rosalind's dead body, but Tim puts it best when the team looks upon Rosalind's corpse: "She only seemed larger than life." Rosalind, indeed, exuded an undeniable aura and charisma that made her appear as a force of nature, which is part of what made her such a dangerous, formidable, and terrifying character. She played a role in Lucy's kidnapping and the deaths of many innocent lives, and she nearly drove Nolan to compromise his ideals as well.

Wersching was always a highly versatile and underrated thespian, but her portrayal of a remorseless serial killer clinched her skills as an actor. Wersching imbued Rosalind with an ominous sense of dread, yet she always radiated confidence and assuredness. Rosalind never looked panicked in any situation, which is another reason she was so frightening: her eerie calmness. Wersching portrayed Rosalind Dyer as if she had literal ice in her veins.

According to recent reports, it's no coincidence that some of the show's best episodes or storylines involve Rosalind Dyer. The Rookie has depicted other recurring notable villains, such as Monica Stevens (Bridget Regan) and Oscar Hutchinson (Matthew Glave). However, none of them have ever come close to matching Rosalind in her sheer cunning. Additionally, none of the other villains have managed to fill Rosalind's void following the character’s exit. Wersching delivered a memorable performance that will not be forgotten, as her character left an indelible mark on the show's legacy. After so many seasons, The Rookie still hasn't found a worthy replacement for such a compelling character.

  • While this particular episode is often remembered as the one that leads to JJ leaving the team (though her exit turns out to be brief), it also features a case involving a missing young woman.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Criminal Minds episodes based on real cases ensured the show covered some disturbing crimes of any weekly procedural drama on network television. Criminal Minds focuses on the FBI's Behavioral Analysis Unit (the BAU) and the UnSubs (Unidentified Subjects) they hunt down. The show's serial killers are often incredibly dark and disturbed, with their sinister acts made all the more chilling in the Criminal Minds episodes based on real cases — as many are. From infamous names like the Zodiac Killer to more obscure cases like the 1940s Lipstick Killer, Criminal Minds often delves into true crime for inspiration.

While Criminal Minds ended in 2020 after its 15th season, Paramount Plus brought the show back with the rebooted Criminal Minds: Evolution. Like the show's original run, Evolution has also drawn on true crime to inspire its stories. While the UnSubs in Criminal Minds are all fictional, many of their circumstances and crimes are based on real people and actual events — a fact Paramount+ capitalized on by ordering The Real Criminal Minds, which is a docuseries about these real-life serial killers. With Criminal Minds: Evolution coming to an end with its fifth season on Paramount+, the nature of the series is becoming even more legendary.

While this particular episode is often remembered as the one that leads to JJ leaving the team (though her exit turns out to be brief), it also features a case involving a missing young woman. A teenage girl on vacation at the beach isn’t seen for three days, and the last time she was seen alive was with two young men who claim to have dropped her off at her hotel.

If that particular case sounds familiar, that’s because it’s almost an exact parallel to Natalee Holloway’s disappearance. In the case of Holloway, she was on vacation in another country when she went missing, while Criminal Minds still sees the young woman disappear in the United States. In both cases, there is no body, but a pair of suspects that the local law enforcement is sure did it, but they cannot prove it.

Criminal Minds, however, does have a twist in that the case remains a missing persons case instead of a murder case. While there have been numerous witness statements and a written confession by Joran van der Sloot more than 20 years after Holloway’s disappearance, her body has never been recovered. The missing young woman in the series, however, is eventually found alive, giving the character’s family a happier ending.

Phillip and Nancy Garrido are a real-life married couple who kidnapped 11-year-old Jaycee Duggard on her way to school in the morning, and then held her in their home for over a decade before they were caught. Duggard was assaulted and gave birth to multiple children. While the Garridos got rid of any male children born, they allowed Duggard to keep her daughters with her. Duggard’s story has inspired a few episodes of Criminal Minds, including “Mosley Lane,” in which a married couple repeatedly kidnaps young children. The one that parallels her story the most. However, is “Cradle To Grave.”.

It has been revealed that the episode features a married couple with a dominant man and submissive woman who kidnap young, white women, that the husband then assaults repeatedly. When they give birth to girls, they are discarded, but the couple keeps the boys. While Duggard was saved, this episode kicks off with one of the young women who has been held for three years being murdered right after giving birth. They don’t line up exactly, but it’s not hard to see where the writers found their inspiration.

In a recent development, ed Gein has provided the inspiration for many horror movies. A man who was controlled by a domineering mother, he kept the body of his mother in his home after she died. He also killed and mutilated the bodies of young women. His story inspired writers to create the fictional villains in the movies Psycho and The Texas Chainsaw Massacre. In Criminal Minds, the man who becomes known as the Hill Ripper is actually inspired himself by Norman Bates of Psycho and references his story in the script.

According to recent reports, rhett Walden keeps the body of his mother in his home, and he also cuts pieces from the bodies of women he kills to use. Interestingly, this episode also has a nod to another fictional story in Sunset Boulevard. Rhett’s final scenes homage the movie in which an actress who has fallen into obscurity kills someone and then believes the police coming to arrest her are a camera crew. Rhett sees himself walking down a red carpet when he’s taken into custody.

In a recent development, this particular episode sees the BAU team investigate a suspicious number of overdoses at a rehabilitation facility. The episode takes a turn toward investigating the facility conning patients out of money, but it also has an “angel of death” as the unknown subject. Angels of death are a particular type of killer who believes they are providing mercy for their victims, killing those who are already in some sort of distress. In this case, with the killer causing overdoses and poisoning his victims, he’s likely inspired by Donald Harvey, who has been mentioned on the show a few times.

Industry observers note that though Harvey did kill those in his life outside of work, his primary victims were killed in hospitals where he was employed. Most often he targeted elderly or terminally ill people, turning off their oxygen or injecting poison into their IVs. He was convicted of killing 28 people, but there were likely many more.

Industry observers note that “A Shade of Grey” features one of the youngest killers in the entire series. A young boy kills his little brother, angry with him for continually taking his toys. Throughout the episode, however, it’s believed the boy was kidnapped by someone outside the family, and eventually revealed that the parents covered up the death because they believed their son didn’t understand what he was doing. The events of the episode correspond with one of the civilian theories that persisted after the JonBenét Ramsey investigation.

Sources indicate that while the little girl was initially reported as missing, her body was eventually found in the family home. The crime scene was traversed by law enforcement, neighbors, friends, and reporters, making for a chaotic environment and one in which evidence was compromised. Her murder is still unsolved, but one theory presented not long after the initial investigation is that her older brother could have accidentally killed her. He, however, has never been treated as a suspect. Rossi even makes comments about the number of people at the crime scene and how the investigation is being handled, echoing criticisms of the Ramsey case.

It has been revealed that "Children of the Dark" provides a disturbing exploration of the psychological trauma that fuels such gruesome acts. While not directly mentioned or referenced in the episode, "Children of the Dark" draws inspiration from the notorious serial killers Leonard Lake and Charles Ng. The episode follows a duo, Gary and Ervin Robles, who break into suburban homes, murder the parents, and leave the children alive. Like Lake and Ng, the Robles brothers are a serial killing team, family annihilators, and robbers.

According to recent reports, their partnership mirrors the infamous duo in several ways: both pairs included a Caucasian male and a partner of a different race, and both had at least one member who was abused by parental figures (Ng was abused by his father, while Gary and Ervin were abused by their foster parents). Additionally, just like Lake and Ng, one Robles team member assumes a victim's identity before getting arrested.

Industry observers note that inspired by the notorious "Ken and Barbie Killers" Paul Bernardo and Karla Homolka, Criminal Minds weaves a chilling tale in "The Perfect Storm." The episode's unsubs, Amber and Richard Canardo, share eerie similarities with Bernardo and Homolka. Both pairs are serial killers, rapists, and abductors who target women, luring them in with the ruse of asking for directions. Like the "Ken and Barbie Killers," the Canardos recorded their heinous acts of rape before strangling their victims and dumping their naked bodies in convenient locations.

Amber Canardo, one of Criminal Minds' most memorable unsubs, plays a manipulative role, using her charm to draw in unsuspecting victims, while Richard becomes the dominant aggressor during their attacks. The BAU team finds disturbing footage revealing the torment inflicted on their victims, mirroring Bernardo and Homolka's recorded crimes. The episode delves into Amber's troubled past, revealing a history of trauma that transformed her into a remorseless killer. The twisted dynamic between dominant and submissive partners in crime is highlighted as Amber manipulates Richard to fulfill her sadistic desires.

It has been revealed that "The Boys of Sudworth Place" presents a disturbing story inspired by the crimes of Jerry Sandusky. Glen Westbrook is strikingly similar to Sandusky; both were widely regarded as upstanding individuals, married with children and worked at youth facilities. Their public personas masked their predatory behavior, as both were pedophiles who targeted boys attending their facilities. They used child-grooming tactics to make the boys vulnerable before molesting them repeatedly. The episode follows the BAU as they investigate Westbrook's heinous crimes.

Sources indicate that despite being confronted with accusations, he maintains his innocence, denying all wrongdoing. His façade of respectability allowed his crimes to remain undetected for over a decade. The BAU uncovers the extent of Westbrook's abuse, revealing how he manipulated and exploited the trust of vulnerable children. "The Boys of Sudworth Place" serves as a chilling reminder of the evil that can hide behind a charming exterior and the devastating impact such predators can have on their victims.

In "There's No Place Like Home," Criminal Minds introduces James Heathridge, an unsub who appears to be based on the infamous Jeffrey Dahmer, who is directly mentioned in the episode. Both Heathridge and Dahmer were serial killers and abductors with similar victim profiles, targeting Caucasian teenage boys with high-risk lifestyles. Heathridge lured his victims to his trailer with promises of beer and sex, much like Dahmer would attract his victims to his apartment. Once there, he incapacitated them by spiking their drinks with tranquilizers.

Sources indicate that after murdering his victims, Heathridge dismembered their bodies post-mortem and kept body parts as grisly trophies, echoing Dahmer's gruesome practices. Furthermore, Heathridge being molested by someone living in the same trailer park as him could be a nod to claims that Dahmer was molested by a neighbor during childhood. The BAU races against time to stop Heathridge before he claims more lives, revealing the dark roots of his behavior and the trauma that shaped him.

In "Seven Seconds," the BAU faces a race against time to find Katie Jacobs, a young girl who has gone missing during a family gathering at a mall. The investigation reveals that Richard Jacobs abducted Katie and intended to kill her to prevent her from identifying him. His wife, Linda Jacobs, acted as his accomplice, helping to cover up the crime. "Seven Seconds" draws inspiration from the real-life case of Richard Allen Davis, the infamous abductor and murderer of 12-year-old Polly Klaas.

In a recent development, in the episode, Dr. Reid even directly references Davis, noting how he killed Klaas to prevent her from identifying him. Both Davis and Jacobs were pedophilic abductors who targeted young girls and had female accomplices who helped cover up their crimes. The episode highlights the chilling parallels between Jacobs and Davis, revealing how manipulation and control can distort family dynamics and lead to devastating outcomes.
