#28244. Industry News: Why Do AI Posters All Look Like That?

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1287 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Lifehacker ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: Why Do AI Posters All Look Like That?

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1287 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Lifehacker

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Every poster for a business or event has pictures of uncanny-looking people, buildings that don’t look right, and always that one font.
  • Recent findings suggest that at this point, gone are the days of chatbots like ChatGPT, Claude, or Gemini simply generating text immediately in response to a prompt.
  • Industry observers note that to borrow a classic and implausible example, if you were to give an AI chatbot the instruction “Make a peanut butter and jelly sandwich,” it would start by generating step-by-step instructions on how to make the sandwich before trying to make one (if it could).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

You know “the look” by now. Every poster for a business or event has pictures of uncanny-looking people, buildings that don’t look right, and always that one font. But why? If generative AI is supposedly able to “think” and be “creative,” why do so many of its results come out looking exactly the same? The answer is complicated, and it has to do with what chatbots define as “thinking.”.

Recent findings suggest that at this point, gone are the days of chatbots like ChatGPT, Claude, or Gemini simply generating text immediately in response to a prompt. Some very fast models do, but most employ what’s known as “thinking models”, which are a bit of a misnomer. The “thinking” really just consists of generating a set of sub-prompts before executing the main one. And it’s in that hidden, generated text that most of the “choices” (to the extent that we can call the statistical output of an AI model a “choice”) occur that determine how a design looks.

Industry observers note that to borrow a classic and implausible example, if you were to give an AI chatbot the instruction “Make a peanut butter and jelly sandwich,” it would start by generating step-by-step instructions on how to make the sandwich before trying to make one (if it could). Most of this happens invisibly in the background, and many proprietary chatbots won’t show you their in-process “thinking” prompts even if you ask.

In the case of an AI poster, it might break down “make a poster” into smaller steps such as “create a design brief for a poster.” To demonstrate this while doing some testing for this piece, I added additional prompts for ChatGPT to explain the “design briefs” it generated, which included details like layout, colors, and typography.

The problem is those instructions are still subject to the same flaws as any other AI-generated text. They can’t properly fact-check; they can’t walk into the real world and see the thing they’re describing; and they can hallucinate or fall back on stale formats that become easy to notice after a while.

For example, while testing, I had ChatGPT generate a poster for a Lifehacker-themed nightclub. In every case, the underlying brief it generated outlined some basic details, but occasionally it added things I hadn’t asked for. This included additional text, iconography, and in one case it even added the “design brief” explanation I had requested as the bottom half of the poster.

It has been revealed that those mistakes filter into the final product, when the brief is then fed into the image generator that ultimately makes the poster. In my case, ChatGPT showed me the underlying explanations for its reasoning (though even that could be different from what was actually sent to the image generator), but most people who use a chatbot for this task won’t see these factors before getting the final result.

While most chatbots won’t show you exactly what underlying “thinking” they use, most can be coaxed into describing the vague outlines of how they reached certain outcomes. And those descriptions provide some insight into why certain chatbots keep outputting similar results over and over. It doesn’t take long for some patterns to emerge. For example, any prompt to generate a poster for a nightclub almost invariably generated a brief that had specifications for a color palette including “electric purple,” “electric yellow,” and “electric pink.”.

In a recent development, the reason for this should be pretty obvious: When the statistical model underlying LLMs needs to come up with an example for “colors for a nightclub poster,” the most obvious answers are neon, high-energy colors. Unless you know something about the specific club’s vibe (and write that out and feed it to the chatbot), the AI will have to fill in the gaps with something. And that something will be based on the same statistics it uses to predict any word.

This pattern of repetition was everywhere in all the design rationale ChatGPT gave me. Across multiple attempts to generate a Club Lifehacker poster, the generated design brief added an overarching “concept” that described the fictional club’s atmosphere as “high-energy” and “futuristic.” Every bot mentioned using images with the “silhouette” of either the DJ or a dancing crowd (often both). All the text had to be “bold” and “futuristic.".

If there's one dead giveaway that a poster was made with AI, it's that one brush-stroke font that they all seem to use. Now, this is a bit more speculative, but I have a theory on where that specific design comes from. And it’s worth noting upfront that this seems to only apply to posters generated by ChatGPT specifically.

One of the most common factors I found in my design brief testing was the use of phrases like “brush lettering” or “brush script.” Brush lettering is a design term that refers to using any number of methods like markers, paint brushes, or brush pens to write text. In digital design, that can take the form of fonts that are designed to emulate the look of fancy, handwritten text.

It has been revealed that in every test poster I created, however, ChatGPT seemed to take the phrase “brush lettering” rather literally. Every instance I encountered of a design brief that mentioned any kind of “brush” text generated an image with letters that looked as though they were created with a broad paint brush. A human designer would understand “brush lettering” to mean “something that looks handwritten," but ChatGPT didn’t seem capable of understanding the phrase as anything other than using an actual paint brush.

The generated posters aren’t even using a “font,” strictly speaking. (Often, letters that should be identical had slight variations.) The image generator part of the chatbot is still a diffusion model, so it can’t employ a vector-based font, per se. But the brush-style font is so common that its look surfaces in any statistical model.

According to recent reports, this is an odd quirk of ChatGPT specifically, and it’s possible that it could change in the future. Especially if OpenAI intentionally tries to train this behavior out of its chatbot. However, it’s helpful to illustrate the underlying mechanism. The only way a chatbot can conceptualize design elements in a visual medium is to generate more specific text to feed to the image generator. And that text is just as prone to mistakes and blandness as any other AI model.

According to recent reports, I’ve been examining this with a focus on the kinds of posters ChatGPT generates because they’re very common, but posters (or any AI-generated content) from other models might look different. Every model has its own tendencies. For example, a lot of vibecoded websites are made with Anthropic’s Claude, and you can often tell by the tiny text, buttons with rounded corners, and tile-based layouts.

To a certain extent, this is inevitable. While AI models are very different from humans and do not make “choices” in the same way people do, design elements still have to come from somewhere, and whether human or AI, it’s impossible to make these decisions in a vacuum. Humans will have preferences based on the things they like or emotionally resonate with, and AI models will have tendencies based on what their statistical model determines is the most appropriate output.

Sources indicate that that means that an AI model’s “style” is naturally going to change over time. Even if a model improves or makes fewer mistakes, it’s impossible to ever change the fact that all ChatGPT images are made by ChatGPT. Whatever you generate with any particular model will have a lot in common with what everyone else who uses the same tool generates.

The new season adapts The Titan's Curse, the third book in Rick Riordan's original series and the first to have never been adapted before. With the first two episodes having just premiered, it's pretty cool to see all the great nods and references to the original material, as well as the key changes that have been made.

Kicking off with Percy, Annabeth, and the newly revived Thalia Grace answering Grover's call for help about a pair of fresh demigods in need of saving, the first two episodes of Percy Jackson season 3 waste no time getting to the action with a major monster fight, just like in the original novel, teeing up the book's major villain, and debuting a brand-new faction of heroes beyond the demigods of Camp Half-Blood.

Keeping that in mind, here are over 30 of the biggest and most notable Easter eggs, references, and key book changes in the first two episodes of Percy Jackson and the Olympians season 3.

"My Rescue Operation Goes Very Wrong" — The title of Percy Jackson season 3's first episode matches the first chapter title in The Titan's Curse.

Recent findings suggest that aegis — Shown fighting a Laestrygonian giant, Thalia Grace wields Aegis for the first time on-screen, an impressive shield from Greek mythology connected to Zeus and Athena, bearing the face of the gorgon Medusa, capable of instilling fear in even the most fearsome of monsters. When Thalia isn't using it, the shield rests on her arm as a bracelet, which she can activate by saying the shield's name.

Industry observers note that guests of Grover— While Percy, Annabeth, and Thalia are introduced to Dr. Thorn as guests of Grover's and potential recruits to Westover Hall, the book saw Thalia manipulating the Mist to convince Thorn and a fellow teacher that they were already students of the school.

Winter Dance Punch— While scouting the Westover Winter Dance, Percy and Annabeth stand near the punch bowl, which feels like a fun nod to Grover's improvisation in the opening of The Titan's Curse novel, backtracking after exclaiming that his friends "made it" by claiming they made the punch (not realizing Thalia had already used the Mist to mask their arrival).

It has been revealed that mrs. Gottschalk— While Mrs. Gottschalk isn't with Dr. Thorn to greet Percy, Annabeth, and Thalia as she does in the book, she's hilariously shown as the school dance's DJ instead.

Mythomagic — Just like in the books, Nico di Angelo is obsessed with the Greek mythology card game known as Mythomagic, which also features dice and minifigures. However, Nico reveals in the first episode of Percy Jackson season 3 that his dice and minis were confiscated by Dr. Thorn. Additionally, some of Camp Half-Blood defectors working for Luke in season 2 (The Sea of Monsters) were shown playing the game as well.

Annabeth Invited To Hunters— In the book, Annabeth was interrupted during the dance before she could tell Percy that she had been invited to join the Hunters and Artemis' Eternal Hunt. Percy doesn't find out till later, when Grover finds the brochure in her backpack. However, the show sees Annabeth telling Percy everything during the dance itself, confirming her intention to remove herself from the equation so she can't be used against Percy or Thalia and the Great Prophecy.

Italy, Washington D.C., Las Vegas—As Annabeth talks with Bianca di Angelo during the dance, it's confirmed that she and her brother Nico originally lived in Italy before they moved to Washington D.C. and then Las Vegas. However, Bianca's memories are fuzzy on the timeline. This is thanks to the manipulations of her and Nico's godly father and his efforts to protect them from Zeus, having had their memories wiped, with the duo then spending years in Las Vegas' Lotus Casino, which was featured in Percy Jackson's first season (The Lightning Thief).

"I Serve At The Pleasure Of The General" — Just like in the book, Dr. Thorn confirms to Percy at Westover that he works for "The General", the major villain of The Titan's Curse who's ultimately revealed to be Atlas, lead commander of Kronos' armies.

“We’re Not Here For Thee” — Despite her younger appearance, Zoë Nightshade has been a member of Artemis' Eternal Hunt and the goddess's top lieutenant for an incredibly long time, as evidenced by her use of older English vocabulary.

Thalia’s Spear — Just like Percy's sword and its more innocuous form as a ballpoint pen, Thalia's spear appears as a can of mace when not in use.

Industry observers note that artemis vs Helicopter— When Artemis and her immortal Hunters arrive to face the manticore that is Dr. Thorn, Artemis waves her hand to turn the incoming helicopter meant to pick Thorn up into a flock of birds, just like in The Titan's Curse.

"An Old Dead Friend Comes To Visit" — The title of Percy Jackson and the Olympians season 3, episode 2 is the same as the title of the sixth chapter in The Titan's Curse.

Industry observers note that wolves Standing Guard— When the Hunters make camp outside of Westover Hall, wolves are shown standing guard. This mirrors the book, which also had falcons in the trees acting as sentries for Artemis and her Hunters.

Recent findings suggest that A Quest Granted By Artemis— Unlike in the book, Percy Jackson convinces Artemis to grant him and Thalia a quest to save Annabeth after she was taken by Thorn via Titan magic. In the book, the Oracle grants the quest to Zoë Nightshade specifically.

Apollo’s Sun Chariot— Artemis summons her twin brother Apollo to transport the Campers and Hunters to Camp Half-Blood. Arriving in his sun chariot, Apollo's ride initially has the form of a Maserati before turning into a large bus, mirroring The Titan's Curse novel. However, both the car and bus are orange, while the car in the book was cherry red.

In a recent development, god of Poetry— Beyond the sun, Apollo is also the god of archery, prophecy, and poetry, hence his recitation of an original poem: "Forbidden children in the melting snow, cannot go where they do not know." However, his haiku in the book is much funnier: "Green grass breaks through snow. Artemis pleads for my help. I am so awesome.".

The Winter Solstice— Before leaving, Apollo tells Artemis that he'll see her at the Winter Solstice, an imminent gathering of the gods in just a few days where Artemis' presence will be crucial to motivate the other gods to take the threat of Kronos more seriously.

Thalia’s Dangerous Driving— In both the book and the new season of Percy Jackson, Apollo lets Thalia drive his sun chariot, which she does rather dangerously before crashing it into the lake near Camp Half-Blood. However, the show makes things more interesting with Apollo giving up the driver's seat midway to make a point about fate, the Great Prophecy, and Percy and Thalia's role within it.

Always Summer— Once they hit the borders of Camp Half-Blood, the snow is gone, and everything is nice and sunnier, with the comment being made that it's "always summer" at the camp for demigods. While it's true that the entire camp is magically climate-controlled, snow was allowed to fall during the winter months in The Titan's Curse novel.

It has been revealed that bianca’s Potential— Making their way to camp, Zoë notes that she sees Bianca's potential and the "strength of a lioness", teeing up Bianca eventually becoming one of the Hunters. This is a solid improvement from the book, as Bianca joined the Hunters while they were still camping at Westover, a decision many felt happened much too quickly with very little thought towards her brother. It seems the show plans to expand and present a more natural decision for Bianca going forward.

Travis & Connor Stoll— Travis and Connor Stoll make their official debut in Percy Jackson season 3. Both are sons of Hermes with the same mother. Travis is the older brother, while Connor is a couple of years younger (despite them looking like twins).

Clarisse’s Secret Mission— In Percy Jackson season 3, Clarisse meets up with Percy before she heads out on a secret mission for Chiron. In the book, Clarisse is already gone before Percy arrives at Camp Half-Blood. The mission itself involves setting up the events of the fourth book, Battle of the Labyrinth (fingers crossed for a fourth season!).

Annabeth Takes The Burden— In the show, Annabeth is far more willing and understanding of what it means to take on the Titan's Curse/Burden of Atlas, and she's not necessarily tricked or manipulated by Luke as it's depicted in the novel.

Quest for the Golden Apple— Luke mentions his past quest to retrieve a Golden Apple, the quest he received from his father Hermes, where he failed and received his scar from a dragon. This was the event that began his animosity toward his father and the gods.

Percy vs Thalia — While it doesn't happen during a game of Capture the Flag between the Hunters and Campers like in the book, Thalia and Percy still come to blows over losing Annabeth and Luke, with both featuring impressive displays of their power before Chiron intervenes.

Bessie— While searching for Annabeth's dagger in the lake, Percy finds and rescues a cute baby sea cow he ends up naming Bessie in The Titan's Curse, otherwise known as The Ophiotaurus, a creature that is far more crucial than Percy realizes.

It has been revealed that the Golden Fleece (No Dragon)— Thalia visits the tree she once inhabited before she was revived at the end of The Sea of Monsters. However, no baby dragon is protecting the Golden Fleece like there is in the book.

"Regulation Capture The Flag" — Seeing Thalia chained by the Hunters who'd been given orders from Artemis to keep the Forbidden Children at Camp, Mr. D notes, "That doesn't look like regulation capture the flag," a clear nod to the aforementioned game that happens in the book.

In a recent development, the Bane of Olympus — Just like on the page, Mr. D has no idea who or what "The Bane of Olympus" is, the creature Artemis went off to hunt alone.

Industry observers note that oracle Walking Around Camp Half-Blood— Another key parallel to the book, the Oracle of Delphi leaves the Substantial House's attic and walks around Camp, something it had never done before. Spewing green mist, the Oracle reveals Artemis being captured by the General/Atlas. Naturally, the Oracle walking around Camp explains the aforementioned chapter and episode title.

The Titan’s Curse Prophecy — The Oracle uses a vision of Annabeth to give this season's prophecy, and the wording is the same as it is in The Titan's Curse book:.

"Five Shall Go West To The Goddess In Chains, One Will Shall Be Lost In The Land Without Rain, The Bane of Olympus Highlights The Trail, Campers and Hunters Combined Prevail, The Titan’s Curse Must One Withstand, And One Shall Perish By A Parent’s Hand".

Industry observers note that the Oracle Chooses The Five — While a big meeting was held to decide the five quest-goers in the book, the Oracle chooses the five herself in Percy Jackson season 3. The first four chosen are Zoë, Phoebe, Bianca, and Grover, with tendrils of green mist wrapping around each of them. The fifth member will either be Thalia or Percy, with the episode cutting to the credits before the choice is revealed. In the book, Thalia is officially chosen, while Percy ignores the rules and joins the quest anyway after Phoebe's incapacitated via a prank from the Stoll brothers before the quest even begins. It will be interesting to see how this plays out on-screen.

End Credits Mural— Like the previous two seasons of Percy Jackson, the end credits feature a large frieze/mural depicting the events of The Titan's Curse in its entirety, featuring major moments like the fight at the Air and Space Museum, the giant bronze automaton Talos, San Francisco, and more.

The 10 Most Important Rock Albums of All Time, Ranked

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1809 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Collider

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • You can look at rock in relatively recent years and feel as though it’s dropped off a bit in terms of influence and popularity, but it’s never truly died.
  • Industry observers note that this sort of music did matter even more some decades ago, and also, with those historically key releases, you can look back and see what they influenced, thereby gaining an even greater appreciation for them.
  • It has been revealed that there’s an argument to be made that The Who released their two best albums in the 1970s (Who’s Next and Quadrophenia), but the stuff they did in the 1960s was also pretty great, especially so when you consider Tommy came out right at the decade’s end.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

You can look at rock in relatively recent years and feel as though it’s dropped off a bit in terms of influence and popularity, but it’s never truly died. There’s been classic rock, progressive rock, punk rock, alternative rock, and then indie rock, for starters, and all sorts of other sorts. You know it when you hear it. This is the part where there might usually be a definition, but like, come on.

Industry observers note that this sort of music did matter even more some decades ago, and also, with those historically key releases, you can look back and see what they influenced, thereby gaining an even greater appreciation for them. So, relating to all that, these are some of the most important rock albums of all time, not always being the best in music history (though some are), but inevitably doing the most for moving rock, as a genre, forward.

It has been revealed that there’s an argument to be made that The Who released their two best albums in the 1970s (Who’s Next and Quadrophenia), but the stuff they did in the 1960s was also pretty great, especially so when you consider Tommy came out right at the decade’s end. This was an influential rock opera/concept album that also happened to be a double album, and that sense of it feeling so unusual and ambitious for its time is why it’s here, rather than one of those two potentially better The Who Albums.

Narratively, there’s a lot here, since Tommy tells an odd story about one man’s rise to becoming some kind of leader/messiah, dramatized in a way that’s actually not as out-there as the 1975 movie of the same name, which is… well, it’s still kind of interesting and cool. But just considering the music and the album, Tommy is mostly very good, and it’s also hard to deny just how much this was doing as a seminal/early large-scale rock opera.

According to recent reports, this is probably the most divisive and least “good” in the traditional sense album being included here, but with the topic at hand being influence, Never Mind the Bollocks, Here's the Sex Pistols does have to be here. Its title heralds The Sex Pistols, obviously, but then the band itself barely held together for the recording of one album, and then this debut did ultimately end up being the only studio album from The Sex Pistols.

Recent findings suggest that still, it heralded a certain kind of punk, and if you hear the term punk rock, you might think of some of the songs here, or just the look of The Sex Pistols, or both. And punk is a part of rock, and there have been so many different kinds of punk music and artists in the decades since Never Mind the Bollocks, Here's the Sex Pistols. So many exceeded this one in terms of quality, but nonetheless, this album is quintessentially punk, so never mind those others, here it is.

Recent findings suggest that with The Clash, there’s a punchiness to the band’s self-titled debut album (the one that feels the most traditionally punk of all their albums), and then a real extravagance and eclectic quality to the fourth album, Sandinista!, and then album #3, London Calling, is a happy medium. It’s also a bit more rock-focused, and then there’s some new wave stuff thrown in alongside the punk rock, and a few other things.

Sources indicate that but it doesn’t tackle an overwhelming number of genres like all the songs on the absolutely exhausting Sandinista! Still, anything’s better than their final album, which is like Voldemort, because its name shouldn’t be said. Focus on the good times. London Calling is nothing but good times. Never Mind the Bollocks, Here's the Sex Pistols walked so London Calling could run, fly, do whatever you want, just whatever it was it did, it was a hell of a lot faster than walking.

Industry observers note that it’s hard to know how to label Doolittle beyond saying it’s alternative rock, which is a pretty broad sub-genre that’s meant different things at different points in time. But it’s the best there is here. It’s a bit too late to be classic rock necessarily, though a bit early to be grunge. It doesn’t even really sound super grunge or anything, but Pixies did influence a certain grunge band that’ll be mentioned and talked about more (very) shortly.

Industry observers note that doolittle is wonderfully punchy, because it’s made up of 15 songs, and clocks in at about 38 minutes all up, meaning the average song length isn't much longer than about two and a half minutes. It’s extremely energetic and engaging, and you can also look back on it now and see how it was influential on the kind of indie/alternative rock that would become mainstream (or pretty close to it) in the 1990s, and then a bit further, throughout much of the 2000s.

It has been revealed that grunge and the alternative rock of the 1990s more or less signified that classic rock’s dominance was over, and Nirvana was at the center of it, being that previously alluded-to band that took influence from Pixies. The band’s debut was Bleach, and that did technically come out at the very end of the 1980s, but it was Nevermind that really exploded in popularity and made Nirvana one of the most legendary bands of the final decade of the 20th century (even that might be a bit of an understatement).

Nirvana was only active for part of the decade, since Kurt Cobain took his life in 1994, making In Utero the final studio album of Nirvana’s (and it’s the trendier pick for the title of “best Nirvana album,” admittedly). Nevermind is sort of untouchable though, even if some people might want to hit it with an “actually, it’s a bit overrated.” It more or less is the grunge sound condensed into an album, and hey, it became utterly iconic for a reason.

Industry observers note that since heavy metal is a kind of rock, including something by Black Sabbath here doesn’t feel too outrageous. It might be more outrageous to not include something like Black Sabbath’s Paranoid, honestly. And sure, the heaviness found in this particular album isn't quite as alarming or oppressive nowadays as it might've been 50+ years ago, so you have to take that into account, and think about what this album did so future metal albums could push everything further.

Black Sabbath was groundbreaking and undeniably influential for this type of rock going forward, and Paranoid is the best showcase of what made the band special (well, at least the band during its classic/essential era). Almost every song here is great on its own, then taken together, Paranoid as a whole ultimately flows remarkably well throughout.

In a recent development, there were some truly massive rock albums released in 1967, so honorable mentions are in order for the likes of The Doors (the self-titled debut) and Sgt. Pepper’s Lonely Hearts Club Band (another album by that album’s artist will be featured later on). Worthiest when looking at influence and importance, 1967-wise, is probably The Velvet Underground & Nico, since so many alternative rock artists since feel influenced by this album in one way or another.

You shouldn't overlook the other Velvet Underground albums, unless that album’s Squeeze. Overlook that one. Those others were crucial for music going forward, but The Velvet Underground & Nico most of all, you know? It’s one of those albums that’s kind of always been there, but before 1967, it literally wasn’t, which is crazy to think about. Albums from this whole era don’t get much more significant, really.

It’s inevitable that Pink Floyd is going to get a shout-out when talking about rock, and The Dark Side of the Moon feels the worthiest of praise, out of all their albums, for present purposes. The Wall might be even more ambitious, but not by much, and in any event, The Dark Side of the Moon feels a bit more revolutionary, coming earlier and doing just about everything an album potentially can in 40 minutes while remaining consistent.

And it all just flows so remarkably well, taking on all sorts of difficult topics and addressing them poetically, with everything backed up by some immense and out-of-this-world-sounding instrumentation. The Dark Side of the Moon is an album about the stresses of life, human nature, and some other stuff. It’s challenging thematically but still so easy to listen to from front to back without feeling any sort of temptation to skip a single track.

Sure, Led Zeppelin borrowed quite heavily from blues rock, which pre-dated classic rock, technically, but the band did make that sort of rock bigger and louder. Maybe they played a role in reshaping blues rock, which is something. There’s that real hard/classic rock sound that Led Zeppelin played a big role in establishing and perfecting, and you definitely see that in the band’s first self-titled album.

Any of the first six Led Zeppelin albums could go here, but their first is particularly punchy and consistent, and it being the OG makes it feel extra worthy of praise and mention.

Industry observers note that all that rock of a blues variety was made harder, so that makes the album undeniably hard rock (as a side note, I almost accidentally typed another word there ending with “ock” that would have changed that sentence tremendously… don’t type while tired, kids). Any of the first six Led Zeppelin albums could go here, but their first is particularly punchy and consistent, and it being the OG makes it feel extra worthy of praise and mention when you're talking about truly key rock albums.

It’s a testament to how good The Beatles were that it’s hard to name just one album of the band’s as their undeniable best, but as for most influential? No, that’s also pretty hard, albeit slightly easier, since their self-titled double album sometimes known as The White Album is so huge and influential in all these different ways. It’s almost cheating to pick it, but it’s epic, at over 90 minutes long, and eclectic in a way that still feels mind-blowing.

Recent findings suggest that the Beatles, on The Beatles (1968), had a go at just about every different type of rock they could, and might well have played a role in influencing some new ones (much has been written about “Helter Skelter” being a proto-heavy metal song). This is before getting to “Revolution 9,” which is something entirely other than rock, but still a good indication of how bold this album was willing to be. Maybe some other Beatles albums are better, but none feel as important within the overall history of pop/rock music.

The Out-of-Touch Adults' Guide to Kid Culture: Looksmaxxing With Dangerous Drugs

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (900 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Lifehacker

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • First, there's the looksmaxxing trend where teenagers are taking dangerous chemicals to correct perceived physical shortcomings.
  • In a recent development, you can judge a generation by the illegal drugs it pioneers.
  • Would-be muscle-men have been injecting themselves with black market ‘rhoids since the Eisenhower administration, but that was a small cult of adult weirdos with a specific goal.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This week's column is bleak. First, there's the looksmaxxing trend where teenagers are taking dangerous chemicals to correct perceived physical shortcomings. Then there are the AI job interviewers. Depressing, but at least some young people are having a little fun with their dystopian hellscape.

In a recent development, you can judge a generation by the illegal drugs it pioneers. In the 1960s, hippies smoked weed and dropped acid to expand their consciousness; the yuppies of the go-go '80s fueled their drive to acquire with Colombian cocaine; but kids today don’t want to go deeper or work harder. They have a smaller, sadder goal: They take drugs to look better. The substance of choice for a growing number of teenage boys are steroids, peptides, and other exotic chemicals designed to enhance appearance.

Would-be muscle-men have been injecting themselves with black market ‘rhoids since the Eisenhower administration, but that was a small cult of adult weirdos with a specific goal. In 2026, kids are into it, and they aren’t using steroids to win a $500 prize in the Mr. Topeka contest; they’re using unapproved research chemicals to looksmaxx. Looksmaxxing is an online movement of young men trying to maximize their physical appearance. Teenagers are taking the normal desire to look their best to dangerous, pathological levels. Driven by a combination of undiagnosed body dysmorphia and relentless social media algorithms that turn amoral “red pill” kooks into gurus, teenage boys are ingesting a panoply of exotic and dangerous compounds in a quest to fix the angle of their jawlines, change their skin tone, lose weight, grow taller, and otherwise “correct” perceived physical problems.

In the "good old days" of steroid abuse, people generally stuck to abusing anabolic-androgenic steroids that had at least been tested for decades. Teens today are buying SARMs (Selective Androgen Receptor Modulators) and synthetic peptides marked "not for human consumption" from shady laboratories online. Steroids primarily affect the muscles, but many of these newer substances target different biological systems. A recent Rolling Stone article reports that kids are “heightmaxxing” by swallowing erdafitinib, a drug that treats advanced urothelial cancer, because the drug is known to trigger growth spurts (that can result in a curvature of the spine and other nasty side effects). They’re also trying MK-677 to get taller, an experimental growth hormone secretagogue that carries the risk of insulin resistance, water retention, and high blood pressure. Others are injecting Melanotan II, a synthetic peptide that forces a long-lasting deep tan, with side effects of extreme nausea and the sudden, aggressive darkening of moles. (And they're doing steroids too.).

In a recent development, in the looksmaxxing community, softmaxxing is doing generally-considered-acceptable things to look better, like getting enough sleep, exercising regularly, and eating a balanced diet. Hardmaxxing is taking more extreme measures like plastic surgery, smashing your face with a hammer, or taking experimental drugs.

In the bodybuilding and looksmaxxing community, “natty” refers to a natural, non-steroid-enhanced physique.

Here's something more lighthearted than the growing popularity of illicit self-esteem chemicals: the bicep heart and waist heart trends. The Bicep heart came first. Thirst trap videos started appearing on Instagram and TikTok in October in which dudes make a heart with their hand and bicep. Then people started posting variations where they frame the shot with someone they love inside the heart. The bicep heart rapidly led to women posting the waist heart.

Industry observers note that okay. So maybe it's not that lighthearted of a trend. While there are some videos of dudes with skinny arms doing the bicep heart, it's mostly jacked dudes. And the waist heart doesn't seem like it would work at all unless you are a specific shape, as this video illustrates. So maybe this isn't a silly meme but an illustration of how young people are inundated with content that can trigger feelings of physical unworthiness, even if they're just looking for silly memes.

As if searching for a job wasn't alienating and horrible enough, some companies have begun using AI agents to conduct interviews. Begging a robot to let you work in a cubicle farm is as dystopian as anything Phillip K. Dick ever imagined, but don't count humanity out yet. Young people are sticking a finger in the eye of the machine by creating comedy videos that focus on trolling these AI job interviewers. They're hilarious because AI is the ultimate straight person in a comedy team, and the raw compute costs to run these interviews means corporate money is burning with each second of wasted time. Here are some of the top creators in the genre.

Bo Bongo: This YouTuber reveals up to AI interviews shirtless but insists he's wearing a "corporate tube top," then focuses on daring the interviewer to notice he's doing things like smoking a cigarette or eating a rotisserie chicken.

Cam Whitt likes to wind up AI by arguing, interrupting, telling outrageous lies, and asking the dumbest questions imaginable, like, "When does the interview actually start?" and "How do I figure out what my name is?".

Grahamn Raabe: Among this YouTuber's schticks is speaking only in nonsense, like describing his professional background as "freight cadence, walnut, a little bit of Richard, spruce wood—six years of spruce wood.".

Sources indicate that nick Reid: Is so obnoxious, he seems to make the AI furious at him, even though it's a computer without emotions. Two thumbs up!

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Amazon is running early Black Friday deals on its Fire TV streaming devices, with the Fire TV Stick HD down to $15.99 and the Fire TV Cube at $89.99, $110 off its current list price. The discounts follow an August price increase across the Fire TV lineup. For more editor-vetted tech deals, check out the rest of our Black Friday coverage.

It has been revealed that the newest Fire TV Stick HD is $15.99, down from $39.99. This 2026 version of Amazon's entry-level stick is about 30% slimmer than before and able to run off a TV's USB port. It streams in 1080p with HDR10+ over Wi-Fi 6 and adds Alexa+ for more conversational voice search. That said, with the 4K Select costing $2 more and the latest Stick 4K $5 more, the HD makes the most sense for TVs that top out at 1080p. This PCMag review has more on its performance.

According to recent reports, fire TV Stick 4K Select is $17.99, down from $49.99, and brings 4K HDR10+ streaming and Alexa+ to Amazon's lowest-priced 4K stick. It introduced in October 2025 as the first Fire TV stick to run Vega OS, and it skips Dolby Vision, Dolby Atmos, and Wi-Fi 6, using Wi-Fi 5 instead.

Sources indicate that the latest Fire TV Stick 4K is down to $19.99 from $59.99 and is the version Amazon released in September with a quad-core processor, Wi-Fi 6, and Vega OS. According to Amazon, apps launch over 35% faster than on the previous model, while the ability to draw power directly from your TV's USB port makes setup a little easier. The redesigned remote also has buttons that are easier to identify by touch, and you get support for HDR10, HDR10+, and HLG content at up to 4K and 60fps. Check out PCMag's review for a closer look at its performance and features.

Recent findings suggest that the Fire TV Stick 4K Plus with AI-powered Fire TV search is $29.99, down from $69.99, and is built on the second-generation Fire TV Stick 4K hardware that PCMag reviewed in 2023, now paired with AI-powered search that finds titles by actor, plot, or a remembered quote. It supports Dolby Vision and Dolby Atmos, which the 4K Select lacks, and it runs Fire OS rather than Vega OS, so sideloading still works.

According to recent reports, fire TV Cube is $89.99, down from $199.99, the largest discount in this roundup and $30 below its 2022 launch price. It's Amazon's fastest streaming device, with an octa-core processor, Wi-Fi 6E, a built-in Ethernet port, and far-field microphones for hands-free Alexa. Its HDMI input and IR blaster also let it connect to and control a cable box. For more on its performance, check out this PCMag review.

Yes, Amazon has Black Friday sales, and we vet our deals to make sure they’re the best ones. You can also refer to guides like our live blog that have already done all of the vetting for you. And if you have an Amazon Prime membership, make the most of it.

According to recent reports, black Friday sales officially begin Friday, Nov. 27, 2026, and run throughout “Cyber Week,” the five-day period that runs from Thanksgiving through Cyber Monday,  Nov. 30, 2026. But Black Friday and Cyber Monday dates have expanded as retailers compete for customers. You can get the same Black Friday sales early, and we expect sales to wind down by Dec. 2, 2026.

Sources indicate that no. If you find the product you're looking for with a major discount right now, get it. It's not likely to drop any lower, but it could always run out of stock. Take advantage of price matching or guarantees instead of waiting. Remember, you can always return products later if you change your mind. For the majority of products, the deal from Black Friday will be the same one on Cyber Monday.
